What you need

Before you read a chapter, have these to hand.

  • A Root, the end module: it gives a unit its power and its sound, and your headphones plug into it.
  • One unit, flashed as the synth whose chapter you're reading. Every unit is the same box until you choose what it becomes, and you can change it as often as you like: flash it as Glass for chapter 3, then as Volt for chapter 4, and so on. The Quick Start guide in the box says how. Your sounds aren't lost when you do: they're kept kind by kind (most of them on the Root, section 1.8), so when you flash your unit back as Glass, your Glass sounds are there, just as you left them.
  • Headphones, or speakers, with an ordinary 3.5 mm plug, into the Root's PHONES socket. Use headphones if you can: a lot of what this book asks you to listen for is small.

That's everything the book needs: the starter pack, a Root and one unit, and a pair of headphones. Every synth in it makes its sounds on its own.

Optional

  • A MIDI keyboard: not essential, but a big help. Each unit's own keys are for trying sounds out: they play every note at the same strength, and they're two octaves wide. A MIDI keyboard plugged into the Root gives you more keys, pitch bend and mod wheels, a sustain pedal, and notes that get louder or brighter the harder you play, which several chapters ask you to try. Any keyboard with a MIDI OUT socket will do, however small (which cable, below).
  • A second unit, for effects. Chorus, echo and reverb come from Haze, a module of its own (chapter 2, section 2.5, and chapter 10). With one unit you can read about them and hear them in this book's examples; to put them on your own sounds, join Haze on beside your synth.
  • A microSD card in the Root, for keeping copies of your sounds and loading other people's (Glass's banks, chapter 3, section 3.13).
  • A computer, for updating the firmware, and for sending sounds to a unit from editing programs.
  • Step, the sequencer, which plays patterns on your synths, with accents and slides: the subject of the Music Production manual.

Which keyboard, and which cable

The Root's MIDI IN is a small 3.5 mm socket, like a headphone socket. Plenty of small keyboards have exactly that socket for their MIDI OUT, and a plain 3.5 mm stereo cable joins them. Bigger keyboards have the big round five-pin MIDI OUT socket instead, so you'll need an adapter: a "TRS MIDI Type A" one, which is the commonest kind.

A keyboard with only a USB socket

Look for a keyboard with a MIDI OUT socket. Most small ones get their power from their USB socket, and any phone charger or power bank will do for that: no computer needed.

A keyboard that only has USB can't plug straight into the Root: the Root's USB socket is for a computer (and for the power). Plug the keyboard into a computer, and the computer into the Root, and the computer passes the notes on. Or use a small "USB MIDI host" box, which turns a USB keyboard's notes into an ordinary MIDI OUT.

Before you start - why make your own sounds?

The sounds are half the music.

If you want to make music, whether that's techno, acid, film music, rock or anything else, the sounds you use matter as much as the notes you play. A tune on a piano and the same tune on a distorted bass synth aren't the same piece of music. Every unit in this range comes with factory sounds, and they're good: good enough to make whole tracks with, and good places to start. Everybody uses presets, and always has.

But presets only take you so far. One electric piano sound on one 1980s synthesiser turned up on so many hit records that you can still date a song by it. The music people remember, and keep coming back to, very often has a sound in it that nobody had heard before, because somebody went looking for it. Wendy Carlos made a bestseller of Bach in 1968 by building every sound from scratch on a big modular synthesiser. Kraftwerk spent years shaping the sounds that made them Kraftwerk. Vangelis's music for Blade Runner is as much the sound of one synthesiser, played and shaped by him, as it is the notes.

That's what this book is for. Not to make you a scientist, but to give you the handful of ideas every synthesiser is built from, so that when a sound is nearly right you know which control to reach for, and when you stumble on something wonderful you know how to find it again.

The best sounds were mistakes

Here's something worth knowing before you start: a lot of the most famous sounds in music were never meant to happen.

In 1980 Roland brought out the TR-808 drum machine. It was meant to sound like a real drummer, for musicians to practise and make demos with, and it didn't: its kick drum was a long electronic boom, its handclap was a burst of hiss, its cowbell sounded like nothing on earth. It sold badly, and Roland stopped making it after about three years. Then, second-hand and cheap, it fell into the hands of people who didn't care that it sounded wrong. They loved how it sounded. Marvin Gaye's "Sexual Healing" and Afrika Bambaataa's "Planet Rock", both in 1982, were built on it, and its boom has been under hip hop ever since.

Roland's TB-303 Bass Line, a little box meant to play bass lines for guitarists practising on their own, failed the same way and was gone by 1984. A few years later, in Chicago, a group called Phuture turned its knobs while it played, and "Acid Tracks" (1987) began acid house. Distorted guitar went the same way: in 1964 the Kinks' Dave Davies slashed a speaker cone with a razor blade to get the fuzzy sound on "You Really Got Me", and a fault became the sound of rock.

None of those people were following instructions. They were playing, and they kept what they liked. So use this book to learn the ideas, then go and break them. Turn things too far. Use controls for the "wrong" job. The only measure of success is whether you've found a sound you like.

How to use this book

Chapter 1 is how every unit works, and chapter 2 is what's in a sound, whatever makes it. Then there's a chapter for each synth, and each one stands on its own: if you've got one unit, read chapters 1 and 2 and then its chapter. Each unit chapter starts with a little history of its way of making sounds, who uses it and what for, and the famous instruments that made it. A Tessel unit isn't any of those instruments, but what it teaches will serve you well on all of them.

Instrument names in this book (such as TR-808 and TB-303, which belong to Roland Corporation, and DX7, which belongs to Yamaha Corporation) are trademarks of their owners. They're mentioned for their history. Tessel isn't connected with any of these companies or endorsed by them.

Chapter 1 - Getting around

Everything that's the same on every unit. Learn it once.

Every Tessel synth is the same box. The screen is in the same place, the four encoders are in the same place, the keys run down the same side, and the buttons that matter most, SOUNDS and SETUP, sit in the same spots. What changes from one unit to the next is what the buttons are called and what they do. So this chapter is about the box, and every chapter after it is about one thing you can turn the box into.

If you've just built your first unit and flashed it, you already know where the headphones go and how to turn it up. That's all you need. Have it in front of you as you read: everything here is quicker to learn by doing than by reading.

1.1 How this book tells you what to press

Most of this book is instructions of the "press this, then turn that" kind, and writing them out in full sentences gets tiring for everybody very quickly. So instead they're written as a little strip of coloured shapes, in the order you do them. Here's one:

VCF›2RES›5.0

That reads: press the button marked VCF, then turn encoder 2 (the box on the screen it changes is called RES) until it says 5.0. Every route in the book is built from the same few pieces:

VCFA button: press it. White with a small dark square, like a button on the panel's white strip.
VECTORVECTOR ENVA button with a page name on it: press the button until the bar along the top of the screen says that name. Some buttons have two pages, and pressing again flips between them, so you might need one press or two. The name in the pill is the name you'll see at the top of the screen.
CHORUSagainPress a button again to switch something on or off rather than to change page.
holdOCT+Hold a button down.
2RESAn encoder, by its number, and the name of the box on the screen it changes: turn it.
push1Push an encoder, like a button, and let go.
hold4Hold an encoder pushed in until the bar on the screen fills up.
5.0The value to set, written exactly as the screen shows it.
C3A key, by its note.

Apart from the routes, there are three kinds of box, and they always mean the same thing.

Try this

Something to do with your hands. These are the most important part of the book, and they're short.

Watch out

A trap, or something that surprises nearly everybody the first time.

Keep

Something worth remembering after you've closed the book.

1.2 A tour of the box

Everything on the panel is numbered in the picture.

  • 1The screen, at the top right. It shows one page at a time, and every page is laid out the same way, which section 1.5 is about.
  • 2The four encoders, two above the screen and two below. They turn forever in either direction, with no end stop, and they push in like buttons as well.
  • 3The function buttons, the grid of buttons under the screen, three across and six down. Each one takes you to a page: on Ember they're called things like LFO, DCO and VCF, on Glass OP1 to OP6, and so on.
  • 4The keys, down the left-hand side: white keys along the edge, black keys beside them.
  • 5OCT- and OCT+, the two small buttons above the keys. They move the keys down or up; section 1.4 has the details.

Two of the function buttons are the same on every unit, and they're always in the same place:

  • 6SOUNDS, in the middle of the bottom row, where you choose a sound and keep your own (section 1.8).
  • 7SETUP, at the bottom right, for the settings that aren't part of any sound (section 1.9).

Where's the Root?

The pictures in this book show a unit on its own, to keep things clear, but a unit on its own does nothing at all: it has no battery, no socket and no speaker. It needs the Root, the end module, joined onto its left-hand side, the side with the keys. The Root gives it power and sound, and that's where your headphones plug in.

Your buttons, your labels

If your unit has the plain top panel, the words under the buttons are the ones you wrote on the white strip when you built it. This book uses the names each button has in the firmware, the same ones that appear in the top bar of the screen, so if the book says VCF and your strip says something else, the screen will settle it.

1.3 Two ways to hold it

Upright, the way the pictures in this book show it, is for setting a sound up: the screen's at the top and the encoders fall nicely under your fingers.

Turned a quarter of the way round to the left, it becomes a little piano: the lowest note on the left, the white keys nearest you. That's for playing a sound to hear what it's like. The screen doesn't turn round with it, so it'll be on its side, but you won't be reading it much while you play.

When you turn the unit round to play it, the Root comes round too, and lies along the front, between you and the keys. That's why the turned picture shows it: it's the one time you need to know where it'll be.

Once you've got a few units joined together, you'll mostly be playing them from a MIDI keyboard or from Step, the sequencer, and the keys on each unit are just for trying a sound out. That's what they're for.

1.4 The keys

There are twenty-seven keys: two octaves and a little bit, from C3 at the top (when the unit's upright) to D5 at the bottom. Middle C, C4, is the eighth white key down, just above halfway. They aren't touch-sensitive, so every note plays at the same loudness however hard you press. A MIDI keyboard plugged into the Root fixes that, and section 1.10 says how.

OCT- and OCT+ move the keys down or up:

  • ·Tap one to move the keys an octave, up to three octaves either way. While the keys are moved, the light beside that button is on, so you can always see that you've moved them.
  • ·Hold one, and the KEYBOARD page appears for as long as you hold it: encoder 1 moves the keys by octaves, encoder 2 by single semitones, and the screen shows the lowest and highest notes the keys now play.
  • ·Press both together and the keys go back to where they started.

Moving the keys only changes what your fingers play. It isn't part of the sound, and it doesn't change notes coming from a MIDI keyboard. Strike, the drum unit, has no OCT buttons at all, because its keys are drums rather than notes.

1.5 Pages, and the four corners of the screen

Each function button has its own page. Press VCF on Ember and the VCF page comes up, with the filter's settings on it. Press ENV and you're on the envelope page instead. There's no menu to dig through, and nothing to scroll: one button, one page.

A few buttons have a second page, which you get to by pressing the same button again. Press it once more and you're back on the first. You'll meet these as they come up, and they're always written as a route with the page's name in it, like VECTORVECTOR ENV. Press until the top bar says VECTOR ENV.

Now the most useful thing in this whole chapter. Every page has up to four boxes, one in each corner of the screen, and each box belongs to an encoder. The encoders sit in the same pattern as the boxes: two above the screen, two below.

  • 1Encoder 1, top left, changes the top-left box.
  • 2Encoder 2, top right, changes the top-right box.
  • 3Encoder 3, bottom left, changes the bottom-left box.
  • 4Encoder 4, bottom right, changes the bottom-right box.

That's it. You never have to remember which encoder does what: look at the screen, find the box you want, and turn the encoder in that corner. When you turn one, the name in its box changes colour, so you can see which one you touched last.

Try this

Press any function button. Look at the four boxes, then turn each encoder in turn, a few clicks one way and back again, and watch which box changes. Do it on two or three different pages. After about a minute you'll stop thinking about it, which is the point.

Encoders do three things:

  • ·Turn. Slowly, and each click moves the value by one step. Quickly, and it moves several steps a click, so you can cross a big range in one sweep and then slow down for the last bit.
  • ·Push. On some boxes, pushing the encoder in does a second job: switching something on and off, or moving to the next letter of a name. The book says when.
  • ·Hold. Anything that can't be undone, such as copying over one of your sounds or resetting the unit, needs the encoder held in. A bar appears along the bottom of the screen and fills up, and only when it's full does the thing happen.

Changed your mind?

Let go before the bar is full and nothing happens at all. That's what the bar is for.

1.6 The top bar

Along the top of every page there's a dark strip with two things in it.

On the left, the name of the page. It's the same name the button has, and it's the name in the route pills. If you're ever not sure where you are, look here.

On the right, where the sound you're playing lives, as a short code: FA01, UB07. The first letter is F for one of the factory sounds or U for one of your own; the second letter is which bank (A, B, C...); the number is which sound in that bank. FA01 is the first factory sound, UB07 is the seventh of your own in your second bank.

A small padlock next to the code means it's a factory sound: you can change it while you play, but nothing you do is ever kept in it. A small star in the padlock's place means the sound has changes that aren't kept anywhere yet. Section 1.8 explains both.

1.7 The lights

Every key and every button has a small red light beside it, and the lights are always telling you something.

  • ·Bright beside a function button: that's the page you're on. Beside a key: that note is playing. Beside OCT- or OCT+: the keys are moved that way.
  • ·Dim and blinking mean different things on different units: on Glass, a dim light means a part of the sound has been switched off, and a blinking one means you're editing a part that's switched off. Each unit's chapter says what they mean there.
  • ·Off: nothing to say.

When you first turn a unit on, the screen shows its name and the firmware version for a moment. Press anything, or turn anything, and it goes away at once.

If the Root carries newer firmware for the unit than the unit has, the next screen says NEW FIRMWARE, with the old and new version numbers. Hold encoder 4 until the bar fills to update it: your sounds are kept. Or press or turn anything else to carry on as you were; it will ask again the next time the unit is turned on.

1.8 Sounds: the factory's and your own

Every unit comes with its own collection of sounds, made at the factory, and room for plenty of your own. They live in banks of up to 32 sounds each: one or more factory banks (FAC A, FAC B...) and four banks of your own (USER A to USER D). The SOUNDS button is where you choose between them.

On the SOUNDS page:

  • 1BANK, encoder 1: which bank.
  • 2SOUND, encoder 2: which sound in it. The sound changes the moment you turn it, so you can play a few notes, turn, play again.
  • 3COPY TO, encoder 3: turn it to choose one of your own slots, then hold it in to copy the sound you're playing into that slot.
  • 4NAME, encoder 4: on one of your own sounds, turn it to change a letter of the name, and push it to move on to the next letter.

Try this

SOUNDS›2SOUND and go through the first factory bank, playing a few notes on each sound. Don't be careful about it. Find two or three you like and remember their codes from the top bar. We'll be coming back to them.

Changing a factory sound

Turn something on a factory sound and you'll hear it change. Go ahead: that's the quickest way to find out what a knob does. But the factory sound itself never changes. The padlock in the top bar turns into a small star, which means "changed, but not kept anywhere". That's deliberate: the factory sounds are the book's examples, and they're also what you can always go back to, exactly as they came.

So the undo is simple: choose the sound again on the SOUNDS page (turn SOUND away and back), and it's as it came. Your changes also go when you choose any other sound, so the first time you turn away from a changed sound the screen says EDITS NOT KEPT and stays where it is: copy it if you want to keep it, or turn again to move on. They do survive turning the unit off, so you can unsnap it and carry on later.

To keep what you've done, copy it into one of your own slots:

SOUNDS›3COPY TO›UA01›hold3

The copy takes your changes with it. The unit switches to the copy, the star disappears from the top bar, and the code changes to UA01. From now on, every change you make to it is kept.

The habit

Like what you've done to a factory sound? Copy it before you choose another one. And before you change one of your own sounds that you care about, copy it to a spare slot first: there's no undo button on your own sounds, so the copy is the undo.

Where your sounds are kept

Your own sounds aren't kept in the unit alone: they're kept on the Root, which every unit of the same kind shares. Two Glass units joined to one Root have the same banks of your sounds, and a change on one shows on the other straight away. Every kind of unit works this way, Taste and Grit with their samples too.

Join a unit to a different Root, a friend's or a new one, and if its sounds aren't the same as the ones that Root keeps, the unit asks before anything happens. Turn encoder 1 to choose one of three: ROOT OVERWRITES GLASS (the unit takes the Root's sounds), GLASS OVERWRITES ROOT (yours replace the Root's) or DON'T OVERWRITE (both stay as they are, and the unit uses its own until it's next turned on). Then hold encoder 4 for three seconds. Nothing is ever mixed together, and a brand-new Root, with nothing on it, simply takes your units' sounds without asking.

Every one of your own slots starts as a plain, simple sound called INIT SOUND (on Glass it's INIT VOICE, on Strike INIT KIT, on Haze INIT FX). It's the blank page you build a sound from scratch on.

It saves itself

There's no SAVE button. A unit saves your sounds, and which page and sound you were on, a moment after you change anything. You can unplug it whenever you like, even halfway through turning a knob, and when you plug it back in it'll be exactly where you left it.

1.9 SETUP

SETUP, at the bottom right, is where the settings that aren't part of any sound live. It has two parts, and pressing SETUP again (or pushing any encoder) moves on through their pages.

THIS UNIT comes first: the settings that belong to this one unit. Encoder 1 is always the unit's MIDI channel (section 1.10), and the others are that unit's own settings, such as how far pitch bend goes, or (VELO) whether notes from a MIDI keyboard play louder when you hit them harder. Each unit's chapter lists its own. A unit with more settings than fit has a second THIS UNIT page; the top bar shows which page you're on as a small number.

The last THIS UNIT page is RESET, which puts things back the way they left the factory, and looks after the unit itself. Encoder 1 chooses what to do:

  • ·SETTINGS puts back SETUP's settings, the MIDI channel and the keys' octave, and keeps your sounds.
  • ·EVERYTHING does that and wipes your sounds as well, so every one of your slots goes back to INIT SOUND. Your sounds are kept on the Root (section 1.8), so this wipes them for every unit of that kind on the Root, as the screen warns.
  • ·REFLASH turns the unit into another kind of unit: encoder 3, in the bottom-left box that shows what the unit is now, chooses which, from the ones the Root carries. This kind's sounds stay in the unit, for when you flash it back.
  • ·Another type's name, such as TASTE, if the unit has been flashed as that type before: each type keeps its own sounds in the unit (see "What you need"), and this clears that type's, leaving the rest alone. The screen says how much room they take.
  • ·EVERY TYPE wipes every type's sounds and settings: for when you pass a unit on to someone else.
  • ·TOTAL RESET wipes everything: every kind's sounds and settings, and its MIDI channel. The unit becomes a blank unit, as it came out of the box, ready to be flashed as anything.
  • ·TEST checks the unit is working: every unit carries the same test it was given in the factory. The unit restarts into the test, which shows the screen in five plain colours, plays a short note through the Root's headphones, then draws a picture of the panel. Press every button and turn every encoder both ways (the picture shows how many clicks are left) and push it, until nothing is left. At the end it says PASS or FAIL, and encoder 4 brings the unit back exactly as you left it: nothing is lost. If you ever need help with a unit, this is the first thing to try, and encoder 1 on the results shows a QR code that tells us what we need.

Then hold encoder 4 for three seconds. The firmware version is on this page too, in the bottom-left box.

EVERYTHING means everything

There's no getting your sounds back after a reset to EVERYTHING, unless you've made a BACKUP to the Root's memory card first (ROOT, encoder 4, below). If you've got a card, do that first.

ROOT comes after THIS UNIT, and it's the settings of the Root, the end module, which has no screen or buttons of its own: which input it listens to (LINE, MIC, or its own BUILT-IN microphone) and how loud (GAIN), what its MIDI output sends, and jobs for its memory card. Every unit's SETUP can reach them, and they're the same whichever unit you use. A second ROOT page, ROOT2, decides how MIDI from outside reaches the units, which is the next section.

  • ·MIDI OUT sends what's playing to a computer or another synth: NOTES (Step's notes, each on the channel of the unit it plays), CLOCK (Step's tempo, with start and stop), BOTH, THRU (a copy of what comes in at MIDI IN), or ALL of them.
  • ·CARD: hold encoder 4 to run a job on the Root's memory card. BACKUP copies every unit on the chain, every type each one has been, and the Root's own settings, into a new folder, BACKUP-1, BACKUP-2 and so on, never over an old one. RESTORE puts the newest backup back into the units that are on the chain, and says if any from the backup weren't there; each unit then starts up again with its things back. FORMAT empties the card. A big backup takes a while: the screen shows how far it's got.
  • ·INPUT chooses which of the Root's inputs units record from: LINE (the LINE/MIC socket, at line level), MIC (the same socket, with more gain and power for a plug-in microphone) or BUILT-IN (the little microphone in the Root's top). GAIN sets how loud it comes in. Both are also on Taste's and Grit's recording pages, where you need them.

ROOT2 also has SOUNDS, for a Root that already has sounds on it, such as a second-hand one. Encoder 3 chooses UNITS' (each kind's sounds come from the leftmost unit of that kind on the chain, replacing the Root's) or ROOT'S (every unit takes the Root's); hold encoder 4 for three seconds. It settles every kind at once, without the question each unit would otherwise ask.

1.10 Playing from a MIDI keyboard

Plug a MIDI keyboard into the Root's MIDI IN socket ("What you need", at the start of the book, says which keyboards and which cable) and you can play any unit from it: with the pitch bend and mod wheels, a sustain pedal, and notes that can get louder the harder you play: most units have a VELO setting for that on SETUP, and on Glass each sound decides for itself.

Each unit has a name made of what it is and a number, such as EMBER 2 or GLASS 1. The number is its MIDI channel, and that's how a keyboard or a computer picks which unit it's talking to. Units are given a channel automatically, each its own, so you don't need to do anything; but you can choose one yourself on THIS UNIT, encoder 1, and a channel you've chosen is never changed.

On ROOT2, MIDI IN decides how the Root passes notes on: CHANNELS, where each unit plays only the notes on its own channel (the usual way, with a computer), or FOLLOW, where the Root sends your keyboard's notes to whichever unit you last touched. FOLLOW is the easy way to play several units from one keyboard: turn a knob on the unit you want and play.

1.11 When something seems wrong

  • ·There's a star in the top bar. The sound has changes that aren't kept anywhere. Copy it to one of your own slots to keep them, or choose the sound again on the SOUNDS page to throw them away (section 1.8).
  • ·The screen says COPY IT TO RECORD or COPY IT TO LOAD. On Taste and Grit, a new sample has to belong to one of your own sounds, so copy the factory sound to one of your slots first (section 1.8).
  • ·There's no sound. Check the volume on the Root, and that the unit is joined on properly (its screen will be lit). On a few units, some sounds play what another unit is playing and make no noise by themselves; their chapters say so.
  • ·The keys play the wrong notes. Look at OCT- and OCT+: if one is lit, the keys are moved. Press both together to put them back.
  • ·You're lost. Look at the top bar. It always says which page you're on.
  • ·The screen says FLASH FULL. The unit's memory is full, almost always of samples (Taste's or Grit's) or songs, perhaps from when it was another type. Nothing is ever thrown away to make room: save what you want to keep to the card, then clear what you don't need on SETUP's RESET page, which lists what's using the space.
  • ·The screen says CARD NEEDED. The Root keeps about 40 seconds of your own samples, Taste's and Grit's together, and that's full. Put a memory card in the Root and there's room for as many as the card holds; or delete samples you no longer use (Taste's and Grit's SAMPLES pages).
  • ·The screen says LOADING. On Taste and Grit: the sound you've chosen uses a sample this unit hasn't got yet, and it's being fetched from the Root (or its card). It takes a few seconds, more for a long sample; until it's here, the notes that need it are silent.
  • ·You've made a mess of a sound. On a factory sound, choose it again on the SOUNDS page. On one of your own, copy the factory sound you started from again (section 1.8). That's what they're for.

That's chapter one, and it's the same on every unit, so you'll only ever need to learn it once: whichever unit you pick up next, it works the same way. Next, a short chapter about what a sound is actually made of, and then one chapter for each unit, each starting from a sound you like and ending with one you've made yourself.

Chapter 2 - What's in a sound

Six things your ears are listening for, all the time, without being asked.

Before any of the units, a chapter about sound itself. It's short, it's mostly listening, and everything in the rest of the book leans on it.

Here's the idea. When you hear a note, your ears are quietly answering six questions about it. How high is it? What colour is it: bright and buzzy, or dark and soft? How does it change, from the moment it starts to the moment it's gone? Does anything in it move while it lasts? Is it close and dry, or swirling, echoing, far off in a big room? And how loud is it?

Every synth in the range is a machine for changing the answers. They go about it in very different ways, which is what the unit chapters are for, but the questions are always the same six. Learn to hear them here and you'll know what you're reaching for on any unit.

Try this

Every sound in this chapter has a player beside it. Use headphones if you can: some of the differences are small, and a phone speaker or a laptop will hide them. Under each one, Make it on your unit says how to make the same thing on the unit in front of you, which is the better way to learn it.

Try this

Every idea in this chapter comes with a sound to try, Sound 2.1, Sound 2.2 and so on, and each one says how to make it on the unit in front of you. Do them as you read: some of the differences are small, so use headphones if you can.

2.1 Pitch

Pitch is how high or low a note is, and it's the one you already know best. Every key plays a different pitch, and that's most of what a tune is.

Sound 2.1  The same note, C, four times, an octave higher each time.

Make it on your unit

Any unit: play C3, then C4 and C5 (the white keys with a gap of seven between them), then press OCT+ and play C5 again.

Those four notes are all called C, and they sound like the same note, only higher each time. That's an octave, and it's the oddest fact in music: count twelve steps up from any key, black and white keys together, and you arrive back at the same note, one floor up. Underneath, the sound is vibrating exactly twice as fast. Each octave doubles it again.

Sound 2.2  Five notes, each a semitone above the last: the smallest step on the keyboard.

Make it on your unit

Any unit: play C4 and the next four keys up, black and white, one at a time.

Strike: in your own kit, EDIT, play LO TOM, and turn 2TUNE a step at a time (section 5.5).

Taste: on MY KEYS (section 8.8), play up and down: one note on every key. A kit key's pitch is TUNE›1COARSE (section 8.5).

Grit: PITCH›1PITCH moves every grain by semitones, without changing the speed (section 9.6).

The smallest step on the keyboard, from one key to the very next, black or white, is a semitone. Twelve of them make an octave.

Almost every unit can move its whole sound up or down without you changing the keys you press, in octaves and in semitones, and many of them can do it in much smaller steps too. Two sounds a hair apart in pitch, played together, rub against each other and make a slow wobble. That's not a mistake: it's one of the oldest ways of making a sound bigger and warmer, and you'll meet it as detune.

Find it on your unit: Glass, section 3.8 · Volt, section 4.4 · Strike, section 5.5 · Ember, section 6.4 · Taste, section 8.5 · Grit, section 9.6

2.2 Tone

Play the same note on a flute and on a trumpet. Same pitch, same loudness, and you'd still never mix them up. What's different is the tone, or the colour of the sound, and it's the thing synths are best at changing.

A note isn't one pitch. It's the pitch you hear, plus a stack of quieter ones above it, called harmonics, that your ear doesn't hear separately but blends into a colour. Few harmonics, and the sound is soft and pure. Lots of them, especially high ones, and it's bright and buzzy.

Sound 2.3  The four basic waves at the same pitch and loudness: sine, triangle, sawtooth, square. Then noise, which has no pitch at all.

Make it on your unit

Glass: INIT VOICE (UA01, section 3.2) is the sine. For something near the sawtooth: VOICE›1ALGO›32, OP1 LEVEL 0, OP6 LEVEL 99, 2FEEDBK›6 (section 3.7).

Volt: on ONE OSC (section 4.3), step OSC 1›3WAVE through TRIANGLE, SAWTOOTH and SQUARE (Volt has no sine: TRIANGLE is the nearest). For noise, switch OSC 1 off and NOISE on with MIXER›push1 and push4 (section 4.5).

Strike: the hats, cymbals and maracas are noise and metallic clang, with no pitch at all; the kick is close to a sine (section 5.2).

Ember: on SAW 1 (section 6.3), WAVES: SAW on its own, PULSE on its own, then SUB alone for a square; NOISE for the hiss (section 6.4). Ember has no sine.

Axis: on CORNERS (section 7.2), each corner is one wave: move the point with VECTOR›3X and 4Y from the sine to the square and on (section 7.3). Waves 0-15 are the plain shapes.

Taste: a sampler plays recordings, not waves: any of the starter set's samples (section 8.4). Its RAIN is close to noise.

Grit: grains are made from samples too; very short ones, GRAIN›1SIZE under 10 MS, turn any sound into a buzz (section 9.4).

Those are the basic shapes most synths start from, all at the same pitch and loudness. The sine is the pure one: no harmonics at all, just the note. The triangle has a few, faintly. The sawtooth has every harmonic there is, and it's the brightest and buzziest, which is why it's the one you'll start from most. The square has every other harmonic, which gives it that hollow, woody sound. The last one is noise: every pitch at once, so no pitch at all. It's the hiss of wind, waves, cymbals and breath.

The filter

Most synths then hand the sound to a filter, which takes harmonics away. Close it a little and the top of the sound goes; close it further and the sound turns dark and muffled, like hearing music through a wall.

Sound 2.4  One sawtooth, four times, with the filter closing a little more each time.

Make it on your unit

Glass: it has no filter, and takes harmonics away by turning a modulator down. On SINE 1 set OP2›OUTPUT›1LEVEL›80, hold a note and turn LEVEL slowly down to 0 (section 3.6).

Volt: on ONE OSC, hold a low note and turn FILTER›1CUTOFF down from +5.0 (section 4.6).

Ember: on SAW 1, hold a chord and turn VCF›1FREQ down from 10 (section 6.5).

Axis: turn FILTER›1CUTOFF down from the top (section 7.5).

Taste: FILTER›1CUTOFF down from 10, on any key (section 8.8).

Grit: FILTER›1CUTOFF down from 10 with TYPE on LOW (section 9.8).

The filter has a second control, usually called resonance. It makes the filter ring at the point where it's cutting, so the harmonics right there stand out. A little gives the sound an edge. A lot makes it whistle.

Sound 2.5  A filter part closed, with no resonance, then some, then a lot: listen for the whistle.

Make it on your unit

Glass: it has no filter, so no resonance. Its nearest thing is a modulator at a high COARSE, which picks out a high harmonic (section 3.6).

Volt: on ONE OSC with CUTOFF at about 0, turn FILTER›2EMPHASIS up: from about 7 it whistles (section 4.6). In ACID, RESONANCE (section 4.12).

Ember: on SAW 1 with FREQ at about 4, turn VCF›2RES up (section 6.5).

Axis: with CUTOFF part way down, turn FILTER›2RES up (section 7.5).

Taste: FILTER›2RES up, with CUTOFF part way down (section 8.8).

Grit: FILTER›2RES up; TYPE on BAND rings like a tuned pipe (section 9.8).

Bright and dark

When people talk about a sound being bright, dark, buzzy, soft, hollow or thin, they're talking about harmonics: how many there are, and which. A filter is the commonest way of changing them, but it isn't the only one. Glass has no filter at all, and makes its harmonics a completely different way (its chapter explains how).

Find it on your unit: Glass, section 3.6 · Volt, section 4.6 · Strike, section 5.2 · Ember, section 6.5 · Axis, section 7.4 · Taste, section 8.10 · Grit, section 9.4

2.3 The shape of a note

Strike a piano key and the note is loudest straight away and then dies away, however long you keep your finger down. Draw a bow across a violin and the note creeps up from nothing. Play an organ and the note stays exactly as loud as long as you hold it, and stops the moment you let go. Hit a bell and it goes on ringing for ten seconds whatever you do.

That difference, how loud a note is at each moment between the key going down and silence coming back, is called the envelope, and it does more to tell your ear what kind of instrument it's hearing than almost anything else.

Sound 2.6  One note, four shapes: an organ, something like a piano, something like a bowed string, a pluck.

Make it on your unit

Glass: the four recipes in section 3.5: ORGAN, PLUCK, BELL and SWELL, on OP1 of SINE 1.

Volt: the four shapes on the LOUDNESS page in section 4.7.

Strike: drums are nearly all attack and decay: in your own kit, EDIT, play KICK, and turn 3DECAY (section 5.6).

Ember: the four shapes on the ENV page in section 6.6.

Axis: the AMP ENV's five points: times and levels (section 7.6).

Taste: ENV's ATTACK, DECAY, SUSTAIN and RELEASE, on top of the sample's own shape (section 8.8).

Grit: ENV's four, for each note's cloud (section 9.8).

Most synths draw the envelope with four controls, and you'll meet these four names on nearly every unit:

  • AAttack: how long the note takes to get going. Short for a piano or a drum; long for strings creeping in.
  • DDecay: how long it takes to fall back from the top.
  • SSustain: the level it holds while your finger stays down. It's a level, not a time, because you choose the time, with your finger. All the way up is an organ; all the way down, and the note dies away whether you hold the key or not, like a piano.
  • RRelease: how long it takes to die away once you let go.

Sound 2.7  A short tap, twice: first with no release, then with a long one.

Make it on your unit

Glass: on SINE 1, OP1›RATES›4R4›40 and play short notes; then put R4 back to 99 (section 3.5).

Volt: the DECAY switch, CONTROL›3DECAY: ON, notes die away after you let go; OFF, they stop (section 4.7).

Ember: on SAW 1, ENV›4R up to 6 and play short notes (section 6.6).

Axis: on AMP ENV, point 4's TIME: how long it takes to die away after you let go (section 7.6).

Taste: on MY KEYS, ENV›4RELEASE (section 8.8).

Grit: ENV›4RELEASE (section 9.8).

Letting go early

Letting go of a key doesn't wait for anything. Whatever the note was doing at that moment, even if it was still creeping up, it heads straight for silence at the release speed. So a sound with a slow attack never reaches full loudness if you play it in short stabs. That isn't a fault: slow sounds want long, held notes.

Brightness over time

Here's the bit that makes synths sound alive. The envelope doesn't have to change only the loudness: it can open and close the filter too. A real plucked string is brightest the instant it's plucked and gets darker as it rings, and a filter that opens at the start of each note and closes again does the same.

Sound 2.8  A dark note, then the same note with the filter opened at the start of each note and closing again: bright, then darker, like a plucked string.

Make it on your unit

Glass: build E PIANO 1 (section 3.6): OP2's envelope dies away sooner than OP1's, so the brightness goes first.

Volt: PLUCK BASS in section 4.7: the filter contour opens the filter on every note and closes it again.

Ember: STAB in section 6.6: the envelope opens the filter on each note and closes it again.

Axis: FILTER's ENV up, and the FILTER ENV's points shape it (sections 7.5 and 7.6).

Taste: FILTER›3ENV above 0: each note starts brighter (MY KEYS, section 8.8).

Find it on your unit: Glass, section 3.5 · Volt, section 4.7 · Strike, section 5.6 · Ember, section 6.6 · Axis, section 7.6 · Taste, section 8.8 · Grit, section 9.8

2.4 Movement

Everything so far does the same thing on every note: press a key, the shape runs, and if you hold the note it sits there being exactly what it is. Real instruments don't. A held violin note shivers. A singer's long note starts straight and then starts to move.

The usual way to put movement into a sound is an LFO, a low frequency oscillator. It's an oscillator like the ones that make the sound, except it runs so slowly you can't hear it as a pitch: a few wobbles a second rather than a few hundred. Because you can't hear it, it isn't used to make sound. It's used to move something else.

Point it at the pitch and you get vibrato. Many LFOs can wait a moment before they start, the way a singer holds a long note steady and only then lets it go.

Sound 2.9  A held note: plain, with vibrato, and with vibrato that waits a moment before it starts.

Make it on your unit

Glass: MOD›1VIBRATO›20, then LFO›2DELAY›40 for the late start (section 3.9).

Volt: oscillator 3 as a slow modulator, with OSC MOD on (section 4.8). Volt has no delayed vibrato.

Ember: DCO›2LFO with the LFO's DELAY up, for the late start (section 6.7).

Axis: MOD slot: LFO 1 to PITCH, with LFO 1's DELAY up (section 7.7).

Taste: LFO›2PITCH, as on VOX PAD (section 8.8).

Grit: a gentle vibrato is PITCH›3RANDOM at a few cents instead: every grain slightly out of tune (section 9.6).

Point it at the filter and the tone goes round and round: brighter, darker, brighter.

Sound 2.10  A filter slowly opening and closing on its own, over and over.

Make it on your unit

Glass: on SINE 1 with OP2 LEVEL 70: OP2›OUTPUT›3AMP MOD›3 and MOD›3TREMOLO›60. The brightness wobbles, the way a filter's would (section 3.9).

Volt: oscillator 3 as a slow modulator, with FILT MOD on (section 4.8).

Ember: VCF MOD›3LFO with RES up a little (section 6.7).

Axis: MOD slot: LFO 1 to CUTOFF (section 7.7).

Taste: LFO›3FILTER (section 8.8).

Grit: LFO›4FILTER, as on MIST MOVING (section 9.8).

Find it on your unit: Glass, section 3.9 · Volt, section 4.8 · Strike, section 5.8 · Ember, section 6.7 · Axis, section 7.7 · Grit, section 9.5

2.5 Effects

Everything so far happens inside the note. Effects happen to the sound after it's made: they take what comes out and do something to all of it, every note at once. A guitarist's pedals are effects, and so is the sound of the room a band plays in.

There are dozens of them, but four do most of the work, and you'll hear them on nearly every record.

Chorus copies the sound, wobbles the copy's pitch very slightly and mixes the two together, the way a choir is never quite in tune with itself. It makes a sound wider and warmer, and it's half the secret of many famous synth sounds.

Sound 2.11  A chord, plain and then with chorus.

Make it on your unit

If you have Haze as well: press its ninth white key, CHORUS, and play: the key sends every synth in. To make your own, MY CHORUS (chapter 10, section 10.9). With one unit on its own, just listen for now (section 2.5).

Ember: press CHORUS I: Ember has a chorus of its own (section 6.8).

Axis: press CHORUS, then again to switch it on (section 7.9).

A phaser is a close cousin: it mixes the sound with a copy that's been shifted slightly, so some harmonics cancel out, and then sweeps where the cancelling happens. You hear it as a slow whoosh, like a jet going over.

Sound 2.12  A chord, plain and then through a phaser: the sweeping, whooshing one.

Make it on your unit

If you have Haze as well: its eleventh white key, PHASER, and hold a chord; MOD's MODE PHASER (chapter 10, section 10.9).

Echo plays the sound back a moment later, then again, quieter each time, like shouting across a valley. Short echoes thicken a sound; long ones make rhythms of their own.

Sound 2.13  A short note, plain and then with echo: the note comes back, quieter each time.

Make it on your unit

If you have Haze as well: its fifth white key, TAPE ECHO, and play short notes; MY ECHO (chapter 10, section 10.8).

Reverb is the room: the thousands of tiny echoes off the walls, floor and ceiling that blur together into a tail. A little puts the sound in a room; a lot puts it in a cathedral.

Sound 2.14  A short chord, plain and then with reverb: the same chord in a big room.

Make it on your unit

If you have Haze as well: its second white key, BIG HALL, and play short notes; MY PLATE and MY HALL (chapter 10, section 10.7).

With one unit, these four have to wait

If you've got one unit, the one in the starter pack, you can't make most of these four sounds yourself yet: in this range, effects come from a second module, Haze. (Ember and Axis each have a chorus of their own: sections 6.8 and 7.9.) That's fine. Listen to them here so you know what they are, and Read what each one does, and when you hear them on a record you'll know what's being done: they're on nearly all of them. Every other sound in this chapter you can make on the unit you've got.

In this range, effects are mostly Haze's job (chapter 10). Join it on and its echo, reverb and chorus are shared by every synth on the chain, each sending in as much as you like. A few units have an effect of their own built in, such as the chorus on Ember and Axis, because it's part of how those sounds were always made.

Find it on your unit: Glass, section 3.11 · Volt, section 4.13 · Strike, section 5.10 · Ember, section 6.8 · Axis, section 7.9 · Taste, section 8.13 · Haze, section 10.7 · Haze, section 10.8 · Haze, section 10.9 · Haze, section 10.11 · Haze, section 10.12 · Haze, section 10.13

2.6 Loudness

Loudness is the sixth thing, and the simplest: every sound has a level, and every unit has somewhere to set it. Only two things about it are worth knowing now. One: louder almost always sounds better at first, so when you compare two versions of a sound, make them equally loud before you decide. Two: loudness can follow how hard you play, if you play from a MIDI keyboard that notices (section 1.10), and that does a lot to make a sound feel like an instrument.

Find it on your unit: Glass, section 3.4 · Volt, section 4.9 · Strike, section 5.9 · Ember, section 6.9 · Axis, section 7.10

2.7 Where next

That's the whole list: pitch, tone, shape, movement, effects and loudness. Every knob on every unit changes one of those, and every unit's chapter will tell you which.

What you have at the end of this chapter

Six questions to ask of any sound you hear, and a name for each part of the answer. At the end of each section above is where your unit's chapter deals with it. Go to that chapter next.

Chapter 3 - Glass

Six sine waves, and everything they can be made to do to each other.

Everything Glass does is made of sine waves. Not "based on" or "a bit like", but literally: there is nothing else inside it. It has six sine wave generators, and every one of its 128 factory sounds is those same six waves arranged in some particular way.

This chapter starts the way chapter 2 said every unit chapter would: with a sound you like, and no theory at all. Then it switches five of the six off, looks very carefully at the one that's left, and builds back up from there. By the end you'll have made an electric piano and a bell from nothing, and you'll be able to open up any of the factory sounds and see how it works.

FM synthesis: where it came from, and who uses it

FM synthesis was discovered by accident, which fits the introduction nicely. In the late 1960s John Chowning, a composer at Stanford University, was experimenting with vibrato on a computer. He made it faster and faster, and at some point it stopped sounding like vibrato and turned into a new tone colour: bright, metallic, bell-like, and controlled by just a couple of numbers. Section 3.6 explains exactly what he heard. Stanford patented it and licensed it to Yamaha.

In 1983 Yamaha brought out the DX7, and it became one of the best-selling synthesisers ever made. Its sounds were nothing like the warm, buzzy analogue synths before it: glassy electric pianos, bells, plucked basses, brass with a bite. They're all over 1980s pop, and Brian Eno, among many others, made a great deal of music with it. FM went into home computers and games consoles too: the sound chips in early PC sound cards, and in Sega's Mega Drive, were FM, so a lot of 1980s and 1990s game music is FM. And a small rack-mounted FM synth from the same family, the TX81Z, gave 1990s house music one of its favourite bass sounds.

FM is good at the sounds other methods find hard: anything that rings, chimes, clangs or plucks, and basses with a hard edge. It's also famous for being hard to program, which is why so many people only ever used the presets. You won't be one of them.

Today you'll find FM on synthesisers such as Elektron's Digitone and Korg's opsix, and in software such as Dexed, which is free. Glass isn't any of those, but it has every setting of the classic six-operator kind, so everything this chapter teaches works on all of them, and it can load the forty years of free sounds made for the DX7 (section 3.13).

3.1 Find a sound you like

Glass comes with four factory banks, FAC A to FAC D: 128 sounds in all, made by people who knew this kind of synth extremely well. The only job in this section is to find out which of them you like.

Try this

SOUNDS›2SOUND and go through all four banks, changing bank with 1BANK. Not carefully: turn, play two or three notes, turn again. It takes about ten minutes, and it's probably the most useful ten minutes you'll spend on Glass all year.

Write down the codes of the five you like best (FA11, FC07 and so on, from the top bar). We'll be coming back to them.

Now one more thing to try before any explanation. Changes to a factory sound aren't kept (chapter 1, section 1.8), and you'll want to keep this one, so copy a sound into your second bank, USER B. In this chapter USER B is your scrapbook, and USER A is where the sounds you build will go.

SOUNDS›1BANK›FAC A›2SOUND›FA11 then 3COPY TO›UB01›hold3

FA11 is an electric piano. You're now playing the copy, UB01, and everything on every page will do what you ask.

Try this

VOICE, hold a note down, and while it's still sounding turn 1ALGO slowly, one click at a time. A diagram appears and changes as you turn, and so does the sound.

Some will sound better than the original. Plenty will sound worse. A few will come out thin, or buzzy, or so quiet you'll wonder whether it's still on. All of that is normal, none of it has broken anything, and by the end you'll have a feel for what this encoder does long before anyone explains it. Push push1 to put the diagram away.

Ignore the diagram for now. We're not going to talk about what it means for a few sections yet, and there's a good reason: it makes far more sense once you've heard what it does than the other way round. If you've made a mess of UB01, copy FA11 over it again. That's what copying is for.

3.2 Six sine waves

Each of the six sine wave generators is called an operator. It's an odd word for something that just makes a tone, but it's what they've been called since the early 1980s and it's what everyone who works with these instruments calls them, so it's worth getting used to. On Glass they're OP1 to OP6, the six buttons down the left of the grid.

We could take a factory sound apart to see how it works, and that's a perfectly good way to learn, but it's much easier to hear what one thing does when there's only one thing there. So we're going to start from a blank sound instead. Every one of your own slots starts as one: INIT VOICE.

SOUNDS›1BANK›USER A›2SOUND›UA01

Play a note. It should be plain, soft and a little dull, not far off the sound of blowing across the top of a bottle. It isn't exciting, and it isn't meant to be. What you're listening to is a single operator, OP1, making a pure sine wave, with the other five turned all the way down to nothing.

If it sounds like something else entirely

Then UA01 has been used before, by you or by someone else. Any slot you haven't touched is INIT VOICE, and the SOUND box lists them by name, so turn 2SOUND until you find one that says INIT VOICE, and use that slot wherever this chapter says UA01.

The operator you can hear is doing the simplest job an operator can do: making a sound and sending it to the output. An operator doing that job is called a carrier.

The other five haven't gone anywhere. They're still sitting there, switched on, set to zero. In section 3.6 we're going to turn one of them up, and it won't get louder: it'll get brighter. That single surprising fact is what this whole instrument is built on.

The sounds you'll build

This chapter builds five sounds of your own, in the first five slots of USER A. Each starts as a copy of SINE 1, the first one, so you're never far from a sound that works:

SlotSoundSectionsWhat it shows
UA01SINE 13.4one operator, one sine wave: the place to start
UA02PLUCK 13.5an envelope that falls away to nothing
UA03SWELL 13.5an envelope that creeps in
UA04E PIANO 13.6a modulator: brightness from a sine you can't hear
UA05THREE OPS3.6 and 3.7two modulators side by side, then stacked

Section 3.4 says how to copy a sound into another slot; after that, each section says which slot to use.

3.3 How Glass is laid out

Glass's eighteen buttons are three columns of six, and each column has one job.

  • 1OP1 to OP6 choose which operator you're working on. They don't change the page: press OP3 while you're on the RATES page and you're on OP3's RATES.
  • 2The operator's pages: OSC, RATES, LEVELS, OUTPUT and KEYS. Each operator has its own set, so these show whichever operator you chose. Then SOUNDS.
  • 3The pages for the whole sound: VOICE, LFO, MOD, P-RATES and P-LEVELS, which belong to the sound rather than to any one operator. Then SETUP.

On an operator's page the top bar says which operator as well as which page, so OP1 OSC is OP1's OSC page. On the other pages it just says the page. One button, one page, every time: no page remembers anything that you have to undo before following an instruction.

The lights tell you the same thing. The operator you've chosen is lit, and so is the page you're on.

Listening to one operator at a time

Hold an OP button for half a second and that operator goes silent; hold it again to bring it back. Its light goes dim so you can see which ones are muted (and blinks if the muted one is the operator you've chosen), and the diagram on the VOICE page fades it out.

This is the most useful button on Glass for learning, because the next few sections argue that some operators are heard directly and some are only heard through others. You don't have to take that on trust. Mute them one at a time and listen: silence one and the sound disappears; silence another and the tone changes without the sound going away. The first kind is a carrier. The second is a modulator, which is section 3.6.

Mutes are kept with your own sounds

On a factory sound a mute is a change like any other: the star appears in the top bar, and it's forgotten as soon as you choose another sound. On one of your own, the mute is part of the sound and saved with it. So if one of your sounds seems to have lost something, look down the OP buttons for a dim light.

Looking inside the factory sounds

Every page works on a factory sound too, so you can open any of them and see exactly how it's made, which, by the end of this chapter, you'll be able to read. Turn something and you'll hear what it does; the star in the top bar says it's changed, and choosing the sound again puts it back.

3.4 One note, louder and quieter

Time to change something. Make sure you're on UA01, your INIT VOICE, and press OP1 then OUTPUT.

OP1›OUTPUT›1LEVEL

  • LEVEL encoder 1, 0-99 how much this operator puts out. Hold a note down and turn it all the way to 0. Silence. Bring it back to 99 and the sound returns.

So LEVEL is the volume of this operator, which might seem a slightly odd thing to have, given there's already a volume control on the Root.

Worth remembering

It isn't really volume. It only looks like volume today, because OP1 is a carrier and there's nothing else switched on for it to work with.

Turn the very same encoder on an operator that isn't a carrier and it changes how bright the sound is instead: same page, same box, entirely different result. Which one you get depends on what job that operator has been given. That's section 3.6.

The other three boxes on OUTPUT come later: KEY VEL and RATE SC in section 3.10, AMP MOD in section 3.9.

The tuning page

OP1›OSC

  • COARSE encoder 1, 0.5 and 1-31 what pitch this operator runs at, compared with the key you pressed. On a carrier all it can do is move the note up in jumps, which is mildly interesting at best.
  • FINE encoder 2, 0-99 the same, in smaller steps. Under both boxes the screen shows what COARSE and FINE make together: X1.00 is exactly the note you played, X2.00 twice it.
  • DETUNE encoder 3, -7 to +7 a very small amount either side of in tune.
  • MODE encoder 4, RATIO or FIXED section 3.6 has this one.

The three tuning controls become some of the most important on Glass in section 3.6, once the operator you're retuning is one you can't directly hear. Put anything you moved back where it was before you go on: COARSE 1, FINE 0, DETUNE 0, LEVEL 99.

Keeping it

You've made a sound. It isn't a very good sound, but it's yours, and the next section builds on top of it, so give it a name. On the SOUNDS page, turn 4NAME to change the letter under the cursor, and push it to move on to the next letter. Call it SINE 1. There's no saving to do: it already has.

Then make two copies of it to work in, because the next section turns them into two other sounds:

SOUNDS›3COPY TO›UA02›hold3 and again to UA03

Copying moves you onto the copy, so go back to UA01 afterwards with 2SOUND.

What you have so far

A sound called SINE 1 in UA01: one operator, one sine wave, nothing else running at all. UA02 and UA03 hold copies. It's the plainest noise Glass can make, and it's also the only sensible place to start from. You'll find yourself coming back to it every time you want to build something new.

3.5 The shape of a note

Play SINE 1. Hold a note. Let go.

Whatever else is wrong with that sound, the biggest problem is that it arrives at full volume the instant you touch the key and vanishes the instant you let go. Chapter 2 (section 2.3) said what's missing: the envelope, the shape of the note. Most synths give you four controls for it, attack, decay, sustain and release. Glass does something more flexible, and it's worth understanding on its own terms rather than squashing it into the usual four.

Four corners

Think of it as drawing a shape. You place four corners, and you say how quickly the sound travels between them.

Reading it from the left: before you press anything, the sound sits at L4. Press a key and it sets off at speed R1 towards L1. When it gets there it turns and heads at speed R2 towards L2, then at R3 towards L3. And there it stays, for as long as you keep the key down: a second, a minute, all afternoon.

Let go and it travels at R4 back to L4, where it started.

Four places to be, four speeds for getting between them. That's the whole system, and every sound Glass makes uses it. Every operator has one of these, so a sound has six of them.

Where to find it

The speeds and the corners are on two pages of whichever operator you've chosen:

OP1›RATES R1 to R4    OP1›LEVELS L1 to L4

  • R1 encoder 1, 0-99 how fast the sound travels from where it starts up to L1.
  • R2 encoder 2, 0-99 from L1 to L2.
  • R3 encoder 3, 0-99 from L2 to L3, where it settles.
  • R4 encoder 4, 0-99 after you let go: from wherever it was back to L4.
  • L1 encoder 1, 0-99 the first corner, which the note heads for as soon as you press the key.
  • L2 encoder 2, 0-99 the second corner.
  • L3 encoder 3, 0-99 where it settles and stays while you hold the key down.
  • L4 encoder 4, 0-99 where it sits before you play, and where it goes back to afterwards.

Both pages show the same picture of the shape, and each number sits on a chip the colour of its part of the picture: change the green number and the green part moves. That correspondence is worth more than anything else on these pages. The picture holds the note long enough to show every stage and then lets go, and a very long shape zooms out to fit (the readout under it, X1.6 and so on, says by how much).

The bit that trips everyone up

Here's the thing to get straight before you touch anything, because it catches out people who've been doing this for years.

The rate numbers are not durations. They're speeds. A high rate means the sound moves quickly, which means that part of the note is shorter.

So turning R1 up makes the attack snappier, not longer. Turning R4 down makes the note hang around after you let go. It's the opposite of what most people expect the first time.

Try this

On SINE 1, OP1›RATES›1R1›45. Play a note and hold it.

Instead of arriving, the sound now creeps in. Turn R1 back up to 99 and it snaps in again. That one encoder is the difference between a bowed instrument and a struck one.

Where the note sits while you hold it

L3 is the level the sound settles at once it's finished travelling: the level you hear for as long as your finger stays down. It's the one corner whose length you don't set, because you set it yourself, with your hand.

L3 at 99 and a held note goes on at full volume, like an organ. L3 at 0 and the note dies away to nothing whether you hold the key or not, like a piano or a bell. That one choice, does the sound sustain or does it die away, accounts for most of the difference between the instrument families you already know by ear.

The strange one

L4 is where the sound sits before you press anything, and also where it goes back to after you let go. It's the same corner doing both jobs.

Which raises a question worth sitting with for a moment: what happens if L4 isn't zero? The answer is that the sound never actually stops. Once you've played a note it sits at whatever level you've set, quietly, all the time, whether you're playing or not: a drone under everything you do.

Try this, then put it back

OP1›LEVELS›4L4›80. Play a note and let go. There it is: a hum that doesn't stop.

This is usually a mistake, and when a sound you're building won't shut up, L4 is the first place to look. But it's also a real effect that people use on purpose, so it's worth having heard it deliberately once rather than only ever meeting it by accident.

Now turn L4 back to 0, and the hum dies away.

Letting go early

Chapter 2 said this about every synth, and it's just as true here. Letting go of a key doesn't wait for anything: whatever the note was doing at that moment, still climbing towards L1 or halfway down to L2, it stops and heads straight for L4 at R4.

So a sound with a slow attack never reaches full volume if you play it in short stabs. That isn't a fault, it's the character of the thing, and it's why slow sounds want long, held notes.

Four shapes worth knowing

Here are four envelopes that between them cover most of what you'll want. Put them in on OP1 of SINE 1 and listen. Every number is a starting point rather than a rule: nudge them until they sound right to you.

Organ

Instant on, full volume for as long as you hold it, instant off.

RATESR1 99R2 99R3 99R4 99
LEVELSL1 99L2 99L3 99L4 0

Pluck

Arrives at once and falls away to nothing, whether you keep holding or not.

RATESR1 99R2 55R3 99R4 99
LEVELSL1 99L2 0L3 0L4 0

Bell

The same fall, far more gradual: so gradual that letting go interrupts it.

RATESR1 99R2 25R3 99R4 30
LEVELSL1 99L2 0L3 0L4 0

Swell

Creeps up from silence, settles just below the top, fades gently when you let go.

RATESR1 35R2 60R3 60R4 45
LEVELSL1 99L2 90L3 90L4 0

Look at what the bell does

Every shape here is drawn with the key held for the same time and let go at the dashed line. Three of them have finished travelling by then and are sitting still. The bell hasn't: it's still on its way down when you let go, which is why its pink release is the only one you can see.

That's also why R4 does nothing at all on the pluck. By the time you let go the sound is already at zero, so there's nowhere left for it to travel.

Try this

Take the pluck and change one number at a time. Bring R2 down to 20: now it's a bell. Bring L2 up to 70: now it's an organ with a bump at the start. Bring R4 down to 20: now every note trails off after you let go, and playing fast makes them pile up on top of each other.

You aren't looking for the right answer here. You're building up a feel for which encoder does what, which is worth more than any table.

Build the pluck in UA02 and the swell in UA03, the two copies of SINE 1, and name them PLUCK 1 and SWELL 1.

What you have so far

Three sounds: SINE 1, PLUCK 1 and SWELL 1. All of them one sine wave, all of them plain, but with completely different characters, because the shape of a note carries more information than the note itself.

3.6 Modulators

Everything so far has used one operator out of six. This section turns on a second one, and the result isn't what you'd expect, which is the whole reason this instrument exists. Chapter 2 said Glass has no filter, and makes its harmonics a completely different way. This is the way.

Go to SINE 1 and let's find out.

Turning up the one you can't hear

OP1 is the one you've been listening to. OP2 has been sitting at zero the whole time.

OP2›OUTPUT›1LEVEL

Play a note again and again, and slowly bring that from 0 up to about 70.

The sound doesn't get louder. It gets brighter: harder, buzzier, more like a real instrument and less like a test tone. Keep going to 99 and it turns harsh and metallic.

This is the thing

Same encoder, same page, same box as the one that changed the volume in section 3.4. Completely different result.

The difference is the job OP2 has been given. It isn't connected to the output at all: it's connected to OP1. An operator wired to the output is a carrier, and you hear it. An operator wired to another operator is a modulator, and you never hear it directly; you only hear what it does to the one underneath. Hold holdOP1 to mute it and the sound vanishes, OP2 and all.

Why brightness, though?

Here's what's actually happening, and it's worth a minute, because everything else in FM synthesis follows from it.

A modulator pushes the carrier's pitch up and down. That's all it does. Turn the modulator's level up and it pushes harder.

If something pushes a note's pitch up and down a few times a second, you hear it as vibrato: a wobble. Speed the wobble up and at some point it stops sounding like a wobble at all. Your ear can't follow it any more, so it does something else with it: it hears a change in tone.

A modulator is doing vibrato several hundred times a second. Far too fast to hear as movement, so you hear it as brightness instead, and the harder it pushes, the brighter the result. That's the trick. That's the whole of it. Everything from here is deciding what to push with, how hard, and when.

What note is it pushing at?

The modulator has its own pitch, and it matters far more than the pitch of a carrier ever would. It's set on OP2's OSC page.

OP2›OSC

  • COARSE encoder 1, 0.5 and 1-31 a multiplier rather than a pitch. At 1 the modulator runs at the same frequency as the note you played; at 2 twice as fast, at 3 three times, and so on.
  • FINE encoder 2, 0-99 fills in the gaps between the whole numbers. The screen shows the result under both boxes: X3.50 is three and a half times.
  • DETUNE encoder 3, -7 to +7 a very small amount of not-quite-right, on purpose.
  • MODE encoder 4, RATIO or FIXED below.

Whole numbers

With OP2's LEVEL at about 70, hold a note and step 1COARSE through 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and on up to about 12. Listen to each one for a few seconds before you move on.

They all sound different, and they all still sound like a musical note: thin, hollow, reedy, nasal, brassy. It's the same instrument playing the same pitch with a different tone each time.

They stay musical because whole-number multiples of a note are exactly the harmonics chapter 2 talked about, the ones real instruments make. Twice the note is the octave above; three times is a fifth above that. Stack them up in different amounts and you get flutes, clarinets, oboes, trumpets: everything that vibrates in a well-behaved way.

Breaking it on purpose

Set COARSE to 3, then turn 2FINE up to about 50, so the screen says X4.50 or so. Play something.

It stops sounding like a note and starts sounding like an object. Bells, gongs, metal bars, glass. Suddenly there's a percussion section in here that wasn't there a moment ago.

The frequencies you've made aren't whole-number multiples any more, so they don't line up with anything your ear expects from a vibrating string or a column of air. It hears metal instead. This is why FM was famous for bells and electric pianos long before it was famous for anything else: it's extremely good at the sounds other kinds of synth find awkward.

Close, but not quite

Put COARSE back to a whole number, 2 is a good one, FINE back to 0, and then move 3DETUNE just a click or two off 0. Play a long held note, and wait.

The sound moves. It shimmers, or beats slowly, or seems to breathe, because two frequencies that are nearly but not quite in step drift in and out of line with each other. This is the difference between a sound that's obviously synthetic and one that seems alive. Real instruments are never perfectly in tune with themselves; strings stretch, air moves, wood warps. That's what DETUNE is for.

When the brightness changes

Now for the part that turns all this into actual instruments.

The modulator has an envelope of its own, on OP2's RATES and LEVELS pages, and it works exactly like OP1's. But because OP2's level changes the brightness rather than the volume, its envelope changes how the brightness changes over time.

Think about hitting a piano key hard: the sound is bright at the very start and then mellows, while the note is still ringing. That's not the volume changing, it's the tone. Almost every acoustic instrument does it.

Build an electric piano

Copy SINE 1 to UA04 (section 3.4 showed how), name it E PIANO 1, then:

OP1: the pluck, with R2 opened out a little.

RATESR1 99R2 40R3 99R4 99
LEVELSL1 99L2 0L3 0L4 0

OP2: OP2›OUTPUT›1LEVEL›75, OSC›1COARSE›2, and its own envelope set to fall away faster than OP1's.

RATESR1 99R2 50R3 99R4 99
LEVELSL1 99L2 0L3 0L4 0

Play it. The note starts bright and clangy and settles almost at once into something soft and round underneath, and it should be recognisably an electric piano.

The two shapes are almost the same. The only number that differs is R2, and the whole instrument lives in the gap between them: the note is still sounding there, but the brightness has already gone. That gap is the clang. Go back to OP2's R2 and slow it down: the clang lasts longer. Speed it up and it becomes a click. That one number is the difference between a whole family of instruments.

Two envelopes, two jobs

The carrier's envelope shapes how loud the note is. The modulator's envelope shapes how bright it is. They're completely separate, and using them against each other, bright and quiet, or dull and loud, is where most good FM sounds come from.

Fixed instead of ratio

One more option on the OSC page: OP2›OSC›4MODE, RATIO or FIXED.

Everything so far has been RATIO: the modulator's frequency follows the note you play, so the sound has the same character wherever you play it. Switch to FIXED and the operator stays at one frequency whatever key you press. COARSE then picks 1, 10, 100 or 1000 Hz, FINE goes up from there, and the screen shows the frequency in Hz.

That sounds like a mistake, and for most instruments it would be, but it's exactly right for anything where part of the sound doesn't move with the pitch: the thump of a bass drum, breath on a flute, the knock of a hammer. Real instruments are full of things that stay the same however high or low you play, and FIXED is how you get them. Put OP2 back to RATIO before you go on.

A second modulator

Adding a third operator is where it starts to get properly interesting, and it needs a different arrangement. Copy SINE 1 to UA05, name it THREE OPS, and on the copy:

VOICE›1ALGO›16

Algorithm 16 has one carrier, OP1, with OP2, OP3 and OP5 all feeding into it directly. For now leave OP5 at 0 and use the other two.

Try this

Set OP2 to LEVEL 65 with COARSE 1, and OP3 to LEVEL 50 with COARSE 7.

Mute each one in turn, holding its OP button, and listen to what disappears. OP2 gives you the body of the sound; OP3 adds a thin, reedy edge on top. Together they make something neither could on its own.

Now give them different envelopes, so the edge fades before the body does.

Two modulators side by side on one carrier behave pretty much as you'd hope: each adds its own character and you hear both. That makes them predictable and easy to work with, which is why this arrangement turns up in a great many factory sounds. There's another way to connect three operators, and it's much less well behaved. That's the next section.

3.7 Algorithms

You've been using algorithms since section 3.1, when you turned ALGO and listened to a sound fall apart and put itself back together. Now for what was actually happening: an algorithm is the wiring diagram, which operators are carriers and which modulate which.

Reading the picture

There are thirty-two of them, and turning ALGO on the VOICE page shows you the one you've landed on. It stays up until you push the encoder, change page or turn another encoder. Every diagram is made of the same parts:

The whole chart is at the end of this section. It's meaningless until you know what the boxes mean, and alarming if you meet it cold, so leave it until you've read the rest.

Tall and thin, short and fat

Look down the chart and the shapes fall into two rough families, and you can predict a great deal from which family an algorithm belongs to.

Short and fat means lots of carriers side by side. Algorithm 32 is the extreme: all six operators are carriers, none of them modulating anything. Six sine waves, added together, and nothing else. That's how a pipe organ works, separate pipes at different pitches sounding at once, and it's what these algorithms are good for: smooth, clean, blending sounds. Organs, strings, choirs, pads.

Tall and thin means operators stacked in a chain, each one modulating the next. Algorithm 1 has a stack four deep. Each stage multiplies the complexity of the one below, so the results are dense, bright, often metallic: bells, chimes, aggressive basses, sound effects.

Most of the thirty-two sit somewhere in between, and that's usually where you want to be: a couple of carriers for body, a stack for character.

Try this

Go back to UB01, your copy of the electric piano from section 3.1, and turn ALGO through them again, exactly as you did then. But this time watch the diagram as it goes past.

You should now be able to see, before you hear it, roughly what's about to happen. That's the whole point of the chart.

Stacking modulators

In the last section you put two modulators side by side. Now for the other way. Stay on UA05, algorithm 16, and look at where OP4 goes: it doesn't feed OP1 at all. It feeds OP3, which feeds OP1.

Try this

Set OP3 to LEVEL 60 with COARSE 1, and put OP2 and OP5 at LEVEL 0. Familiar ground: one modulator, one carrier.

Now bring OP4's LEVEL up slowly from 0.

OP4 is modulating a modulator. You aren't making the sound brighter, you're making the brightening more complicated, and it gets strange much faster than it did before. Small moves make big differences.

Modulators side by side add up in ways you can predict. Modulators stacked on top of each other multiply in ways that are extremely hard to predict, even for people who've been doing this for decades. Which isn't a reason to avoid them. It's a reason to turn the encoder slowly and keep the ones you like.

Feedback

One operator in every algorithm has a pink loop drawn round it. That's feedback: an operator modulating itself.

VOICE ALGO, FEEDBK, OSCSYNC and TRANSP

  • ALGO encoder 1, 1-32 which of the thirty-two wirings the sound uses.
  • FEEDBK encoder 2, 0-7 how hard the looped operator modulates itself.
  • OSCSYNC encoder 3, ON or OFF whether the operators start their waves afresh on every note (ON) or carry on from wherever they happened to be. The difference is in the very first instant of the note, and it's subtle.
  • TRANSP encoder 4, -24 to +24 moves the whole sound up or down in semitones. Unlike OCT- and OCT+, it's part of the sound.

Turn feedback up gradually and the operator's pure sine wave gets more and more jagged: first brighter, then buzzy, and at the top of the range it breaks down into noise. It's a small control with a big range, and it's how you get roaring basses, hissing cymbals and wind out of an instrument that only contains sine waves.

Try this

On algorithm 16 the loop is round OP6. OP6 modulates OP5, OP5 modulates OP1, and OP1 is the only carrier. So three operators have to be up before the loop can be heard at all: OP1, because it's the one that reaches your ears; OP5, because it's what OP6 modulates; and OP6 itself. Set OP5 and OP6 to LEVEL 70 and put OP2, OP3 and OP4 at 0.

Now set FEEDBK to 0 and step it up one number at a time. What's changing is OP6's own wave, and you hear it as a change in OP1's brightness.

Eight settings, and you can hear every step. There's no other control on Glass with that few positions and that much difference between them.

An honest word about all this

Here's something manuals tend not to say. People who are extremely good at FM, people who've made a living at it for thirty years, still spend a lot of their time turning encoders and going "ooh, what's that". The theory tells you roughly where to look. It doesn't tell you what you'll find. Nobody sits down and calculates their way to a good bell sound.

What the theory buys you is this: when something sounds nearly right, you know which encoder to reach for. And when something sounds wonderful by accident, you can work out why, which means you can do it again on purpose. That's genuinely all of it, and it's enough.

All thirty-two

Here they are. You're not meant to learn them, and nobody has. What you're meant to be able to do is glance at one and guess roughly what it'll sound like, which you now can.

Carriers are blue. The pink line is the feedback loop, and it's worth looking for: twenty of the thirty-two come in pairs or threes with identical wiring, differing only in where that loop sits.

Where you've got to

You can start a sound from nothing, shape how it grows and fades, make it bright or dull or metallic or alive, change how that brightness moves over time, and read the wiring diagram well enough to guess what an unfamiliar algorithm will do. That's the heart of Glass. The rest of the chapter is about pitch, movement, and what happens across the keyboard.

3.8 Pitch
