Most of the pitch controls you've met already. On a carrier, COARSE and FINE move the note up or down (in octaves and fifths and so on, which is rarely what you want), and DETUNE nudges it. TRANSP on the VOICE page moves the whole sound in semitones. And a MIDI keyboard's pitch bend wheel bends the note, as far as SETUP's BEND says (section 3.12).

There's one more, and it's odder.

The pitch envelope

P-RATES and P-LEVELS hold a second kind of envelope, built exactly the same way as an operator's, with four rates and four levels. The difference is where it goes: instead of changing how loud the sound is, it changes what pitch it's at, all six operators together. It belongs to the sound, not to any one operator.

One thing to know before you touch it: on the pitch envelope, 50 means no change. Above 50 bends the note up, below 50 bends it down. So a level of 0 isn't silence, it's a long way flat.

The other thing to know is that the numbers are wildly uneven. Going from 50 to 70 buys you about a fifth. The next ten steps buy another third or so, the ten after that most of an octave, and the last few run away entirely. Somewhere around 85 it stops being a pitch control and becomes a special effect. So the useful range is roughly 20 to 80, and it's worth knowing that before you spin the encoder, find yourself several octaves out and decide it's broken.

Try this, on a copy

Copy SINE 1 to a spare slot. On P-LEVELS set L4 to 99 with L1, L2 and L3 at 50, and on P-RATES set R1 to about 75. Play: a note that swoops down into place from above. Set R1 to about 40 instead, and you've got the sound used in every computer game until about 1985.

3.9 Movement

Every sound you've built so far does the same thing on every note: press a key, the envelopes run, and if you hold it the note sits there being exactly what it is. Chapter 2 (section 2.4) said what puts movement into a sound: the LFO, an oscillator too slow to hear, used to wobble something else. Glass's is on two pages.

The LFO page: what the wobble is like

LFO SPEED, DELAY, WAVE and KEYSYNC

  • SPEED encoder 1, 0-99 how fast the wobble is. Human vibrato sits around five or six wobbles a second, which is about 35 to 40 here. The scale doubles roughly every twenty steps: about 2 a second at 10, 4 at 30 and 8 at 50, and past that too fast to count. Equal turns buy equal musical steps of speed, which is why it feels even all the way round.
  • DELAY encoder 2, 0-99 how long the LFO waits after you press a key before it starts, then fades in. This is the one setting that makes vibrato sound like a person rather than a machine. Nobody plays a note with the vibrato already running: a violinist arrives on the note, and then it starts to move.
  • WAVE encoder 3 the shape of the wobble, one of six.
  • KEYSYNC encoder 4, ON or OFF whether the LFO starts its wobble from the beginning on each note (ON) or runs on in the background (OFF). Off, every note catches the wobble at a different point, which sounds natural on single notes and a little chaotic on chords. On, every note starts its wobble together, which sounds deliberate on chords and a little mechanical on tunes.

TRI and SINE both go smoothly up and down, and for vibrato you won't be able to tell them apart; either is right. SQR jumps: straight to the top, straight to the bottom, nothing in between. On pitch that gives a trill between two notes; on volume, a hard on-off stutter. SAW+ climbs and drops back, SAW- falls and jumps back; on pitch, the falling one is the sound of something powering off, over and over. S&H picks a random value, sits on it, then picks another. It's the sound of 1970s computers thinking, it has almost no use in a sound meant to be like an instrument, and it's enormous fun everywhere else.

The MOD page: how far it moves things

MOD VIBRATO, P SENS and TREMOLO

  • VIBRATO encoder 1, 0-99 how far the LFO pushes the pitch up and down. Small amounts are vibrato. Large amounts are a siren.
  • P SENS encoder 2, 0-7 how much of that vibrato this sound lets through. At 0 there's no vibrato at all, however high VIBRATO is. Every INIT VOICE starts at 3, so you'll rarely need it, but if VIBRATO seems to do nothing, look here. It sits right beside VIBRATO for exactly that reason.
  • TREMOLO encoder 3, 0-99 how far the LFO pushes the level up and down. Small amounts are a slight throb. Large amounts are a helicopter.

Try this first

On any of your sounds, MOD›1VIBRATO›20 and LFO›1SPEED›30. Play a note and hold it.

Now wind VIBRATO slowly down towards 0 while the note is still sounding, and find the point where you stop noticing the wobble and just hear a slightly livelier instrument. That point is where you want to be most of the time. Then try a DELAY of about 40.

TREMOLO needs a second setting, on each operator

Vibrato moves the whole sound. Tremolo is chosen operator by operator: each operator's OUTPUT page has AMP MOD encoder 3, 0-3, how much of the tremolo reaches that operator. It starts at 0 on every operator, so TREMOLO on its own does nothing at all. Turn AMP MOD up on the operators you want it on.

That's a feature rather than a nuisance. On a carrier, AMP MOD gives you a wobble in volume, which is plain tremolo. On a modulator it gives you a wobble in brightness: the sound shimmers rather than pulses, which is a much more musical effect, and the reason the setting is per operator.

At the very top of its range the LFO arrives at the edge of what you can hear as a pitch. Turn SPEED to 99 with VIBRATO high and the vibrato stops sounding like movement and starts sounding like a tone colour. That isn't a coincidence or a fault: it's the same thing the operators do to each other in section 3.6, happening slowly enough that you can hear it cross over.

A MIDI keyboard's mod wheel and aftertouch can bring in vibrato and tremolo too, while you play (section 3.12).

3.10 Playing across the keyboard

Play the bottom note of a piano and the top note of the same piano. They aren't the same sound an octave or six apart. The bottom note is long, dark and complicated. The top note is short, bright and thin. Nobody designed that on purpose: it falls out of the fact that one string is long and thick and the other short and tight.

An FM sound has no strings, so nothing falls out of anything. By default, the electric piano you built in section 3.6 does exactly the same thing at both ends of the keyboard, and that sameness is one of the main reasons a sound can be technically right and still sound fake.

This section is about the settings that break the sameness. It's the fiddliest part of Glass and gives the least reward per minute spent, which is why it's this far back. It's also the difference between a sound that's fine and a sound that's convincing. Everything here is per operator, and the interesting effects come from doing it to modulators rather than carriers.

How hard you play

On the OUTPUT page, KEY VEL encoder 2, 0-7 is how much the force of your playing changes this operator's level. At 0, playing hard and playing softly sound the same from this operator. At 7, the difference is dramatic.

Velocity on a carrier is a volume control: play harder, that note is louder. Velocity on a modulator is a brightness control: play harder, that operator modulates more strongly, and the sound gets brighter as well as louder. That second one is what real instruments do. Hit a piano key harder and it doesn't just get louder, it gets harsher. Blow a trumpet harder and it gets brassier. Set velocity on your modulators, leave your carriers alone, and you get an instrument that changes character with how hard you play it.

Glass's own keys can't show you this

Glass's keys play every note at the same strength (velocity 100), however hard you press. To hear KEY VEL you need notes that come in harder and softer: a MIDI keyboard that senses how hard you play, plugged into the Root (section 1.10), or notes from Step, which can give every note its own velocity. Glass has no VELO setting on SETUP because it doesn't need one: each sound decides for itself, operator by operator, with KEY VEL.

Keyboard scaling

The KEYS page does one thing: it makes an operator get quieter, or louder, the further you play from a key you choose.

OP2›KEYS L DEPTH, R DEPTH, BREAK and CURVES

  • BREAK encoder 3, A-1 to C8 a note, which you choose: everything below it is the left side, everything above it the right side.
  • L DEPTH encoder 1, 0-99 how strong the effect is on the left side. At 0 that side does nothing, whatever curve you pick.
  • R DEPTH encoder 2, 0-99 the same, for the right side.
  • CURVES encoder 4 the shape each side takes, left then right, as two pairs of letters: -L, -E, +E or +L, so -L+E is -L on the left and +E on the right. All sixteen pairs are on the one encoder.

The minus curves make the operator quieter as you move away from BREAK; the plus curves make it louder. L is linear, changing evenly; E is exponential, changing slowly at first and then fast.

The classic use is a modulator with BREAK somewhere in the middle of the keyboard, a minus curve on the right and a moderate R DEPTH. Now the top of the keyboard is less brightly modulated than the bottom, which is what nearly every acoustic instrument does: high notes are purer, low notes richer.

Rate scaling, which is the one to set first

Keyboard scaling changes how loud an operator is at different pitches. RATE SC OUTPUT, encoder 4, 0-7 changes how fast its envelope runs at different pitches.

Turn it up and notes at the top of the keyboard die away faster than notes at the bottom, which is the piano fact from the start of this section, made into a single encoder. It's the highest return on effort of anything in this section: if you're going to set one thing here and ignore the rest, set this. It reaches the operator envelopes and nothing else; the pitch envelope runs at the same speed wherever you play.

Hear rate scaling on its own

Take your electric piano, E PIANO 1. Press OCT- once, play a low note and let it ring; then play a note two octaves up and let that ring. Roughly, time them. The high note rings on as long as the low one, or longer, which is the wrong way round for a piano.

Now OP1›OUTPUT›4RATE SC›3 (OP1 is this sound's only carrier). Play the two notes again. The high note now dies away sooner, as it does on a real piano. If it still rings on, go higher.

An order to do this in

All of this is optional, all of it is fiddly, and it's easy to spend an hour here and end up with a sound that's worse. So, in order of how much they repay the effort:

  • 1RATE SC, on whichever operators are carriers. Notes get shorter as they get higher.
  • 2KEY VEL on your modulators. Playing harder gets brighter.
  • 3Keyboard scaling with a minus curve on the right, on your modulators. High notes get purer.
  • 4AMP MOD, only if you're already using TREMOLO and want the shimmer rather than the throb.

You don't have to do any of it, and a sound with none of it set is a perfectly good sound. It just won't change as you move around the keyboard, and now you'll be able to hear that it doesn't.

3.11 Effects

Glass has no effects of its own: every sound in it is the six operators and nothing else, which is exactly how the instruments it's built like always worked. The famous FM sounds of the 1980s were almost never heard dry, though. They went through chorus and reverb on the way to the record, and an electric piano with a little chorus is a different animal.

That's Haze's job. Join Haze onto the chain and it can send Glass into its chorus, echo and reverb, as much as you like (chapter 2, section 2.5). Try E PIANO 1 with a little chorus and a plate reverb.

3.12 Glass's SETUP

SETUP's THIS UNIT pages (chapter 1, section 1.9) have Glass's own settings: the ones that belong to the unit rather than to a sound. Encoder 1 on the first page is the MIDI channel, as on every unit.

  • BEND THIS UNIT 1, encoder 2, 0-12 how far a MIDI keyboard's pitch bend wheel bends the note, in semitones. Two is usual.
  • STEP THIS UNIT 1, encoder 3, ON or OFF OFF bends smoothly; ON bends in whole semitones.
  • MODE THIS UNIT 1, encoder 4, POLY or MONO POLY plays up to 16 notes at once. MONO plays one: the last key you're holding sounds, and a key played while another is held changes the pitch without starting the note again, which is how lead lines are played. Let go and it goes back to the key still held.
  • PORTA THIS UNIT 2, encoder 1, OFF or 1-99 glide: the pitch slides from one note to the next instead of jumping, and this is how long it takes. In POLY each note glides from the one before; in MONO it glides between keys held together.
  • WHEEL THIS UNIT 2, encoder 2, 0-99 how far a MIDI keyboard's mod wheel goes.
  • ROUTE THIS UNIT 2, encoder 3, OFF, PITCH, AMP or BOTH what the mod wheel moves: vibrato (PITCH), tremolo (AMP) or both, through each sound's own P SENS and AMP MOD.
  • TOUCH THIS UNIT 2, encoder 4 the same choices for aftertouch, pressing harder on a key you're holding, if your keyboard sends it.

The last THIS UNIT page is RESET, as on every unit.

3.13 Forty years of free sounds

Here's the fact this section exists for.

Glass has every setting of the most famous FM synth of the 1980s, the DX7, and it can load that synth's sound banks: standard DX7 SysEx files of 32 sounds at a time. The DX7 came out in 1983, sold in enormous numbers, and was programmed by more or less everybody. People have been making banks of sounds for it, and giving them away, for over forty years. There are archives of thousands of them online, free, in a file format that hasn't changed. They were made for a synthesiser that cost as much as a car. All of them load into Glass, and play as they were made.

That's why the algorithms in section 3.7 are those thirty-two, in that order, and why every operator has four rates and four levels instead of the four simple stages other synths use.

From the card

Bank files go on the Root's memory card, in a folder called GLASS. Then press SOUNDS twice: the second press is the CARD page.

  • FILE encoder 1 which bank file on the card, in alphabetical order.
  • INTO encoder 2, USER A-D which of your banks it goes into.
  • LOAD encoder 3, hold loads it. The file's 32 sounds replace all 32 in that user bank, so the screen asks you to hold.
  • SAVE encoder 4, hold saves the user bank chosen in INTO as a new file on the card (USER-A-1.SYX, then USER-A-2.SYX and so on). It never writes over a file that's already there.

A bank always lands in one of your own banks; the factory banks never change, so you can always get back to them. And SAVE is how you keep a copy of your own sounds before you try something risky, such as a RESET to EVERYTHING.

Before you fill all four banks

Loading replaces every sound in the user bank you chose, including the ones you made. Save that bank to the card first if there's anything in it you want.

Also expect a fair share of any forty-year-old bank to be unusable. They were made for a five-octave keyboard that sensed how hard you played, often for one particular record, and a lot of them are one thin sound that made sense in one arrangement. The hit rate is low, and the ones that hit are extraordinary.

Over MIDI

A computer can send Glass a bank or a single sound as SysEx, through the Root's USB socket or its MIDI IN, from an editor or librarian program. A bank doesn't go straight over anything: it waits at the top of the CARD page's list as FROM MIDI, and you load it from there as if it came from the card. A single sound goes into the sound you're on, if it's one of your own (on a factory sound the screen says VOICE: PICK A USER SOUND). Glass listens for SysEx on its own MIDI channel, or, with the Root's MIDI IN on FOLLOW, when it's the unit you touched last.

What to do with all this

Most of this chapter was about building sounds from nothing, which is the slow way and the way you actually learn. This section hands you a shortcut that skips all of it. Use both. Load a bank, find a sound in it that does something you can't explain, and then open it up, operator by operator, and work out what makes it do that. Every sound in every one of those archives is a worked example, made by somebody who knew what they were doing, and you now know how to read them.

DX7 is a trademark of Yamaha Corporation. Tessel isn't connected with Yamaha or endorsed by it; Glass loads sound files in that format.

What you have at the end of this chapter

SINE 1, PLUCK 1, SWELL 1, E PIANO 1 and THREE OPS in your first bank, and a working understanding of the only idea in FM that really matters: some operators are heard, some change the ones that are heard, and the difference between them is nothing but where they're plugged in. Plus a key to forty years of other people's sounds.

Chapter 4 - Volt

Start with something bright and buzzy, and take away what you don't want.

Glass makes its sounds by adding: pure sine waves, pushing each other into brightness. Volt works the other way round, the way most synthesisers have since the 1960s. It starts with waves that are already full of harmonics, bright and buzzy, and then a filter takes away the ones you don't want. It's called subtractive synthesis, and it's the sound of more records than any other kind.

Volt is two instruments in one box, and every sound is one or the other:

  • ·CLASSIC is the classic analogue synth of the early 1970s kind: three oscillators, a mixer, a filter that growls and whistles, and two contours. Basses, leads, brass, even drums.
  • ·ACID is the little bass line machine of the early 1980s kind: one oscillator, a squelchy filter, and accent and slide. The sound of acid house.

Both are our own, but they work the classic way, with the kind of controls synths like these have always had, so what you learn here works on any synth of either kind you ever meet.

Volt plays one note at a time. That isn't a shortcoming: synths of both kinds were made that way, for basses and lead lines, and so much of their character comes from it that section 4.9 is about exactly that.

Subtractive synthesis: where it came from, and who uses it

Subtractive synthesis is the oldest way of making sounds on a synthesiser that's still in everyday use. Robert Moog's modular synthesisers of the 1960s worked this way: cabinets of oscillators, filters and envelopes joined by patch cables. In 1970 his company squeezed the most useful parts into one portable instrument with a keyboard, the Minimoog, and for the first time a synthesiser could go on stage. Kraftwerk, Parliament-Funkadelic, Gary Numan and countless others played it, and its fat basses and singing leads are still everywhere, from funk to the whining leads of 1990s West Coast hip hop.

Most of the famous synthesisers since have worked the same way: the Sequential Prophet-5, Roland's Juno-106 and SH-101, Korg's MS-20, the ARP Odyssey, and a great many made today. Learn it once and you can sit down at almost any synthesiser in the world and make it do something.

Volt's other half, ACID, makes the kind of sound the TB-303 made famous. Its story is in the introduction: a failed bass machine that became acid house, from Phuture's "Acid Tracks" in Chicago in 1987 to the acid house summer in Britain a year later, and it's still the sound of acid techno today.

Subtractive synthesis is good at warm, fat and round: basses, leads, brass, strings, pads, and drums, if you're clever. Volt isn't a Minimoog or a TB-303. But it works the way they do, so what you learn here will serve you on them, and on every subtractive synth you ever meet.

4.1 Find a sound you like

Volt comes with two factory banks: FAC A, the CLASSIC sounds, and FAC B, the ACID ones.

Try this

SOUNDS›2SOUND and go through FAC A, then 1BANK›FAC B and go through that. Play two or three notes on each, and try a few of them lower down with OCT-: Volt is a bass synth as much as a lead one. Write down the codes of the ones you like.

The first seven in FAC A are worth a closer look, because they're classic sounds people have been making on synths like this for fifty years: PROG LEAD, SINE LEAD, FUNK QUACK and DISCO BASS, then three that might surprise you: KICK DRUM, SYNTH TOM and SNARE DRUM. Drums, made with the same three oscillators and a filter as everything else. Once you've read this chapter, open them up and see how.

As you go through, look at the CLASSIC and ACID buttons, top and second in the right-hand column. Whichever the sound is, its button is lit.

4.2 How Volt is laid out

  • 1The left column is CLASSIC's controllers and sound sources, top to bottom: CONTROL, MOD, OSC 1, OSC 2, OSC 3 and MIXER, in the order the sound goes through them.
  • 2The middle column is what happens to the sound after that: FILTER, CONTOUR (the filter's own contour), LOUDNESS (the loudness contour), EXTRA, then SOUNDS.
  • 3The right column is CLASSIC and ACID, then SETUP at the bottom.

The readings on the screen are the classic ones, as a synth of this kind would mark its knobs: most knobs read 0 to 10, an oscillator's range is in feet (16', 8'...), waves are drawn as pictures, and times are in milliseconds and seconds.

Some controls have a little on/off switch that goes with them, and on Volt pushing the encoder works that switch. You'll see it as a small chip under the value, saying ON or OFF. On the MIXER page, for instance, each channel has a level and an on/off switch: turn to set the level, push to switch it on or off.

CLASSIC and ACID

On one of your own sounds, pressing CLASSIC or ACID switches the sound to that mode and shows its pages. A sound keeps both halves, a CLASSIC one and an ACID one, so switching back and forth never loses anything. ACID has two pages: press ACID again for the second, ACID 2.

Press a CLASSIC page's button while the sound is ACID (or the other way round) and Volt shows you that page for as long as you hold the button, with a note saying which mode the sound is in. Let go and you're back where you were. Nothing on it changes while you look.

Factory sounds work as on every unit: turn anything and you'll hear it change, the star in the top bar says so, and choosing the sound again puts it back (chapter 1, section 1.8).

4.3 The journey of a sound

Before you touch anything, here's the whole of CLASSIC in one picture. Once you've got this, every page makes sense.

  • 1Three oscillators make the raw sound: three waves, at pitches you choose. There's a noise source too.
  • 2The mixer decides how much of each goes on.
  • 3The filter takes away the top of the sound: as much or as little as you like, and its own contour can open and close it on every note.
  • 4The loudness contour shapes how loud each note is, from the moment the key goes down to the moment it's gone.

The rest of CLASSIC, the CONTROL and MOD pages, changes how those four behave while you play.

A sound to work on

Your own slots start as INIT SOUND, a plain, useful bass. It's a good sound, but it has all three oscillators on and the filter half closed, so to hear what each part does we'll strip it right down to one oscillator and an open filter first.

SOUNDS›1BANK›USER A›2SOUND›UA01

  • 1MIXER›push2 and push3: OSC 2 and OSC 3 switch off, so only OSC 1 is left.
  • 2FILTER›1CUTOFF›+5.0, 2EMPHASIS›0.0 and 3AMOUNT›0.0: the filter wide open, doing nothing.
  • 3LOUDNESS›3SUSTAIN›10.0: the note stays at full loudness while you hold it.

Play it. That's one sawtooth, raw: bright, buzzy and rather rude. Name it ONE OSC on the SOUNDS page (4NAME: turn for the letter, push for the next one).

The sounds you'll build

This chapter builds ten sounds of your own, one in each section, each in its own slot of USER A. Every one starts as a copy of something you've already made, mostly ONE OSC, so you're never more than a few steps from a sound that works. When a section says "start from a copy of ONE OSC in UA04", that means:

SOUNDS›2SOUND›UA01›3COPY TO›UA04›hold3

Copying moves you onto the copy, so you're ready to work. By the end of the chapter, USER A will hold:

SlotSoundSectionWhat it shows
UA01ONE OSC4.3one raw oscillator, the place to start
UA02THREE SAWS4.4three oscillators a touch apart, and the mixer's growl
UA03WHISTLE4.6the filter playing on its own
UA04PLUCK BASS4.7the filter contour snapping open
UA05BRASS4.7a slow filter contour: the "bwah"
UA06WOBBLE4.8oscillator 3 moving the filter
UA07SOLO LEAD4.9glide, vibrato and a ringing release
UA08KICK4.11a drum from a whistling filter
UA09SNARE4.11a drum from noise
UA10MY ACID4.12the squelch

If you ever lose your way in this chapter, go back to ONE OSC.

Reading the times

Volt's ATTACK and DECAY boxes show a time, not a number: 2 MS, 200 MS, 1.0 S. The recipes in this chapter give them the same way, so turn until the screen says what the recipe says. Each click is a small step, and the steps get bigger as the times get longer, as on the dials of the synths Volt follows.

4.4 The oscillators

OSC 1 RANGE and WAVE    OSC 2 and OSC 3 RANGE, FREQ and WAVE

  • RANGE encoder 1, LO, 32', 16', 8', 4', 2' the octave, in feet, as organ stops are named: 8' is the note you play, 16' an octave below, 4' an octave above. The bigger the number, the lower the note. LO is far below hearing as a note, and section 4.8 is about what it's for.
  • FREQ OSC 2 and OSC 3, encoder 2, -7.0 to +7.0 tunes the oscillator up or down by up to seven semitones, against OSC 1, which is the reference and has no FREQ of its own.
  • WAVE encoder 3 the shape of the wave, drawn on the screen: TRIANGLE, SHARKTOOTH, SAWTOOTH, SQUARE, WIDE and NARROW.
  • OSC 3 CTL OSC 3, encoder 4, ON or OFF whether oscillator 3 follows the keys (ON), or stays at one pitch whatever you play (OFF). Section 4.8.

The whole instrument can be tuned too: CONTROL›1TUNE, up to two and a half semitones either way.

The six waves

On ONE OSC, hold a note and step OSC 1›3WAVE through all six.

TRIANGLE is the soft one: few harmonics, flute-like. SHARKTOOTH is half triangle, half sawtooth, a little brighter. SAWTOOTH has every harmonic there is, which is why it's the one you'll start from most: the brightest and buzziest, the raw material for brass and strings and most basses. SQUARE has every other harmonic, which gives it that hollow, woody sound. WIDE and NARROW are squares that spend longer up than down; the narrower, the thinner and more nasal, down to a reedy buzz.

Put it back on SAWTOOTH before you go on: the next sound starts from ONE OSC as it was.

More than one oscillator

Now the best thing about three oscillators: playing them together. This is the second sound of your own.

Build THREE SAWS

Start from a copy of ONE OSC in UA02. First, bring OSC 1 up to the note you play: OSC 1›1RANGE›8'.

Now switch OSC 2 on, at the same pitch: MIXER›push2, then OSC 2›1RANGE›8' and 3WAVE›SAWTOOTH. Set its FREQ to 2FREQ›+0.0 for a moment. Play a long note: two sawtooths in perfect step just sound like one louder one.

Now turn FREQ up a single click, to +0.1, and play a long note again. Wait.

The sound starts to move: it swirls, or beats slowly, as the two oscillators drift in and out of step. The further apart, the faster the beating; too far and it just sounds out of tune. That slow swirl is the sound of two oscillators slightly apart, and it's in nearly every big analogue sound you've ever heard. Volt's oscillators also wander a few cents on their own, as analogue oscillators always do (DRIFT on the EXTRA page, section 4.10), so even exactly in tune they're never quite still.

THREE SAWS, the third saw

Switch OSC 3 on (MIXER›push3), then OSC 3›1RANGE›8', 3WAVE›SAWTOOTH and 2FREQ›-0.1: a click below the note, where OSC 2 is a click above. Now one oscillator sits in tune and the other two lean either side of it.

Last, the mixer: MIXER and set all three levels to 7.0. (Why 7 and not 10 is the next section.)

THREE SAWS

ONE OSC, plus:

OSC 1RANGE 8'WAVE SAWTOOTH
OSC 2RANGE 8'FREQ +0.1WAVE SAWTOOTH
OSC 3RANGE 8'FREQ -0.1WAVE SAWTOOTH
MIXEROSC 1 7.0 ONOSC 2 7.0 ONOSC 3 7.0 ON

Play a chord's worth of notes one after another, low down and high up. It's big and bright and alive, and still completely raw: the filter is wide open. Name it THREE SAWS.

Two other tricks while you're here. OSC 2's FREQ at +7.0 puts it a fifth above: a chord on every key, an old trick for leads and stabs. And an oscillator's RANGE an octave below the others gives a bass a floor to stand on. INIT SOUND uses that one: two sawtooths a touch apart, and a square an octave below.

4.5 The mixer

MIXER OSC 1, OSC 2, OSC 3 and NOISE

Four levels, 0 to 10, one for each oscillator and one for noise, each with its own switch on the encoder's push. Noise is the hiss of chapter 2: every pitch at once, so no pitch at all. Mix a little in for breath, or use it on its own for wind, waves and the snares of drums (section 4.11 makes one). EXTRA›2NOISE chooses its colour: WHITE, the bright hiss, or PINK, darker and softer.

The mixer is part of the sound

On classic analogue synths, turning the mixer up too far overloads the filter after it, and the sound gets thicker and growlier. Players soon found it out, and it's a big part of why those synths sound the way they do. Volt does the same: past about 5, it growls. So the mixer isn't only a balance: 10 on all three oscillators is a growl, 4 is clean, and you choose.

Hear the growl

On THREE SAWS, hold a low note and turn all three mixer levels from 7.0 up to 10.0 one after another, then down to 4.0. It gets a bit louder as you go up, but listen past the loudness: at 10 the sound is thicker and rougher, at 4 it's smooth and polite. Neither is right. Leave it at 7.0, and remember that the mixer is the first place to make a sound fatter.

4.6 The filter

Here's where the sound gets its character. Chapter 2 (section 2.2) said a filter takes harmonics away. This one is a low-pass filter: it lets the low part of the sound through and cuts the high part, and it cuts steeply, which is why it sounds so smooth.

FILTER CUTOFF, EMPHASIS, AMOUNT and KEYBOARD

  • CUTOFF encoder 1, -5.0 to +5.0 where the filter starts to cut. +5 is wide open, and the sound comes through as the mixer made it. Turn it down and the top goes, then the middle, until at -5 there's hardly anything left.
  • EMPHASIS encoder 2, 0-10 the filter's resonance: it makes the filter ring at the cutoff, so the harmonics right there stand out. A little gives an edge; a lot thins out the bass and gives that vowel-like "wow". From about 7, the filter starts to whistle at its own pitch.
  • AMOUNT encoder 3, 0-10 how far the filter's contour opens the filter on each note. Section 4.7.
  • KEYBOARD encoder 4, OFF, 1, 2, 1+2 how much the cutoff follows the keys. OFF, it stays put, so high notes come out duller than low ones; 1 follows a third of the way, 2 two thirds, 1+2 all the way, so every note is equally bright.

Try this

On THREE SAWS, hold a low note and turn CUTOFF slowly down from +5 to -5 and back. That one control is most of what subtractive synthesis is. Listen to how the three saws' swirl stays, even as the brightness goes: the filter takes away harmonics, not movement.

Now set CUTOFF to about 0 and turn EMPHASIS up slowly while you sweep CUTOFF again. Around 4 or 5 the sweep turns into a "wow". Past 7, you'll hear the whistle come in on top of the note.

Put CUTOFF back to +5.0 and EMPHASIS to 0.0 afterwards: the next sounds start from THREE SAWS as it was.

A sound with no oscillators

That whistle is the filter ringing on its own, and it doesn't need the oscillators at all. Players have used it for fifty years, for eerie, pure leads like a theremin's or a singing saw's.

Build WHISTLE

Start from a copy of ONE OSC in UA03.

  • 1MIXER›push1 until OSC 1 says OFF. Now nothing at all goes into the filter. Play a note: silence.
  • 2FILTER›2EMPHASIS›10.0. Play a note: a pure, high tone, from nothing. That's the filter.
  • 3It plays the same note whatever key you press, because the filter doesn't know about the keys. 4KEYBOARD›1+2, and it follows them all the way: now you can play a tune on it. 1CUTOFF moves the whole thing up or down; put it at 0.0.
  • 4To make it sing: LOUDNESS›1ATTACK›200 MS, so each note fades in a little, and CONTROL›push2 to switch GLIDE on, with 2GLIDE›4.0, so it slides from note to note. Play joined-up notes, each key down before you let go of the last.
  • 5It's a quiet sound, so CONTROL›4VOLUME›10.0.

WHISTLE

ONE OSC, plus:

MIXEROSC 1 OFF
FILTERCUTOFF +0.0EMPHASIS 10.0KEYBOARD 1+2
LOUDNESSATTACK 200 MS
CONTROLGLIDE 4.0 ONVOLUME 10.0

Name it WHISTLE. A sound made of nothing but a filter, ringing.

4.7 The two contours

Chapter 2 (section 2.3) called the shape of a note its envelope, and drew it with attack, decay, sustain and release. Synths of this kind often call their envelopes contours, and have two of them: one for loudness, and one for the filter. Volt has both.

LOUDNESS ATTACK, DECAY and SUSTAIN    CONTOUR the same, for the filter

  • ATTACK encoder 1, 2 MS to 14 S how long the note takes to get to the top.
  • DECAY encoder 2, 2 MS to 14 S how long it then takes to fall to the sustain level.
  • SUSTAIN encoder 3, 0-10 the level it holds while your finger stays down.

Where's the release?

There's no RELEASE knob. Volt has a switch instead, the classic way: CONTROL›3DECAY, ON or OFF.

  • ·ON: when you let go, the note dies away at the speed DECAY says.
  • ·OFF: when you let go, the note stops.

It works on both contours at once. It's a quirk, and it's kept, because it's how the instrument behaves: a long DECAY with the switch ON gives a sound that rings on after you let go, which is lovely for leads and a nuisance for tight basses, so flip it OFF for those.

The loudness contour

Four shapes

On ONE OSC, try these on the LOUDNESS page, with CONTROL's DECAY switch ON. Hold each note a second or two, then let go.

Organ

On at once, full while held, gone when you let go (almost: DECAY is short).

ATTACK 2 MSDECAY 10 MSSUSTAIN 10.0

Piano-ish

Struck, and dying away whether you hold it or not.

ATTACK 2 MSDECAY 775 MSSUSTAIN 0.0

Bowed

Swells in, holds, and fades when you let go.

ATTACK 775 MSDECAY 600 MSSUSTAIN 10.0

Pluck

Short and snappy.

ATTACK 2 MSDECAY 346 MSSUSTAIN 0.0

Then try the piano-ish one with the DECAY switch OFF, and play short notes: each one stops dead when you let go. Put LOUDNESS back to ATTACK 2 MS, DECAY 775 MS, SUSTAIN 10.0 when you're done, and the switch ON.

The filter contour

Now the part that makes analogue synths sound alive. CONTOUR is the same shape, but it moves the filter: on every note, it opens the filter from wherever CUTOFF has it, up by as much as AMOUNT says, and closes it again. Bright at the start, darker as it goes: chapter 2's "brightness over time".

Build PLUCK BASS

Start from a copy of ONE OSC in UA04. It's a bass, so play it low: press OCT- once (that only moves the keys, it isn't part of the sound). Then set:

PLUCK BASS

ONE OSC, plus:

FILTERCUTOFF -3.0EMPHASIS 3.0AMOUNT 7.0
CONTOURATTACK 2 MSDECAY 346 MSSUSTAIN 0.0
LOUDNESSATTACK 2 MSDECAY 775 MSSUSTAIN 0.0
CONTROLVOLUME 10.0

Play a bass line, short notes. Every note snaps open and closes down: a plucked, rubbery bass. Name it PLUCK BASS.

Now change one thing at a time, and put it back each time. AMOUNT up to 10: a bigger snap. CONTOUR's DECAY longer, to 600 MS: a slower "yow". EMPHASIS up to 6.0: the snap gets a squelch. CUTOFF up to 0.0: brighter all the way through, so the snap matters less. That last one is worth noticing: CUTOFF and AMOUNT work together, one setting where the filter rests and the other how far each note opens it.

A slow filter: brass

PLUCK BASS opens its filter at once and lets it fall. Turn that round, so the filter opens slowly at the start of each note, and you get the sound synths have been using for brass since the 1970s: the "bwah" of a horn section, the note getting brighter as it's blown.

Build BRASS

This one starts from THREE SAWS, because brass wants the thickness of three oscillators:

SOUNDS›2SOUND›UA02›3COPY TO›UA05›hold3

  • 1Close the filter most of the way, and give its contour plenty to do: FILTER›1CUTOFF›-2.0, 2EMPHASIS›1.0, 3AMOUNT›6.0.
  • 2The slow opening: CONTOUR›1ATTACK›200 MS, 2DECAY›600 MS, 3SUSTAIN›6.0. Each note now climbs to full brightness over a fifth of a second, falls back a little, and holds there.
  • 3The loudness follows a little behind: LOUDNESS›1ATTACK›10 MS, 2DECAY›600 MS, 3SUSTAIN›9.0.

BRASS

THREE SAWS, plus:

FILTERCUTOFF -2.0EMPHASIS 1.0AMOUNT 6.0
CONTOURATTACK 200 MSDECAY 600 MSSUSTAIN 6.0
LOUDNESSATTACK 10 MSDECAY 600 MSSUSTAIN 9.0

Play slow, held notes, and listen to the start of each: "bwah". Name it BRASS. Then try CONTOUR's ATTACK at 600 MS: a slower, softer blow, more like a swelling string section. And notice that because the DECAY switch is ON, every note dies away in 600 MS when you let go, as a horn's does.

Two contours, two jobs

LOUDNESS shapes how loud the note is. CONTOUR shapes how bright it is. PLUCK BASS and BRASS are almost the same sound with the filter contour turned round: fast-then-falling for a pluck, slow-then-holding for a horn. Most of the classic sounds are one of those two shapes, or the swell.

4.8 Oscillator 3 as a modulator

Chapter 2 (section 2.4) said movement in a sound usually comes from an LFO, an oscillator too slow to hear. Volt has no LFO. It has something cleverer: oscillator 3 can stop being a sound and become the thing that moves the other two.

  • 1OSC 3›1RANGE›LO: so slow it's no longer a note.
  • 24OSC 3 CTL›OFF: it stops following the keys, so the wobble is the same speed on every note.
  • 3MIXER›push3 until OSC 3 is OFF: you don't want to hear it, only use it.

Then the MOD page decides where it goes and how much:

MOD MOD MIX, OSC MOD, FILT MOD and WHEEL

  • MOD MIX encoder 1, 0-10 what does the moving: at 0, oscillator 3; at 10, noise; in between, some of each. Noise makes the movement random.
  • OSC MOD encoder 2, ON or OFF on: it moves the pitch of oscillators 1 and 2. That's vibrato.
  • FILT MOD encoder 3, ON or OFF on: it moves the filter's cutoff. That's a wah, or a wobble.
  • WHEEL encoder 4, 0-10 how much. On a synth like this it's usually the modulation wheel beside the keys; here it's an encoder, and a MIDI keyboard's mod wheel moves it too (section 4.14).

Build WOBBLE

Start from a copy of ONE OSC in UA06, and set oscillator 3 up as above, with OSC 3›3WAVE›TRIANGLE.

First, vibrato: MOD›2OSC MOD›ON and 4WHEEL›1.5. Hold a note: the pitch wavers. OSC 3›2FREQ sets how fast. That's one use; but this sound is going to be the other.

Turn OSC MOD OFF and 3FILT MOD›ON. Close the filter so it has room to move: FILTER›1CUTOFF›-1.0 and 2EMPHASIS›5.0. Now MOD›4WHEEL›5.0. The tone goes round and round: a wobble.

WOBBLE

ONE OSC, plus:

OSC 3RANGE LOWAVE TRIANGLEOSC 3 CTL OFF
MODFILT MOD ONWHEEL 5.0
FILTERCUTOFF -1.0EMPHASIS 5.0

Name it WOBBLE. Then play with it: OSC 3's WAVE on SQUARE and the wobble jumps between two places instead; on SAWTOOTH it sweeps up and drops; MOD MIX up to 10 and it goes random, like a sample-and-hold. OSC 3's FREQ up and down: from a slow sweep to a fast flutter.

Oscillator 3 doesn't have to be slow, either. Put it back in the audio range, OSC 3 CTL ON, and OSC MOD makes it modulate the other two at an audible pitch: the clangs and bells of chapter 3, Glass's own trick, done the analogue way.

4.9 Playing it

Volt plays one note at a time, and the way it does it is part of the sound.

  • The lowest key wins. Hold two keys in CLASSIC and you hear the lower one. So hold a high note and tap lower ones below it: each tap sounds while you hold it, and the high note comes back when you let go, an old trick for trills. (ACID is the other way round: the last key you pressed wins.)
  • Joined-up notes don't start again. Play a new key before letting go of the last, and the pitch changes but the contours carry on where they were, so there's no new snap of the filter. Play them separately and every note snaps. How you join your notes is part of the playing.
  • Glide. CONTROL›push2 switches glide on, and 2GLIDE sets how long the pitch takes to slide from one note to the next.
  • VOLUME CONTROL, encoder 4, 0-10 the sound's own level. Use it to make your sounds sit together: a bass and a lead that should be equally loud.

As classic synths of its kind did, CLASSIC plays every note at the same loudness, however hard you hit a MIDI keyboard. If you'd rather it followed how hard you play, turn VELO on in SETUP (section 4.14).

Build SOLO LEAD

Everything so far, in one lead line. Start from a copy of THREE SAWS in UA07 (SOUNDS›2SOUND›UA02›3COPY TO›UA07›hold3).

  • 1Oscillator 3 becomes the vibrato, as in WOBBLE: OSC 3›1RANGE›LO, 3WAVE›TRIANGLE, 4OSC 3 CTL›OFF, and MIXER›push3 to OFF. Then MOD›2OSC MOD›ON and 4WHEEL›1.5: a gentle waver.
  • 2A little edge from the filter: FILTER›1CUTOFF›+1.0, 2EMPHASIS›2.0, 3AMOUNT›3.0.
  • 3Glide: CONTROL›push2 to ON, and 2GLIDE›3.0.
  • 4A ringing release: LOUDNESS›2DECAY›600 MS, with CONTROL's DECAY switch ON.

SOLO LEAD

THREE SAWS, plus:

OSC 3RANGE LOWAVE TRIANGLEOSC 3 CTL OFF
MIXEROSC 3 OFF
MODOSC MOD ONWHEEL 1.5
FILTERCUTOFF +1.0EMPHASIS 2.0AMOUNT 3.0
CONTROLGLIDE 3.0 ONDECAY ON
LOUDNESSDECAY 600 MS

Name it SOLO LEAD. Now play it properly: a slow tune, high up (OCT+), some notes joined, some apart. Joined, the pitch glides and the filter doesn't snap; apart, each note starts fresh. Hold a high note and tap a lower one underneath for a trill. Let a last note go and hear it ring. That's how a lead line on a synth like this is played: the hands do half the work.

4.10 The EXTRA page

EXTRA EXTERNAL, NOISE and DRIFT

  • EXTERNAL encoder 1, 0-10, push ON or OFF classic synths of this kind had a mixer input for an outside sound. Players discovered that plugging a synth's own output back into it overloaded the filter even harder, for a fatter, dirtier sound, and it became a famous trick. EXTERNAL is that trick: Volt's output fed back into its own mixer, as much as you like.
  • NOISE encoder 2, WHITE or PINK the noise colour (section 4.5).
  • DRIFT encoder 3, ON or OFF on: each oscillator wanders slowly in pitch by a few cents, as analogue oscillators always do. It's what keeps a held chord of oscillators from sounding frozen. Off for a sound that must be dead still.

Try this

On BRASS, push EXTRA›push1 to switch EXTERNAL on, and turn it up slowly while you hold a low note. Somewhere past 5 the brass turns into something much nastier. Back to OFF afterwards, unless you like it: plenty of people do.

4.11 Drums from three oscillators

Section 4.1 pointed at three factory sounds that might have surprised you: KICK DRUM, SYNTH TOM and SNARE DRUM. Long before drum machines, people made drum sounds on synths like this one, and the tricks are all things you've now done: a whistling filter, a burst of noise, and very short contours. Build them yourself, and you'll understand drum machines too (Strike's chapter takes it further).

A kick drum

A kick drum is a low thump that drops in pitch as it dies. WHISTLE was a filter ringing on its own; a kick is a filter ringing very low, pinged by a short, sharp contour.

Build KICK

Start from a copy of ONE OSC in UA08.

  • 1A soft, low oscillator to give the thump some body: OSC 1›1RANGE›32' and 3WAVE›TRIANGLE, and MIXER›1OSC 1›7.0.
  • 2The filter ringing low, the same pitch on every key: FILTER›1CUTOFF›-3.5, 2EMPHASIS›10.0, 4KEYBOARD›OFF.
  • 3The ping: 3AMOUNT›6.0, and CONTOUR›2DECAY›45 MS with 3SUSTAIN›0.0. On every note the filter jumps up and falls straight back, and its whistle falls with it: that's the drop in pitch.
  • 4Short: LOUDNESS›2DECAY›263 MS and 3SUSTAIN›0.0. And loud: CONTROL›4VOLUME›10.0.

KICK

ONE OSC, plus:

OSC 1RANGE 32'WAVE TRIANGLE
MIXEROSC 1 7.0 ON
FILTERCUTOFF -3.5EMPHASIS 10.0AMOUNT 6.0KEYBOARD OFF
CONTOURDECAY 45 MSSUSTAIN 0.0
LOUDNESSDECAY 263 MSSUSTAIN 0.0
CONTROLVOLUME 10.0

Play short notes: thump, thump. Name it KICK. Now tune it: CUTOFF higher and it's a tom; up to about +0.0 and KEYBOARD to 1+2, and you've got a tom you can play tunes on, which is what the factory's SYNTH TOM is. CONTOUR's DECAY longer for a boomier kick with a longer drop; LOUDNESS's DECAY longer for a boom that hangs on.

A snare drum

A snare is two things at once: the drum's skin, a short tone, and the snares underneath it, a burst of rattle. On a synth, the rattle is noise.

Build SNARE

Start from a copy of ONE OSC in UA09.

  • 1The skin, quietly: OSC 1›1RANGE›8', 3WAVE›TRIANGLE, and MIXER›1OSC 1›3.0.
  • 2The snares: MIXER›4NOISE›10.0 and push it to ON.
  • 3A filter that snaps shut on the noise: FILTER›1CUTOFF›+1.0, 2EMPHASIS›1.0, 3AMOUNT›5.0, 4KEYBOARD›OFF; CONTOUR›2DECAY›45 MS, 3SUSTAIN›0.0.
  • 4Short and loud: LOUDNESS›2DECAY›200 MS, 3SUSTAIN›0.0, CONTROL›4VOLUME›10.0.

SNARE

ONE OSC, plus:

OSC 1RANGE 8'WAVE TRIANGLE
MIXEROSC 1 3.0 ONNOISE 10.0 ON
FILTERCUTOFF +1.0EMPHASIS 1.0AMOUNT 5.0KEYBOARD OFF
CONTOURDECAY 45 MSSUSTAIN 0.0
LOUDNESSDECAY 200 MSSUSTAIN 0.0
CONTROLVOLUME 10.0

Name it SNARE. Try the noise PINK (EXTRA›2NOISE) for a softer, darker snare; OSC 1's level up for more ring; LOUDNESS's DECAY at 10 MS and the noise alone for a hi-hat's tick.

Play KICK and SNARE in turn, on the beat and the off-beat, and you've got the start of a drum part, from a bass synth. Now open the factory's KICK DRUM and SNARE DRUM: you'll find you can read every setting.

4.12 ACID

Now the other instrument: one oscillator, a filter that squelches, and two ingredients hidden in the notes, accent and slide. The sound was made famous by producers turning the knobs while a pattern played, and that's still how it's done.

Every sound of your own has an ACID half waiting, so start from a copy of ONE OSC in UA10 and press ACID. The CLASSIC button goes out, ACID lights, and the sound is now an ACID sound. Its ACID half has never been touched, so it starts from INIT SOUND's: a perfectly good acid bass to start from.

ACID TUNING, CUTOFF, RESONANCE and ENV MOD    ACIDACID 2 DECAY, ACCENT, WAVEFORM and VOLUME

  • TUNING ACID, encoder 1 the pitch, fine.
  • CUTOFF ACID, encoder 2, 0-10 where the filter sits.
  • RESONANCE ACID, encoder 3, 0-10 how much it rings: the squelch.
  • ENV MOD ACID, encoder 4, 0-10 how far each note sweeps the filter open. Turning it up also lowers where the filter rests, so the sweep gets wider at both ends.
  • DECAY ACID 2, encoder 1, 0-10 how long that sweep takes to close.
  • ACCENT ACID 2, encoder 2, 0-10 how much harder accented notes hit.
  • WAVEFORM ACID 2, encoder 3, SAW or SQUARE the only choice of wave. The square is made from the saw, so it isn't quite a perfect square, and that's part of its sound.
  • VOLUME ACID 2, encoder 4, 0-10 the sound's level.

Notice what isn't there: no attack, no sustain, no loudness contour. On ACID the loudness of a note is fixed: it comes in, holds while the key's down, and stops. DECAY only shapes the filter. Everything you do to an ACID sound, you do with four knobs: CUTOFF, RESONANCE, ENV MOD and DECAY.

Build MY ACID

Play a run of short notes, low down, all the way through this: the squelch is in the movement.

  • 1ACID›3RESONANCE›8.0. The filter starts to ring on every note: the squelch arrives.
  • 22CUTOFF›2.5 and 4ENV MOD›7.0: the filter rests lower and jumps further, so each note goes "yow".
  • 3ACID 2›1DECAY›4.0: a little tighter, so fast lines stay clear.
  • 44VOLUME›8.0.

MY ACID

ONE OSC's ACID half, with:

ACIDCUTOFF 2.5RESONANCE 8.0ENV MOD 7.0
ACID 2DECAY 4.0WAVEFORM SAWVOLUME 8.0

Name it MY ACID. Now turn the four, one at a time, while you play: CUTOFF and ENV MOD against each other, the filter's resting place and how far it jumps. RESONANCE up and down: more or less squelch. DECAY down to 1.0 for short, tight blips; up to 8.0 for long, slow "yowww"s. Turning these while a pattern plays is how acid house was made, and nobody has ever needed more.

Then the other wave: ACID 2›3WAVEFORM›SQUARE, CUTOFF down to 1.5, RESONANCE to 3.0, ENV MOD to 3.0, DECAY to 6.0. A deep, hollow, rubbery bass, from the same four knobs. Same instrument, nothing like the squelch.

And a reminder of the trick from section 4.2: press CLASSIC on MY ACID and it's ONE OSC again, unchanged; press ACID and it's your acid sound. Each slot keeps both.

Accent and slide

ACID's two secret ingredients don't live on knobs: they're in the notes. Any note can be accented or slid.

  • ·Accent: an accented note is louder, with a sharper, shorter sweep, and a run of accents builds up, each one squelchier than the last (how much, RESONANCE decides). ACCENT sets how strong it is.
  • ·Slide: a slid note glides from the one before, quickly, without starting again: a sliding, rubbery line.

Volt's own keys play every note unaccented. Accents come from a MIDI keyboard played hard (velocity 100 or more) or from Step, the sequencer, which can mark any note ACCENT or SLIDE. Slide comes from joined-up playing: press the next key before letting go of the last, on Volt's keys or a MIDI keyboard.

Try this

On MY ACID, play a line of short notes, then the same line again with every second note joined to the one before it (the next key down before you let go). The joined ones slide: that rubbery "bwoop" between notes is half of acid's sound, and you've just played it with your fingers.

ACID wants a sequencer

You can play ACID from the keys, and it's a fine bass. But the sound everyone knows comes from a pattern of notes, accents and slides going round and round while you turn the knobs. That's what Step is for, and the Music Production manual starts with exactly that.

4.13 Effects

Volt has no effects of its own; nor did classic synths of either kind. With Haze joined on, though, Volt gets chorus, echo and reverb, and one more thing that belongs to it more than to anything: distortion. Acid bass lines were very often driven hard into a distortion pedal, and Haze's ACID DRIVE preset is that. On its own with one unit, Volt's nearest thing is its own mixer overload (section 4.5) and EXTERNAL (section 4.10).

4.14 Volt's SETUP

SETUP's THIS UNIT page has Volt's own settings, beside the MIDI channel:

  • BEND encoder 2, 0-12 how far a MIDI keyboard's pitch bend wheel bends the note, in semitones. Two is usual.
  • WHEEL encoder 3 what moves the WHEEL encoder on the MOD page: a MIDI keyboard's MOD WHEEL, BREATH, EXPRESSION (a pedal), AFTERTOUCH, or OFF, so only the encoder moves it.
  • VELO encoder 4, OFF or ON OFF, the classic way: every CLASSIC note is equally loud. ON: CLASSIC's loudness follows how hard a MIDI keyboard or Step plays. (ACID always uses how hard you play, for its accents.)

What you have at the end of this chapter

Ten sounds of your own: ONE OSC, THREE SAWS, WHISTLE, PLUCK BASS, BRASS, WOBBLE, SOLO LEAD, KICK, SNARE and MY ACID. Between them they use every page on Volt, and they show the idea behind most of the synthesisers ever made: start with something bright, and take away what you don't want. Nearly every factory sound is one of yours with a few numbers changed; open some up and see if you can tell which.

Chapter 5 - Strike

Every drum is a tone, a hiss or a clang, and how quickly it dies.

Strike is a drum machine, and every drum in it is synthesised: there are no recordings inside it at all. Each kick, snare and cymbal is made the moment you hit it, from the same few things chapter 2 was about, a pitch, a tone, a shape. That means every drum can be retuned, lengthened, shortened and brightened, and it means you'll understand exactly what you're changing.

Drum synthesis: where it came from, and who uses it

The first drum machines were rhythm boxes for home organs: Wurlitzer's Sideman, in 1959, played a handful of fixed patterns, and for twenty years most of those that followed did the same, to keep a singer or an organist in time. Roland's CR-78 of 1978 was one of the first you could program with your own patterns, and its soft, ticking sounds are on Blondie's "Heart of Glass" and Phil Collins's "In the Air Tonight".

Then came the TR-808 (its story is in the introduction), and in 1983 the TR-909, whose punchy kick and snare were the backbone of Chicago house and Detroit techno, and still are. In Britain, Simmons built electronic drum kits played with sticks, and their pitch-bending toms are one of the sounds of 1980s pop. At much the same time, the first drum machines that played recordings of real drums arrived, and for a while synthesised drums looked old-fashioned. They came back, because a synthesised drum can be bent into any shape a recording can't.

Hip hop, electro, house, techno, trap, drum and bass, synth-pop: all of them were built on synthesised drums. Strike isn't any of the machines above. Its kits are our own, each with a character of its own. But a kick, a snare or a hi-hat is made the same way on all of them, and what you learn here works on any drum machine, or on any synth, when you want to make a drum from scratch.

5.1 Find a kit you like

The left-hand column is six kit buttons. Press one and that kit is ready on the keys:

  • BOOM a long, deep, booming kick, a snappy snare, handclaps, and hats and cymbal made of a metallic hiss. The sound of electro and hip hop, and of a great deal of pop since.
  • PUNCH a short, punchy kick with a click at the front, a fat snare, and bright, sizzling hats, crash and ride. House and techno.
  • SPARK small, bright and tight: a little kick, a crisp snare, two toms, hats and a cymbal. Lovely with acid bass lines.
  • VELVET soft, ticking, old-fashioned: a gentle kick and snare, bongos and conga, cowbell, claves, maracas, a tambourine, a güiro and a metallic beat. Early synth-pop, and anything lo-fi.
  • NEON electronic drums as a drummer played them in the 1980s: a kick, a snare and three toms, all with a pitch that bends (section 5.8). It has no hats or cymbals, on purpose.
  • TIMBER an acoustic-inspired kit: drums made by working out, roughly, how real drums, cymbals and shakers vibrate. It's still a synthesised kit, with an acoustic flavour, not the sound of a real drummer, and it's at its best when you want something a little less electronic.

Try this

Press each kit and play down the white keys, top to bottom. Then play a simple beat on each: KICK, then SNARE, then KICK, KICK, SNARE, with CL HAT between. You'll hear six completely different bands.

The keys

Strike's 16 white keys are the drums, and each key is the same kind of drum in every kit: the kick is always the top key, the snare always the third, and so on. So a beat played on one kit plays on any other. The black keys do nothing, and Strike has no OCT buttons, because its keys are drums, not notes. When you play a key, the screen shows that drum's name.

KeyDrumKeyDrum
1KICK9LO TOM
2PERC (a kit's extra drum)10MID TOM
3SNARE11HI TOM
4TAMB (tambourine)12CRASH
5RIM13RIDE
6CLAP14COWBELL
7CL HAT (closed hi-hat)15CLAVES
8OP HAT (open hi-hat)16MARACAS

A kit only has the drums it was made with, so some keys are silent in some kits, and the screen says NOT IN THIS KIT. A kit may also put a drum of its own on a key: VELVET's CLAP key is a güiro, for instance, and the screen gives it its own name.

For the sound of a real drum kit

Strike makes every drum by synthesis, so none of its kits is a real kit. For the genuine sound of real drums, recorded, you want Taste, the sampler, which plays recordings of real instruments.

Like a real hi-hat, the closed hat stops the open one: play OP HAT, then CL HAT straight after, and the open one is cut short.

5.2 What a drum is made of

Every drum in Strike is built from chapter 2's pieces. Once you know which, every setting makes sense.

  • ·A kick is a low tone, often close to a pure sine, that starts a little higher and falls quickly to its own pitch, and dies away. Sometimes there's a click at the very front, the beater hitting the drum. Pitch, and a very short shape.
  • ·A snare is two things at once: a short tone, the drum itself, and a burst of noise, the rattle of the metal wires under it. How much of each is most of the difference between snares.
  • ·Hi-hats and cymbals have no pitch you could sing. They're a clang of several square waves at odd, unrelated pitches, plus noise, with the low part filtered away. The closed hat dies at once; the open hat and the cymbals ring.
  • ·A clap is noise, in a few quick bursts, like several people not quite clapping together.
  • ·Toms, congas, bongos, cowbell and claves are tones that ring and die, each at its own pitch.

So when you change a drum, you'll nearly always be changing one of three things: its pitch (TUNE), how long it lasts (DECAY), or what it's made of (TONE, SNAPPY and their like). That's what sections 5.5 to 5.8 are about.

5.3 Looking inside a kit

Press EDIT, then play a key: the screen shows that drum's settings, up to four, one on each encoder, and the key's light stays on so you know which drum you're on. The top bar says which drum and which kit it came from. Play another key to look at another drum. Press EDIT again to go back to playing.

Each drum has only the settings that suit it, so the boxes differ from drum to drum and kit to kit. On BOOM the kick has LEVEL, TUNE, DECAY and TONE, the snare LEVEL, TUNE, TONE and SNAPPY, and the closed hat just LEVEL. SPARK and VELVET have only LEVEL on every drum: they were made that way, simple boxes with nothing to tweak, and their charm is in their sound as it is. An empty box means that drum hasn't got that setting.

On a factory kit EDIT works too, as every unit's factory sounds do: you hear the change, the star in the top bar says it isn't kept, and choosing the kit again puts it back. Copy it to one of your own kits to keep it. Holding a key to swap its drum (below) works only on your own kits.

5.4 A kit of your own

Your own kits live on the SOUNDS page, as every unit's sounds do (chapter 1, section 1.8): FAC A holds the six factory kits, and USER A has room for 32 of your own. Every one of your slots starts as INIT KIT, which is BOOM's drums.

The USER button, at the top of the middle column, always takes you back to the last of your own kits you played, so it works like a seventh kit button. To start from a different factory kit, choose it and copy it: for example PUNCH, then SOUNDS›3COPY TO›UA02›hold3.

In your own kit, EDIT does what you ask, and pushing an encoder puts that setting back to the factory's value. While a setting is away from the factory's, the screen shows the factory's under it.

The kits you'll build

This chapter builds four kits of your own, each for a different kind of music, and each one shows something new:

SlotKitSectionWhat it shows
UA01DEEP KIT5.5tuning: a long, deep kick for hip hop and trap
UA02TIGHT KIT5.6decay: short, tight drums for techno
UA03ELECTRO5.7 and 5.8swapping drums: NEON's drums with BOOM's hats and cymbal, and drums that bend
UA04MIXED KIT5.7 and 5.9a drum from five kits, then balancing a kit

How to change a drum, every time

Every recipe in this chapter works the same way: press EDIT, play the drum's key, and turn its encoders until the boxes say what the recipe says. The recipes list each drum by its key name, and its settings in encoder order. Press EDIT again when you're done, to go back to playing. A setting you don't see in a recipe stays as it is.

5.5 Tuning drums

Start on your first kit, and give it a name: SOUNDS›1BANK›USER A›2KIT›UA01, then 4NAME: DEEP KIT. Press SOUNDS again to close the page. It's INIT KIT, so it starts as BOOM.

A deep kick

Press EDIT, then the KICK key. Turn 3DECAY up to 80 and 2TUNE down to 30, and play: a long, deep boom that you'll feel more than hear, the kick that sits under hip hop and trap. It now rings for about a second and a half, three times as long as before. Bring 4TONE down to 20 to take the edge off the front, so it's all boom.

Bass players tune their notes to a kick like this one, so TUNE matters: play the kick and a bass note together, and turn TUNE until they agree.

The snare

Play the SNARE key. 4SNAPPY is the noise, the rattle of the wires: down to 10 for a dull, boxy drum, up to 90 for a crack. 3TONE changes the body of the drum under it. For DEEP KIT, tune it down a little to sit with the kick, and give it plenty of crack: TUNE 40, SNAPPY 75.

DEEP KIT

INIT KIT (BOOM's drums), with:

KICKLEVEL 90TUNE 30DECAY 80TONE 20
SNARETUNE 40SNAPPY 75
CLAPLEVEL 85

Play a slow beat: KICK, then CLAP and SNARE together, KICK, KICK, CLAP and SNARE. The clap layered on the snare is an old trick for a fatter backbeat.

While you're in DEEP KIT, try the toms: on BOOM's three tom keys, 4TYPE switches each between TOM and CONGA, the same circuit with two characters, and TUNE sets each one's pitch. Other kits' drums have different settings: PUNCH's kick has ATTACK instead of TONE, how much click there is at the front. TIMBER's kick has BEATER (how hard the beater is), and its snare SNARES: at 0, the wires are switched off, and you've got a deep, ringing drum.

Tune the kit, not just the drums

Drums have pitches, and they sound best when the pitches get on with each other and with the song. Tune the kick to the key of your bass line, the toms a pleasant step apart, and the whole kit sounds deliberate. It's the oldest trick of drummers with real drums, and it costs you nothing here.

5.6 How long a drum lasts

A drum is nearly all attack and decay: it starts at once and dies away, and how quickly it dies is most of its shape. Where a drum has DECAY, it's the most useful setting it has. DEEP KIT's kick showed the long end; techno lives at the short end, where every drum is out of the way before the next one arrives.

Build TIGHT KIT

This one starts from PUNCH, the punchy kit with the click at the front. Copy it into your second slot: PUNCH, then SOUNDS›3COPY TO›UA02›hold3, and name it TIGHT KIT.

  • 1The kick: EDIT, KICK, 3DECAY›25. It's over in under a fifth of a second now: a thump, not a boom. 4ATTACK›70 for more click, so it cuts through. 2TUNE›45.
  • 2The hats: CL HAT, 3DECAY›15: a short tick. OP HAT, 3DECAY›30: an open hat that closes quickly, so it doesn't wash over everything.
  • 3The snare: SNAPPY up to 80, for a sharp crack.

TIGHT KIT

PUNCH, with:

KICKTUNE 45DECAY 25ATTACK 70
SNARESNAPPY 80
CL HATDECAY 15
OP HATDECAY 30

Play four kicks to a bar, an open hat between each pair, and the snare on the second and fourth: a techno beat. Now play the same beat on PUNCH itself, then on DEEP KIT. Same notes, three different decays, three different kinds of music.

Try this

Back on DEEP KIT: an open hat with a short DECAY is half closed, with a long one it washes. Try OP HAT's DECAY at 15, then 70. And a cymbal with a short DECAY is a choke, a crash that's grabbed: CRASH's 3DECAY›15. Leave them where you like them best.

5.7 Swapping drums between kits

Here's the quickest way to make a kit nobody else has: take each drum from wherever you like. In one of your own kits, hold a key down for a moment, and the screen says where that drum comes from: SNARE FROM BOOM. Turn any encoder while you hold it, and the drum changes to that key's drum from another kit, or NONE, to silence the key. The kits come round in the order of their buttons, BOOM, PUNCH, SPARK, VELVET, NEON, TIMBER, then NONE, and a kit that hasn't got that drum is skipped.

A swapped drum arrives with its factory settings, and its own set of knobs. When you play a key in one of your kits, the screen says where it's from.

Build ELECTRO

NEON's drums are made for bending, and it has no hats or cymbals at all. BOOM has a fine metallic hi-hat and cymbal. Put them together, and you've got a kit for electro and 1980s pop that neither kit is on its own.

Go to your third slot, SOUNDS›2KIT›UA03, and name it ELECTRO. It starts as BOOM, so the hats and cymbal are already there.

  • 1Hold the KICK key and turn an encoder until the screen says KICK FROM NEON (four clicks on). Let go.
  • 2The same for SNARE, then LO TOM, MID TOM and HI TOM: each one FROM NEON.
  • 3Leave CL HAT, OP HAT and CRASH as they are: FROM BOOM.

Play a beat: NEON's kick and snare, BOOM's hats over them. Then the three toms in a quick roll, top to bottom. Two kits' worth of character in one.

Build MIXED KIT

Now take it further: a kit from five. In your fourth slot, UA04, named MIXED KIT: hold KICK and turn until it says FROM PUNCH. Hold SNARE: leave it FROM BOOM. Hold CL HAT and OP HAT: FROM TIMBER. Hold the three toms: FROM NEON. Hold COWBELL: FROM VELVET. Five kits, one band.

It won't sit together yet: some drums will be much louder than others. Section 5.9 fixes that.

5.8 Drums that bend

NEON's drums have one setting the others don't: 3BEND, how fast the pitch falls after the hit. A little, and the kick and toms get a natural thud. A lot, and they swoop down with that "pew" that every electronic drum kit of the 1980s had. Their settings are LEVEL, TUNE, BEND and DECAY.

ELECTRO, bending

On ELECTRO, press EDIT and play the MID TOM key. Turn 3BEND up to 90 and play it: "pew". Then 4DECAY up to 85, so you hear the whole swoop. Do the same to the LO TOM and HI TOM, and play the three in a quick roll.

ELECTRO

INIT KIT, with KICK, SNARE and the three toms FROM NEON, and:

LO TOMBEND 90DECAY 85
MID TOMBEND 90DECAY 85
HI TOMBEND 90DECAY 85
KICKBEND 80

The kick with a little more bend gets a deeper thud. Now try the opposite: BEND all the way down to 0 on a tom, and it's a plain, steady tone, nothing like a drum. The fall in pitch is what makes it sound hit.

5.9 Loudness and accents

Every drum has LEVEL, on encoder 1, 0 to 99, and getting the levels right is what turns a pile of drums into a kit. A good rule to start from: the kick and snare loudest, the hats well under them, everything else somewhere between.

MIXED KIT, balanced

On MIXED KIT, press EDIT and play a beat you know with one hand while you set each drum's 1LEVEL with the other. Start here, then trust your ears:

MIXED KIT

The drums of section 5.7, with:

KICKLEVEL 90
SNARELEVEL 80
CL HATLEVEL 50
OP HATLEVEL 50
TOMSLEVEL 70
COWBELLLEVEL 45

Then tune it, as in section 5.5: the toms a step apart, the cowbell somewhere that doesn't fight the kick. The kit becomes one band rather than five.

Strike's own keys play every hit at the same strength. From a MIDI keyboard, or pads that sense how hard you hit them, harder is louder. From Step, any step can be marked ACCENT, and an accented hit is louder by as much as SETUP says:

  • ACCENT SETUP, THIS UNIT, OFF or +1 to +10 dB how much louder an accented step is: +6 to start with. Accents are what make a programmed beat feel played.

5.10 Effects

Strike has no effects of its own. With Haze joined on, though, a drum kit is transformed by a room: a little plate reverb behind the snare, an echo on a rim shot, and Haze's PUMP can make one of your synths duck in time with Strike's kick, the breathing sound of so much dance music.

5.11 Playing Strike from Step or a keyboard

Strike takes MIDI channel 10 automatically, the channel drums have always used, so it's usually STRIKE 10. Notes arrive by the General MIDI drum map that almost every keyboard, computer and drum pad follows: C2 (note 36) is the kick, D2 the snare, F#2 the closed hat and so on, whatever kit you're on. So a beat programmed for any General MIDI drum kit plays on Strike as it is.

With Step, the sequencer, you play the drums on Strike's own keys while Step's ENTRY page is open, and Step writes them in. That's the Music Production manual's job, and its first chapter starts there.

What you have at the end of this chapter

Four kits of your own: DEEP KIT for hip hop and trap, TIGHT KIT for techno, ELECTRO for the 1980s, and MIXED KIT from five kits, tuned and balanced. And the three questions to ask of any drum: what's its pitch, how long does it last, and what's it made of?

Chapter 6 - Ember

Six voices, one filter each, and a chorus that makes them sing.

Ember plays chords. That's what sets it apart: Volt and Strike play one sound at a time, Glass plays many but builds each one from sine waves. Ember is a polyphonic synthesiser, a polysynth: up to six notes at once, each with its own oscillator, filter and envelope, all following the same settings. Press three keys and you've got three complete synthesisers playing together.

It works the subtractive way: start with a wave that's bright and full of harmonics, take away what you don't want with a filter, and shape it with an envelope. If you've read Volt's chapter you'll know the idea; this chapter teaches it again from the start, Ember's way, so it works on its own.

Polysynths: where they came from, and who uses them

The first synthesisers played one note at a time. Playing chords meant a synthesiser for every note, and early polyphonic instruments were huge and expensive: Yamaha's CS-80 of 1977, the instrument behind Vangelis's Blade Runner, weighed about as much as a person. In 1978 Sequential's Prophet-5 brought five voices and, for the first time, a memory that kept every setting of a sound, so a player could build a sound once and call it back on stage.

In the early 1980s Roland's Juno-6, Juno-60 and then the Juno-106 (1984) made polysynths cheap: one oscillator per voice, digitally controlled so it stayed in tune, and a built-in chorus that made even a plain sound wide and warm. They sold in their thousands, and second-hand they became one of the sounds of house music, as well as of countless pop records. Lush pads, glassy strings, fat brass stabs, rubbery basses: the polysynth's whole vocabulary.

Ember isn't any of those instruments. But it's a six-voice polysynth of that early-1980s kind, and it works the way they do, so what you learn here will serve you on any of them, and on any synthesiser with a filter and an envelope.

6.1 Find a sound you like

Ember has one factory bank, FAC A: 32 sounds, from pads and strings to basses, organs and stabs.

Try this

SOUNDS›2SOUND and go through all 32. This time, play chords: three or four keys at once, and hold them. Ember is made for it. Write down the codes of the ones you like.

Listen out for FA26, SHIMMER, and FA02, STRINGS: both lean on the chorus, which is section 6.8.

6.2 How Ember is laid out

  • 1The left column is the sound's path, top to bottom, in the order the sound goes through it: LFO, DCO (the oscillator), WAVES, VCF (the filter), VCF MOD (what moves the filter) and ENV (the envelope).
  • 2The middle column has VCA, the loudness, at the top and SOUNDS at the bottom.
  • 3The right column has the two CHORUS buttons, then SETUP.

Most settings read 0 to 10, like the sliders on a synthesiser of this kind; a few are switches, ON or OFF, or a short list of choices. Every setting has its own encoder: turn it.

6.3 The journey of a sound

Each of Ember's six voices makes its sound the same way:

  • 1The oscillator makes the raw waves: a pulse, a sawtooth, a sub-oscillator an octave lower, and noise. WAVES mixes them.
  • 2The filter takes away the top of the sound.
  • 3The VCA sets how loud it is.
  • 4One envelope shapes both: it opens and closes the filter, and it shapes the loudness.

Then all six voices are added together and go through two more things they share: a high-pass filter, which can thin out the bass, and the chorus.

A sound to work on

Your own slots start as INIT SOUND, and on Ember that's already the plainest sound there is: one sawtooth, the filter wide open, full loudness while the key is down. A perfect blank page.

SOUNDS›1BANK›USER A›2SOUND›UA01

Play a chord. Bright, buzzy, rather harsh: that's a sawtooth, raw. Name it SAW 1 on the SOUNDS page (4NAME: turn for the letter, push for the next one).

The sounds you'll build

This chapter builds seven sounds of your own. One of them, WARM PAD, grows section by section, a piece at a time, the way you'd build any sound; the others are made in a single section each. Every one starts as a copy of SAW 1. When a section says "start from a copy of SAW 1 in UA03", that means:

SOUNDS›2SOUND›UA01›3COPY TO›UA03›hold3

Copying moves you onto the copy, so you're ready to work. By the end, USER A will hold:

SlotSoundSectionsWhat it shows
UA01SAW 16.3the raw sawtooth, the place to start
UA02WARM PAD6.4 to 6.8every part of Ember, added one at a time
UA03STAB6.6the envelope snapping the filter open
UA04SYNTH BASS6.6the sub-oscillator, and the high-pass filter's bass lift
UA05ORGAN6.6the VCA on GATE
UA06SWEEP6.7the LFO moving the filter
UA07BELL KEYS6.8both choruses at once

6.4 The oscillator

Ember has one oscillator per voice, set on two pages.

  • PULSE WAVES, encoder 1, ON or OFF a pulse wave: a square whose width you can change (below). Hollow and woody.
  • SAW WAVES, encoder 2, ON or OFF the sawtooth: every harmonic there is, the brightest, the one most sounds start from. Pulse and saw can be on together.
  • SUB WAVES, encoder 3, 0-10 a square wave an octave below the note, for weight: the floor under a bass or a pad.
  • NOISE WAVES, encoder 4, 0-10 hiss, for breath, wind and the snap of a stab.
  • RANGE DCO, encoder 1, 16', 8', 4' the octave, in feet: 8' is the note you play, 16' an octave below, 4' an octave above.
  • LFO DCO, encoder 2, 0-10 vibrato: how much the LFO moves the pitch (section 6.7).
  • PWM DCO, encoder 3, 0-10 the pulse's width: at 0 a square, turning up makes it narrower, thinner and more nasal.
  • PWM MODE DCO, encoder 4, LFO or MANUAL MANUAL: PWM sets the width and it stays put. LFO: the LFO sweeps the width back and forth, and PWM sets how far: the pulse seems to move and thicken, almost as if there were two oscillators.

Try this

On SAW 1, switch SAW off and PULSE on, and hold a chord while you turn PWM from 0 up to about 8: the sound gets thinner and more nasal. Now set PWM MODE to LFO and PWM to about 5: the sound comes alive, moving slowly. Put SAW 1 back as it was afterwards (SAW ON, PULSE OFF, PWM 0.0, PWM MODE MANUAL): everything else starts from it.

With only one oscillator per voice, Ember gets its thickness in other ways: the sub-oscillator underneath, the moving pulse width, and above all the chorus (section 6.8). The pad you're about to start uses all three.

WARM PAD, part 1: the waves

Start from a copy of SAW 1 in UA02, and name it WARM PAD.

  • 1Both waves at once: WAVES›1PULSE›ON, with SAW still ON. Hold a chord: brighter and fuller than either alone.
  • 2A moving pulse: DCO›4PWM MODE›LFO and 3PWM›5.0. Listen to the chord start to breathe.
  • 3Weight underneath: WAVES›3SUB›4.0.

Hold a low chord. Still harsh, and it starts and stops like a switch, but there's a lot going on in it now. The next three sections tame it.

6.5 The filter

The filter is where the sound gets its tone. It's a low-pass filter: it lets the low part of the sound through and cuts the high part, steeply.

  • FREQ VCF, encoder 1, 0-10 where the filter starts to cut. 10 is wide open; turn it down and the sound darkens, until there's almost nothing left.
  • RES VCF, encoder 2, 0-10 resonance: the filter rings at FREQ, so the harmonics there stand out. A little gives an edge, more gives a "wow", and near the top the filter whistles on its own.
  • KYBD VCF, encoder 3, 0-10 how much the filter follows the keys. At 0 it stays put, so high notes come out duller than low ones; at 10 it follows them all the way.
  • HPF VCF, encoder 4, 0-3 the high-pass filter, after all six voices: 0 lifts the bass a little, 1 is flat (does nothing), 2 and 3 cut the bass away, for thinner, brighter sounds that sit above a bass line.

Try this

On SAW 1, hold a chord and turn FREQ slowly from 10 down to 2 and back. Then set FREQ to about 4 and turn RES up while you sweep again. Try HPF at 3 on a full chord: the low end goes, and what's left is bright and airy. Put SAW 1 back afterwards: FREQ 10.0, RES 0.0, HPF 1.

WARM PAD, part 2: the filter

Back on WARM PAD (UA02): VCF›1FREQ›5.5, 2RES›1.0 and 3KYBD›3.0. The harshness has gone and it's warm; the little resonance keeps it from sounding dull, and KYBD keeps high chords from going muddy.

6.6 One envelope

Ember has one envelope, and it does two jobs at once: it shapes how loud each note is, and it can open and close the filter.

ENV A, D, S and R

  • A encoder 1, 0-10 attack: how long the note takes to get to the top.
  • D encoder 2, 0-10 decay: how long it takes to fall to the sustain level.
  • S encoder 3, 0-10 sustain: the level it holds while the key is down.
  • R encoder 4, 0-10 release: how long it takes to die away after you let go.

The loudness follows the envelope as long as VCA›1VCA›ENV. Set it to GATE instead and the loudness ignores the envelope: on while the key is down, off when you let go, like an organ. The envelope then works on the filter alone. 2LEVEL is the sound's own volume.

Four shapes

On SAW 1, with VCA on ENV, try these on the ENV page, and put A 0.0, D 0.0, S 10.0, R 1.0 back afterwards:

Organ

A 0.0D 0.0S 10.0R 1.0

Piano-ish

A 0.0D 5.0S 0.0R 4.0

Pad

A 5.0D 6.0S 8.0R 6.0

Pluck

A 0.0D 3.0S 0.0R 2.0

WARM PAD, part 3: the shape

On WARM PAD: the pad shape, ENV›1A›5.0, 2D›6.0, 3S›8.0, 4R›6.0. Now each chord swells in over about a second, and fades away when you let go. Play slow chords, one into the next, and let them overlap as they fade.

The envelope on the filter

Now the part that makes a synth sound alive. On the VCF MOD page:

  • ENV VCF MOD, encoder 1, 0-10 how far the envelope opens the filter on each note, from wherever FREQ has it.
  • POLARITY VCF MOD, encoder 2, NORMAL or INVERT NORMAL opens the filter; INVERT closes it instead, so the note starts dark and brightens as it fades.
  • LFO VCF MOD, encoder 3, 0-10 how far the LFO moves the filter (section 6.7).

WARM PAD, part 4: brightening as it swells

On WARM PAD, VCF MOD›1ENV›2.0: a touch of the envelope on the filter, so each chord gets a little brighter as it swells in, and darker as it fades. Small, but it's the difference between a pad that sits there and one that breathes.

Build STAB

Start from a copy of SAW 1 in UA03, and set:

STAB

SAW 1, plus:

VCFFREQ 3.0RES 4.0KYBD 5.0
VCF MODENV 5.0
ENVA 0.0D 3.5S 1.0R 3.0
VCALEVEL 10.0

Play short chords: every one snaps open and closes, the stab of a hundred house records. Name it STAB. Then try ENV higher for a brighter snap, D longer for a slower "yow", and PULSE on with PWM MODE on LFO for a thicker one.

WARM PAD and STAB use the same envelope, turned round: slow and held for the pad, fast and falling for the stab. Nearly every polysynth sound is one of those, or somewhere between.

Build SYNTH BASS

Polysynths play basses too, and the sub-oscillator is the reason. Start from a copy of SAW 1 in UA04.

  • 1An octave down, with a square underneath that: DCO›1RANGE›16', WAVES›1PULSE›ON and 3SUB›8.0.
  • 2Dark, with a pluck from the envelope: VCF›1FREQ›2.5, 2RES›3.0, 3KYBD›5.0, and VCF MOD›1ENV›4.0.
  • 3The shape: ENV›1A›0.0, 2D›4.0, 3S›3.0, 4R›2.0.
  • 4The bass lift: VCF›4HPF›0. HPF 0 isn't a cut at all: it gently lifts the lowest notes. On a bass, that's what you want.

SYNTH BASS

SAW 1, plus:

DCORANGE 16'
WAVESPULSE ONSAW ONSUB 8.0
VCFFREQ 2.5RES 3.0KYBD 5.0HPF 0
VCF MODENV 4.0
ENVA 0.0D 4.0S 3.0R 2.0

Play single notes, low down, a bass line. Name it SYNTH BASS. Then play a chord on it and hear why basses are usually one note at a time: a low chord turns to mud.

Build ORGAN

The VCA on GATE: loudness on while the key is down, off when you let go, nothing in between, like an organ's. Start from a copy of SAW 1 in UA05.

  • 1A hollow square and its octave below: WAVES›1PULSE›ON, 2SAW›OFF, 3SUB›6.0. PWM stays at 0.0 and PWM MODE on MANUAL, so the pulse is a square.
  • 2The filter fairly open, and following the keys all the way, so every note has the same tone: VCF›1FREQ›7.0, 3KYBD›10.0.
