  • 3VCA›1VCA›GATE, and 2LEVEL›5.5.
  • 4Press CHORUS II: the faster chorus, for the swirl of an organ's rotating speaker.

ORGAN

SAW 1, plus:

WAVESPULSE ONSAW OFFSUB 6.0
VCFFREQ 7.0KYBD 10.0
VCAVCA GATELEVEL 5.5
CHORUSII ON

Name it ORGAN. Play chords, and short ones: every note starts and stops dead, exactly as long as your finger. Now turn the ENV page's settings: nothing changes, because on GATE the loudness ignores the envelope, and VCF MOD's ENV is at 0, so the filter does too. Give the envelope a job on the filter alone: ENV›2D›2.0 and 3S›0.0, then VCF MOD›1ENV›3.0. Each note still lasts exactly as long as your finger, but now starts with a flash of brightness: an organ's key click. Keep it or put ENV back to 0.0, as you like

One envelope, two jobs

Because one envelope shapes both the filter and the loudness, a long attack makes a note swell in loudness and brightness together, and a short decay makes both snap. That's most of the classic polysynth sounds. When you want the loudness to stay put while the filter moves, set the VCA to GATE, as ORGAN does.

6.7 Movement

Ember's LFO, one slow wobble shared by every voice, can move three things: the pitch (vibrato), the pulse's width (PWM MODE LFO, section 6.4) and the filter.

LFO RATE and DELAY

  • RATE encoder 1, 0-10 how fast it wobbles.
  • DELAY encoder 2, 0-10 how long it waits after you start playing before it fades in. The wait starts again with the first key of each new phrase, after every key has been let go, so a held chord starts steady and only then begins to move.

How much it moves each thing is set where that thing is: LFO on the DCO page for vibrato, PWM with PWM MODE on LFO for the pulse, and LFO on the VCF MOD page for the filter.

Build SWEEP

Start from a copy of SAW 1 in UA06.

First, vibrato, to hear the delay: LFO›1RATE›5.5, 2DELAY›6.0 and DCO›2LFO›1.5. Hold a note: it starts straight, then the vibrato arrives. That's for leads and strings; this sound is going to be the other kind.

Now DCO›2LFO›0.0 and LFO›2DELAY›0.0. Close the filter so it has room to move: VCF›1FREQ›4.0 and 2RES›5.0. Then VCF MOD›3LFO›6.0, and LFO›1RATE›3.0.

SWEEP

SAW 1, plus:

LFORATE 3.0DELAY 0.0
VCFFREQ 4.0RES 5.0
VCF MODLFO 6.0

Hold a chord: the tone goes round and round, slowly opening and closing. Name it SWEEP. Try the RATE faster for a wah-wah, slower for a sweep you only notice after a while.

WARM PAD, part 5: a slow drift

On WARM PAD, the LFO is already sweeping the pulse width (PWM MODE LFO). Slow it right down, so the pad drifts instead of wobbling: LFO›1RATE›3.0. It was already 3.0 if you never changed it; turn it either way and listen to what it does to the pad.

A MIDI keyboard's mod wheel adds vibrato too, as much as SETUP's WHEEL allows (section 6.10).

6.8 The chorus

Here's Ember's secret ingredient, and the reason chapter 2 said a chorus is "half the secret of many famous synth sounds". A chorus copies the sound, sways the copy's timing back and forth very slightly, and plays it beside the original. On Ember the copy sways one way on the left and the other way on the right, so the sound spreads wide, warm and shimmering, as if it were several instruments, not one.

Two buttons control it, each on or off, lit while on:

  • ·CHORUS I on its own: a slow, gentle sway, about once every two seconds. Wide and warm.
  • ·CHORUS II on its own: faster, a little less deep. Richer, more obviously moving.
  • ·Both on (I+II): something else again, a fast, shallow shimmer, nearer to vibrato than to chorus. Lovely on pads and electric pianos.

Switch the chorus on and you'll also hear a faint hiss in quiet moments. That's on purpose: the circuits these choruses grew from always hissed, and on dark, quiet sounds the hiss breathing in time with the sway is part of the swirl.

WARM PAD, part 6: the chorus

On WARM PAD, hold a chord and press CHORUS I. That's it: the pad goes wide and warm, and that's the sound people mean when they talk about this kind of synth. Press CHORUS I again to switch it off and listen to how flat the pad was without it; then on again.

Last, the level: with everything on, the pad is loud, so VCA›2LEVEL›5.0.

WARM PAD

SAW 1, plus everything from sections 6.4 to 6.8:

WAVESPULSE ONSAW ONSUB 4.0
DCOPWM 5.0PWM MODE LFO
VCFFREQ 5.5RES 1.0KYBD 3.0
VCF MODENV 2.0
ENVA 5.0D 6.0S 8.0R 6.0
VCALEVEL 5.0
CHORUSI ON

Six changes, one at a time, and you've built a pad. Compare it with the factory's WARM PAD, FA01: they're close cousins.

Build BELL KEYS

Now the third chorus. Start from a copy of SAW 1 in UA07.

  • 1A thin pulse: WAVES›1PULSE›ON, 2SAW›OFF, DCO›3PWM›3.0 (PWM MODE stays MANUAL).
  • 2Struck, and ringing away: ENV›1A›0.0, 2D›6.0, 3S›2.0, 4R›5.0.
  • 3Bright at the strike and mellowing as it rings: VCF›1FREQ›6.0, 3KYBD›5.0, VCF MOD›1ENV›3.0.
  • 4Both choruses: press CHORUS I and CHORUS II, so both are lit. And VCA›2LEVEL›5.5.

BELL KEYS

SAW 1, plus:

WAVESPULSE ONSAW OFF
DCOPWM 3.0
VCFFREQ 6.0KYBD 5.0
VCF MODENV 3.0
ENVA 0.0D 6.0S 2.0R 5.0
VCALEVEL 5.5
CHORUSI ONII ON

Name it BELL KEYS, and play chords, held and let go. That quick shimmer is I+II. Switch one chorus off and then the other, and hear how each sounds on its own on the same sound.

The chorus belongs to the sound, so each sound keeps its own setting. With Haze joined on, Ember can also send into Haze's echo and reverb, as every synth can (chapter 2, section 2.5).

6.9 Playing chords

Ember has six voices, so six notes at once. Play a seventh, and the voice that has been playing longest gives way to the new note, fading out quickly so the change doesn't click. Ember also uses its voices in turn, so a note you've let go of carries on ringing through its release while the next notes start on other voices.

  • Sustain pedal. From a MIDI keyboard, the sustain pedal holds notes as a piano's does.
  • How hard you play. Ember's own keys play every note at the same loudness. From a MIDI keyboard, turn VELO on in SETUP (section 6.10) and harder is louder.
  • LEVEL VCA, encoder 2, 0-10 the sound's own volume, to make your sounds sit together. Each step is about 2 dB, which is why the recipes above set it: a full chorused pad with four notes held is much louder than a single plucked note.

Try this

On WARM PAD, play a chord and, while it's still fading, a second chord: both ring together, because the second chord takes free voices. Then hold four notes and play three more, one by one: you'll hear the first notes give way. Six is plenty for chords; it's a thing to know when the release is long.

6.10 Ember's SETUP

SETUP's THIS UNIT pages have Ember's own settings, beside the MIDI channel:

  • BEND encoder 2, 0-12 how far a MIDI keyboard's pitch bend wheel bends the notes, in semitones.
  • VCF BEND encoder 3, 0-10 how far the same wheel moves the filter too: bend the wheel and the sound brightens or darkens.
  • WHEEL encoder 4, 0-10 how much vibrato the mod wheel can add.
  • VELO second page, encoder 1, OFF or ON OFF: every note equally loud. ON: harder is louder, from a MIDI keyboard or from Step.

What you have at the end of this chapter

Seven sounds of your own: SAW 1, WARM PAD, STAB, SYNTH BASS, ORGAN, SWEEP and BELL KEYS. Between them, every page on Ember, and the shape of nearly every polysynth sound there is: a wave, a filter, one envelope moving both, and a chorus to make it sing. Open the factory's STRINGS, BRASS and HOUSE ORGAN, and see how close you already are.

Chapter 7 - Axis

Four waves at the corners of a diamond, and a point that moves between them.

Every synth so far makes a sound and then changes it. Axis makes four sounds at once and moves between them. Each voice has four oscillators, A, B, C and D, sitting at the four corners of a diamond, and a point on the diamond decides how much of each you hear. Put the point at a corner and you hear that oscillator alone; in the middle, all four equally; anywhere else, a blend. Then let an envelope move the point while the note plays, and the sound travels: from a bell to a voice to a buzz and back again, on every note. That's vector synthesis.

Vector synthesis: where it came from, and who uses it

Vector synthesis began with Sequential Circuits' Prophet VS in 1986: four digital waves per voice, mixed by a joystick, the joystick's moves remembered by an envelope, then an analogue filter. Its waves were made by computer, with a gritty, glassy, slightly metallic sound that nothing else had, and its evolving pads turned up in film music and on records of the late 1980s. Sequential didn't last much longer, but its ideas did: some of the same people went on to Korg's Wavestation (1990), which strung waves together in sequences, and Yamaha put vector mixing into its SY22 and TG33. Software versions are still made today.

Axis isn't any of those instruments. It's a vector synth of the late-1980s kind and works the way they do, so what you learn here will serve you on any of them. But its waves are its own: all 128 were made for Axis, from our own recipes, and none is copied from anywhere. They're in families of sixteen, so you can move through related sounds, and section 7.8 has a trick that the vector synths of the 1980s couldn't do.

7.1 Find a sound you like

Axis has one factory bank, FAC A, with 32 sounds.

Try this

SOUNDS›2SOUND and go through all 32. Hold the notes this time, for a few seconds each: a lot of Axis's sounds change as they go, and you'll miss it in short notes. FA01, VECTOR PAD, travels round all four corners for ever; FA12, WAVE SWEEP, sweeps through bright, resonant waves; FA14, VOWELSCAN, changes vowel as each note opens.

7.2 How Axis is laid out

  • 1The left column is the four oscillators: OSC A, OSC B, OSC C and OSC D.
  • 2The middle column is what happens to the sound: FILTER, FILTER ENV, AMP ENV (the loudness), LFO 1, LFO 2, then SOUNDS.
  • 3The right column is VECTOR (press it again for its envelope), MOD, CHORUS, KEYS, then SETUP.

A sound to work on

Your own slots start as INIT SOUND: four sawtooths, all the same, with the point in the middle, so it sounds like one plain sawtooth. Give its corners four different waves, and you've got something to explore:

SOUNDS›1BANK›USER A›2SOUND›UA01

  • 1OSC A›1WAVE›0 SINE: the pure one.
  • 2OSC B›1WAVE›3 SQUARE: hollow.
  • 3OSC C›1WAVE›65 AH HI: a voice.
  • 4OSC D›1WAVE›96 BELL 1: a bell.

Name it CORNERS on the SOUNDS page (4NAME: turn for the letter, push for the next one).

The sounds you'll build

This chapter builds seven sounds of your own. Most start as a copy of CORNERS, so you'll always know what's at each corner. When a section says "start from a copy of CORNERS in UA03", that means:

SOUNDS›2SOUND›UA01›3COPY TO›UA03›hold3

Copying moves you onto the copy, so you're ready to work. By the end, USER A will hold:

SlotSoundSectionWhat it shows
UA01CORNERS7.2four different waves, one at each corner
UA02WIDE PAD7.4 and 7.5waves from different families, tuned apart, and the filter
UA03PULSER7.6a rhythm from a looping envelope
UA04TRAVELLER7.7the vector envelope going round the diamond
UA05DRIFTER7.7two LFOs through the MOD list
UA06SCANNER7.8WAVE SCAN
UA07UNISON LEAD7.10all eight voices on one note

Reading the numbers

Axis shows every setting as it is: times in MS and S, rates in HZ, the cutoff in HZ and KHZ, levels from 0.0 to 10.0, X and Y from -100 to +100 (two at a click). The recipes give them the same way, so turn until the screen says what the recipe says. Times and rates move in small steps at the bottom and bigger ones at the top, so a recipe's 0.10 S or 1.02 S is exactly a value the screen can show.

7.3 Four waves on a diamond

The VECTOR page is the diamond itself. A is on the left, C on the right, D at the top and B at the bottom. The square dot is the point, and beside each corner is how much of it you're hearing.

  • X VECTOR, encoder 3, -100 to +100 left and right: towards A, or towards C.
  • Y VECTOR, encoder 4, -100 to +100 down and up: towards B, or towards D.

The point is on the bottom encoders on purpose: your hands stay below the screen and you can watch the diamond while you turn. Move the point beyond the diamond's edge and the two corners nearest it share the sound between them.

Try this

On CORNERS, hold a chord and turn X slowly all the way left (the sine), then right (the voice); then Y down (the square) and up (the bell). Then find places in between that you like: a little voice in the bell, a little square in the sine. Every point on the diamond is a different sound.

Put X and Y back to 0 when you're done: the copies of CORNERS start with the point in the middle.

7.4 The oscillators

Each corner's oscillator has its own page, all four alike:

  • WAVE encoder 1, 0-127 which of Axis's 128 waves it plays: its number and name (64 AH LO), and the wave drawn.
  • COARSE encoder 2, -24 to +24 its pitch, in semitones: 12 is an octave up, 7 a fifth.
  • FINE encoder 3, -100 to +100 a fine adjustment, in cents (a hundredth of a semitone): a little apart from another corner and they beat slowly against each other.
  • LEVEL encoder 4, 0-10 how loud this corner is when the point is on it.

The waves

The 128 waves come in eight families of sixteen, and the waves in a family are related, so turning WAVE moves you through sounds that belong together:

WavesFamilyWhat they sound like
0-15Plain shapesSine, triangle, sawtooth, square, pulses: the basics.
16-31OrganPipe and electric organ registrations, from a soft flute to a full organ.
32-47HollowOdd harmonics: clarinets, reeds, woody and nasal sounds.
48-63Octaves and evenOctave stacks, even harmonics, whistles and sparkle.
64-79VocalVowels, low and high: AH, EH, EE, OH, OO and more.
80-95ResonantA sawtooth with one bright peak that climbs through the family.
96-111Bells and metalBells, glass, chimes, vibes, marimba, gongs.
112-127DigitalDense digital waves, sync sounds, folded and clipped waves, buzz and grit.

The waves are played at a fairly low resolution (12 bits), as vector synths of this kind did, which gives them a slight grain and glassiness. That's part of the sound, not a fault.

Try this

On CORNERS, hold a note and turn OSC C›1WAVE slowly from 64 to 79, through the vocal family: one voice singing sixteen vowels. Then put it back to 65.

A pad from four families

CORNERS uses four very different waves, so the point decides what you hear. A pad wants the opposite: four waves that blend into one, tuned a little apart so they move against each other, with the point in the middle to hear them all.

WIDE PAD, part 1: the corners

This one starts from INIT SOUND itself, not CORNERS: go to UA02 and name it WIDE PAD.

  • 1A and C, the left and right, a soft sawtooth each, pulled a few cents apart: OSC A›1WAVE›8 SOFT SAW, 3FINE›-8 CT; OSC C›1WAVE›8 SOFT SAW, 3FINE›+8 CT. Hold a chord: a slow, warm beating.
  • 2B, the bottom, a hollow wave an octave down for body: OSC B›1WAVE›33 HOLLOW 2, 2COARSE›-12.
  • 3D, the top, a glassy shine an octave up, quieter: OSC D›1WAVE›100 GLASS 1, 2COARSE›+12, 4LEVEL›6.0.

Leave the point in the middle, X 0 and Y 0, so all four play equally. Bright and big, but buzzy: the filter's next.

7.5 The filter

After the diamond, each voice goes through a resonant low-pass filter, which takes away the top of the sound.

  • CUTOFF FILTER, encoder 1 where the filter starts to cut, shown in Hz: all the way up, it's wide open.
  • RES FILTER, encoder 2, 0-10 resonance: the filter rings where it cuts, giving an edge, then a "wow".
  • ENV FILTER, encoder 3, -100 to +100 how far the FILTER ENV opens it (or, below 0, closes it) on each note.
  • KEYBOARD FILTER, encoder 4, 0-10 how much the filter follows the keys; 8.5 to start, so high notes stay nearly as bright as low ones.

WIDE PAD, part 2: filter, shape and chorus

  • 1Take the buzz off: FILTER›1CUTOFF›2.3 KHZ and 2RES›1.5.
  • 2A slow swell and a long fade: on AMP ENV, 1POINT›1 and 2TIME›1.02 S (the time to reach full loudness), then 1POINT›4 and 2TIME›1.22 S (the time to fade after you let go). Section 7.6 explains these pages properly.
  • 3CHORUS, and press it again so it's lit: on.
  • 4KEYS›4LEVEL›10.0: a soft pad needs its full level.

WIDE PAD

INIT SOUND, with:

OSC AWAVE 8 SOFT SAWFINE -8 CT
OSC BWAVE 33 HOLLOW 2COARSE -12
OSC CWAVE 8 SOFT SAWFINE +8 CT
OSC DWAVE 100 GLASS 1COARSE +12LEVEL 6.0
FILTERCUTOFF 2.3 KHZRES 1.5
AMP ENVPOINT 1 TIME 1.02 SPOINT 4 TIME 1.22 S
CHORUSON
KEYSLEVEL 10.0

Play slow chords and let them fade into each other. Then move the point while one holds: towards D and the glass comes up; towards B and the body thickens. The same pad, four ways.

7.6 Envelopes with five points

Axis's envelopes are more than attack, decay, sustain and release. Each has five points, 0 to 4, each with its own level, and a time to travel to each one from the last. One of them is the sustain point, where the note waits while you hold the key; when you let go, it carries on through the points after it.

AMP ENV (the loudness) and FILTER ENV (the filter, by FILTER's ENV): POINT, TIME, LEVEL and SUSTAIN

  • POINT encoder 1, 0-4 which point the other boxes are about. The picture marks it.
  • TIME encoder 2 how long it takes to get to this point from the one before, from 4 ms to 41 seconds. (Point 0 is where it starts, so it has no time.)
  • LEVEL encoder 3, 0-10 this point's level.
  • SUSTAIN encoder 4, point 1-4 the point it holds at while the key is down.

INIT SOUND's AMP ENV is the plainest shape: up to full at point 1 almost at once, along to point 3, held there, then down to silence at point 4 when you let go. Five points let you draw much more: a swell that overshoots and settles, a pluck with a second, softer bump, a note that fades and then rises again while you hold it.

Loops

Push encoder 1 on any envelope page and the boxes become its loop settings (push again for the points):

  • SUSTAIN encoder 1 the sustain point, as before.
  • LOOP AT encoder 2, point 0-3 where a loop goes back to.
  • REPEATS encoder 3, OFF, 1-7, FOR EVER how many times it goes round, from LOOP AT to the sustain point, before settling.
  • BOUNCE encoder 4, ON or OFF ON: back and forth between the two, instead of jumping back to the start.

Build PULSER

A rhythm made by the envelope alone. Start from a copy of CORNERS in UA03, and go to AMP ENV.

  • 1Point 1: 1POINT›1, 2TIME›0.10 S, 3LEVEL›10.0.
  • 2Point 2: 1POINT›2, 2TIME›0.10 S, 3LEVEL›2.0. The note dips.
  • 3Point 3: 1POINT›3, 2TIME›0.10 S, 3LEVEL›6.0. It comes back up, not quite as far. SUSTAIN stays at point 3.
  • 4The loop: push encoder 1, then 2LOOP AT›POINT 1 and 3REPEATS›FOR EVER.
  • 5It's a single-note sound with gaps in it, so KEYS›4LEVEL›10.0.

PULSER

CORNERS, with an AMP ENV of:

POINT 1TIME 0.10 SLEVEL 10.0
POINT 2TIME 0.10 SLEVEL 2.0
POINT 3TIME 0.10 SLEVEL 6.0
LOOPSUSTAIN POINT 3LOOP AT POINT 1REPEATS FOR EVER
KEYSLEVEL 10.0

Name it PULSER. Hold a note: it pulses, loud-quiet-softer, loud-quiet-softer, for as long as you hold it. Each time round it jumps from point 3 back to point 1. Now push encoder 1 and turn 4BOUNCE›ON: instead of jumping back it goes back the way it came, 1-2-3-2-1-2-3, and the rhythm changes shape. Then try the times: all three at 0.40 S for a slow throb, or point 2's at 0.40 S and the others short for a swing.

7.7 The vector envelope, and movement

Here's the heart of Axis. Press VECTORVECTOR ENV (VECTOR again) and the diamond comes back with five points on it: this envelope moves the point on the diamond while the note plays, so the sound travels between the corners. It works like the other envelopes, five points with a time to each, a sustain point and a loop, except that each point is a place on the diamond, its X and Y, instead of a level.

VECTORVECTOR ENV POINT, TIME, X and Y (push encoder 1 for its loop)

Build TRAVELLER

A sound that goes round all four corners, for ever. Start from a copy of CORNERS in UA04, and press VECTORVECTOR ENV. Set the five points to the four corners, a second apart, and back to where it started:

TRAVELLER

CORNERS, with a VECTOR ENV of:

POINT 0X 0Y +100the bell (D)
POINT 1TIME 1.02 SX +100Y 0the voice (C)
POINT 2TIME 1.02 SX 0Y -100the square (B)
POINT 3TIME 1.02 SX -100Y 0the sine (A)
POINT 4TIME 1.02 SX 0Y +100the bell again
LOOPSUSTAIN POINT 4LOOP AT POINT 0REPEATS FOR EVER
KEYSLEVEL 5.0

X and Y move two at a click, so +100 is fifty clicks; turn fast. Name it TRAVELLER, hold a chord, and watch the point on the screen go round as the sound goes from bell to voice to square to sine and back. Every note goes round on its own, from the moment it starts, so play a second chord a little after the first and they'll be in different places on the diamond at once. That's FA01, VECTOR PAD, made by you.

Then try BOUNCE ON in the loop settings: round and back again instead of round and round. And the times: all four at about 4 S for a slow, evolving pad, or at 0.10 S for a strange, warbling buzz.

The LFOs and the MOD list

Axis has two LFOs, each with its own page:

  • RATE LFO 1 or 2, encoder 1 how fast, in Hz.
  • SHAPE encoder 2 TRIANGLE, SAW UP, SAW DOWN, SQUARE or RANDOM (a new random value each time round).
  • DELAY encoder 3 how long it waits after a note starts before fading in.

An LFO on its own moves nothing. What it moves, and how much, is set on the MOD page: a list of six connections, each one a SOURCE moving a DESTINATION by an AMOUNT.

  • SLOT MOD, encoder 1, 1-6 which of the six connections the other boxes show.
  • SOURCE encoder 2 what does the moving: LFO 1, LFO 2, FILT ENV, AMP ENV, VELOCITY (how hard a key is played), WHEEL (the mod wheel), KEY (which note), PRESSURE (pressing harder on a held key), or NONE.
  • DEST encoder 3 what it moves: PITCH, CUTOFF, RES, LEVEL, X, Y, PAN, and the WAVE destinations of section 7.8.
  • AMOUNT encoder 4, -100 to +100 how much, either way.

Some sources need a MIDI keyboard

Axis's own keys play every note at the same strength and have no mod wheel, so VELOCITY, WHEEL and PRESSURE only move when you play from a MIDI keyboard (one that sends aftertouch, for PRESSURE). The LFOs, the two envelopes and KEY all work from Axis's own keys.

Build DRIFTER

Two LFOs, two jobs. Start from a copy of CORNERS in UA05.

  • 1A vibrato that arrives late: MOD›1SLOT›1, 2SOURCE›LFO 1, 3DEST›PITCH, 4AMOUNT›+3. Then on LFO 1: 1RATE›5.0 HZ and 3DELAY›0.48 S. Hold a note: it starts still, then wavers.
  • 2A point that wanders: MOD›1SLOT›2, 2SOURCE›LFO 2, 3DEST›X, 4AMOUNT›+60; and LFO 2›1RATE›0.20 HZ, once every five seconds.
  • 3KEYS›4LEVEL›7.0.

DRIFTER

CORNERS, with:

MOD 1LFO 1PITCH+3
MOD 2LFO 2X+60
LFO 1RATE 5.0 HZDELAY 0.48 S
LFO 2RATE 0.20 HZ
KEYSLEVEL 7.0

Name it DRIFTER, and hold a chord for a long time, watching the point: it drifts from the sine side to the voice side and back on its own, while the vibrato wavers on top. Change LFO 2's SHAPE to RANDOM, and it jumps to a new place every five seconds instead.

TRAVELLER and DRIFTER both move the point, in different ways: the vector envelope draws a path that starts again with every note; an LFO sways back and forth whatever the notes do. Put both on one sound and you've got movement inside movement.

7.8 WAVE SCAN

Here's something the vector synths of the 1980s couldn't do. The MOD list has five more destinations: WAVE A, WAVE B, WAVE C, WAVE D and WAVES (all four together). Send a source there and it pushes that oscillator's wave along its family of sixteen, blending smoothly from each wave into the next, never leaving the family. At AMOUNT +100, a source at full moves it fifteen waves: the whole family.

Build SCANNER

Start from a copy of CORNERS in UA06.

  • 1Corner A gets the first of the resonant family: OSC A›1WAVE›80 RESO 3.
  • 2Listen to A alone: VECTOR›3X›-100.
  • 3The scan: MOD›1SLOT›1, 2SOURCE›FILT ENV, 3DEST›WAVE A, 4AMOUNT›+100.
  • 4Slow the filter envelope down, so you can hear it work: FILTER ENV, 1POINT›1 and 2TIME›0.64 S, then 1POINT›2 and 2TIME›1.02 S.
  • 5KEYS›4LEVEL›10.0.

SCANNER

CORNERS, with:

OSC AWAVE 80 RESO 3
VECTORX -100Y 0
MOD 1FILT ENVWAVE A+100
FILTER ENVPOINT 1 TIME 0.64 SPOINT 2 TIME 1.02 S
KEYSLEVEL 10.0

Name it SCANNER, and hold a note: the resonant peak sweeps up through the family as the filter envelope rises, then falls back part of the way as it settles at point 2's level. Notice that the filter itself isn't moving: FILTER's ENV is still 0. The FILTER ENV is only being used as a source, to scan the waves. Change its times and the sweep follows.

An LFO makes a steady sweep that never stops; KEY moves the wave further along the higher you play; FILT ENV and AMP ENV sweep on every note. With a MIDI keyboard, WHEEL scans by hand (FA17, DRAWBARS, pulls in organ stops this way) and PRESSURE scans as you press. Seven other factory sounds scan too: SCAN PAD, VOWELSCAN, RESO SWEEP, SCAN BASS, BELL SCAN, FOLD BASS and COMPUTER. Open their MOD pages to see how.

7.9 Chorus

Axis has a stereo chorus of its own: press CHORUS to see its page, and press it again to switch it on or off (lit while on). WIDE PAD has it on.

  • CHORUS encoder 1, ON or OFF the same switch.
  • RATE encoder 2 how fast it sways, in Hz.
  • DEPTH encoder 3, 0-10 how deep.
  • SPREAD encoder 4, 0-10 how far apart the eight voices sit, left and right, so a chord is wide even with the chorus off. (PAN in the MOD list moves a voice as it plays.)

Try this

On WIDE PAD, hold a chord and switch the chorus off and on: off, it's smaller and plainer; on, it fills the room. Then try DEPTH at 10.0 and RATE faster for a seasick wobble, and back.

With Haze joined on, Axis can also send into Haze's echo and reverb, as every synth can.

7.10 Playing it

KEYS MODE, DETUNE, GLIDE and LEVEL

  • MODE encoder 1, POLY, UNISON or MONO POLY: up to eight notes at once. UNISON: all eight voices on one note, slightly apart, for one enormous sound (FA27, SUPER SAW). MONO: one note at a time, joined-up notes gliding without starting again.
  • DETUNE encoder 2, 0-10 in UNISON, how far apart the voices are.
  • GLIDE encoder 3, OFF or a time how long the pitch takes to slide from one note to the next.
  • LEVEL encoder 4, 0-10 the sound's own volume. Eight voices on one note are loud, which is why UNISON sounds want it low.

Build UNISON LEAD

This one starts from INIT SOUND: four sawtooths. Go to UA07 and name it UNISON LEAD.

  • 1Turn the level down first, because the next step makes it very loud: KEYS›4LEVEL›3.5.
  • 2All eight voices on one note: 1MODE›UNISON, 2DETUNE›3.0. Play a note: one enormous, swirling sawtooth.
  • 3Glide between notes: 3GLIDE›0.18 S.
  • 4An edge from the filter, opening on each note: FILTER›1CUTOFF›1.6 KHZ, 2RES›3.0, 3ENV›+40.

UNISON LEAD

INIT SOUND, with:

KEYSMODE UNISONDETUNE 3.0GLIDE 0.18 SLEVEL 3.5
FILTERCUTOFF 1.6 KHZRES 3.0ENV +40

Play a tune high up. One note at a time, every one huge, sliding into the next. DETUNE up to 6.0 for a wilder swirl, down to 1.0 for a tighter, more focused one. Then go back to CORNERS and try UNISON there: a unison of four different waves.

From a MIDI keyboard, harder is louder while SETUP's VELO is ON (as it starts); VELOCITY in the MOD list can make harder brighter, too.

7.11 Axis's SETUP

  • BEND THIS UNIT, encoder 2, 0-12 how far a MIDI keyboard's pitch bend wheel bends the notes, in semitones.
  • VELO THIS UNIT, encoder 3, ON or OFF ON: harder is louder; OFF: every note the same.

What you have at the end of this chapter

Seven sounds of your own: CORNERS, WIDE PAD, PULSER, TRAVELLER, DRIFTER, SCANNER and UNISON LEAD. Between them, every page on Axis, and the idea behind every vector synth: not one sound changed, but four sounds and a path between them.

Chapter 8 - Taste

Any sound in the world, on a key: then chop it, bend it and play it.

Every synth so far makes its sounds from scratch. Taste doesn't make sounds at all: it records them, and plays them back from the keys. A drum hit, a chord from another unit, a word, rain on a window: once it's in Taste, it's on a key, and you can play it higher and lower, chop it into pieces, play it backwards, stretch it, loop it and filter it. That's a sampler, and a short recording is a sample.

Taste plays samples two ways, and every sound of Taste's holds one of each:

  • ·A KIT puts a different sample on every key: 27 keys, 27 samples. Drum kits, chopped-up loops, a word on each key.
  • ·An INSTRUMENT puts one sample across all the keys, played higher up the keyboard and lower down it, so you can play tunes and chords with it.

Sampling: where it came from, and who uses it

People were cutting up recorded sound long before computers: in the 1940s and 50s, composers of musique concrète in Paris spliced tape by hand, and the Mellotron of the 1960s played a strip of tape for each key, the strings and flutes on records by the Beatles and the Moody Blues. The first digital samplers, the Fairlight CMI of 1979 and the E-mu Emulator of 1981, cost as much as a house; Peter Gabriel, Kate Bush and Stevie Wonder used them to put real-world sounds into songs.

Then samplers got cheap. Ensoniq's Mirage (1984) and Akai's S900 (1986) brought them into bedrooms and small studios, and in 1987 and 1988 two machines changed music for good: E-mu's SP-1200 and the Akai MPC60, which Roger Linn designed. Both put sampling and a sequencer in one box with pads, and both had a gritty sound of their own: the SP-1200 recorded at 12 bits and a low rate, which made drums crunchy and bass heavy. Producers such as Marley Marl, Pete Rock and later J Dilla built hip hop from them, sampling drum breaks from old funk records, chopping them into hits and playing them back in new orders. A few seconds of drumming from The Winstons' "Amen, Brother" (1969), sampled, chopped and sped up, became the backbone of jungle and drum and bass.

Since then, samplers have played everything: whole orchestras, drum kits recorded one hit at a time, and vocal chops in pop. Taste isn't any of those machines. It's a sampler of the late-1980s kind, with that kind's character (CHARACTER, section 8.10), and it works the way they do, so what you learn here will serve you on any sampler you ever meet, or in any music software, which all sample the same way.

8.1 Find a sound you like

Taste has one factory bank, FAC A, with 32 sounds, all made from the samples built into Taste (the starter set, section 8.4): drum kits, chopped breaks, instruments, and many of them the same sample turned into something quite different.

Try this

SOUNDS›2SOUND and go through them. A kit (BOOM KIT, STUDIO KIT, BREAK CHOP) wants every key played, top to bottom; an instrument (KEYS, PAD, STRINGS) wants chords and tunes. Look at the KIT/INSTR button at the top of the middle column: lit, the sound's a kit; out, an instrument.

Then listen to the families: KEYS, KEYS BACK, KEYS PLUCK and KEYS DRONE are all one sample of a piano-like sound. TWO SPEEDS plays the same drum loop on eight keys at four speeds, two ways (section 8.7 says why they sound so different).

8.2 How Taste is laid out

  • 1The left column is the sample itself: SAMPLE (getting one), TRIM (which part plays), LOOP, CHOP and TUNE.
  • 2The middle column is KIT/INSTR at the top, then how it sounds: FILTER, ENV, LFO and MIX, then SOUNDS.
  • 3The right column is CHARACTER at the top and SETUP at the bottom.

In a kit, the pages work on one key at a time: the last one you played. Its name is in the top bar (TRIM C3), and its light stays dim so you can see which it is. Play another key and the pages show that one instead. In an instrument, the top bar says INST: there's only one sample to work on.

The pages with a waveform (TRIM, LOOP, SAMPLE and CHOP) draw the sample across the middle of the screen, the part that plays dark, the rest pale, so you can see what you're doing.

8.3 The sounds you'll build

Your own slots start as INIT SOUND, and on Taste that's truly empty: a kit with nothing on any key. This chapter fills seven of them:

SlotSoundSectionsWhat it shows
UA01MY KIT8.4 and 8.5putting samples on keys, and making them a kit
UA02MY BREAK8.6 and 8.7chopping a drum loop, and fitting it to the tempo
UA03MY KEYS8.8an instrument from one note
UA04VOX PAD8.8a loop that holds a note for ever
UA05SLOW CHOIR8.9STRETCH: pitch and length apart
UA06DUSTY BREAK8.10CHARACTER: the old machines' grit
UA07HELLO8.11a sample you record yourself

Every one starts from an empty slot, so there's no copying to do: just go to the slot. And there's nothing to save: Taste keeps everything as you go.

8.4 The starter set

Taste comes with 37 samples built in, ready to use on any key: drum hits (from Strike's kits, and a real acoustic kit, the ST... ones), a drum loop (BREAK), notes and chords from the other units (KEYS C4, PAD C4, BASS C3, STRINGS, BELLS C4, VOX C4, EXPANSE, SWEEP), and some real-world sounds (RAIN, CHOIR, and a spoken line, WORDS). Press SAMPLE twice for the SAMPLES page, the list of every sample Taste has:

  • SAMPLE encoder 1 which sample: the list below shows it, with its length in seconds. A star (*) means one of the starter set; your own come first, without one.
  • NAME encoder 2 your own samples only: turn to change the letter, push for the next one.
  • USE hold encoder 3 puts the sample on the key being edited (or makes it the instrument): the whole of it, with every setting back to the start.
  • SAVE hold encoder 4 writes it onto the Root's card as a WAV file (section 8.12).

MY KIT, part 1: samples on keys

Go to SOUNDS›1BANK›USER A›2SOUND›UA01 and name it MY KIT. It's a kit with nothing on it. Now put a drum on each of five keys, the same keys Strike uses, so a beat for one plays on the other:

  • 1Press the top key, C3, to choose it. Then SAMPLE, SAMPLEagain for SAMPLES, 1SAMPLE until it shows ST KICK, and hold 3USE. The screen says ON THIS KEY NOW. Play C3: a real kick drum.
  • 2Press E3 (the third white key), find ST SNARE, hold USE.
  • 3A3 (the sixth white key): CLAP, Strike's handclap.
  • 4B3 (the seventh): ST CL HAT. And C4 (the eighth): ST OP HAT.

Play a beat: kick, hats, snare. Half a real drum kit and a drum machine's clap, on one unit. That's already more than most drum machines could do.

8.5 Trimming, tuning and mixing a key

Every key has its own settings, on the pages from TRIM to MIX, for the key being edited.

TRIM START, END, REVERSE and TRIGGER

  • START, END encoders 1 and 2, in seconds where the key starts and stops playing in its sample. Each click moves a thousandth of the waveform shown; push the encoder to zoom in on its marker (×8, ×64, back) for finer moves.
  • REVERSE encoder 3, ON or OFF plays it backwards, from END to START.
  • TRIGGER encoder 4, 1-SHOT or GATE 1-SHOT: one press plays it all, as a drum should. GATE: it plays while the key is held and stops when you let go.

TUNE COARSE, FINE, BEATS and ROOT

  • COARSE encoder 1, -24 to +24 semitones up or down. On a sampler, up also means faster and shorter, down slower and longer, as with a tape or a record played at the wrong speed (unless TIME is STRETCH, section 8.7).
  • FINE encoder 2, -50 to +50 cents, for tuning by ear.
  • BEATS encoder 3, OFF or 1-64 section 8.7.
  • ROOT encoder 4 instruments only: section 8.8.

MIX LEVEL, PAN, CHOKE and NORMAL

  • LEVEL encoder 1, 0-10 how loud this key is.
  • PAN encoder 2, L50 to R50 where it sits, left to right.
  • CHOKE encoder 3, OFF or GROUP 1-4 kits only: keys in the same group cut each other off, as a closed hi-hat stops an open one.
  • NORMAL hold encoder 4 shows how loud the sample is at its loudest; hold to make it as loud as it can go without distorting. Your own recordings only: the starter set's are full already.

MY KIT, part 2: making it a kit

  • 1The hats choke each other: play B3, then MIX›3CHOKE›GROUP 1; play C4, the same. Now play the open hat and the closed one straight after: the open one is cut short.
  • 2Spread them, as a drummer's kit is spread: on B3, 2PAN›L15; on C4, 2PAN›L25.
  • 3A deeper kick: play C3, TUNE›1COARSE›-3. Lower and a little longer, because it plays slower.
  • 4The clap under the snare: play A3, MIX›1LEVEL›7.0.

MY KIT

An empty kit, with:

C3ST KICKCOARSE -3
E3ST SNARE
A3CLAPLEVEL 7.0
B3ST CL HATCHOKE GROUP 1PAN L15
C4ST OP HATCHOKE GROUP 1PAN L25

Then the trick drum machines can't do: play E3, TRIM›3REVERSE›ON, and play it. A backwards snare, swelling up into nothing. Put it back OFF, or keep it on a key of its own (CHOP's COPY, section 8.6, puts a copy on another key).

8.6 Chopping

Here's the trick hip hop was built on. Take a drum loop, cut it into pieces, one hit each, and put each piece on a key. Now you can play the drummer's hits in any order you like.

CHOP SLICES, MODE, SENS and CHOP

  • SLICES encoder 1, 2-27 how many pieces (EVENLY only).
  • MODE encoder 2 EVENLY: equal pieces, START to END, which suits a loop with a steady beat (16 for a bar of sixteenths). AT HITS: a new piece wherever the sound jumps up, a drum hit or a word. COPY: not a chop at all, but the key's sample and settings copied onto another key (encoder 1 becomes TO).
  • SENS encoder 3, 0-10 AT HITS only: higher finds quieter hits.
  • CHOP hold encoder 4 does it: the pieces go on the key being edited and the keys above it, one each. The waveform shows the cuts first, dashed, so you can see before you hold.

MY BREAK, part 1: a loop, kept whole

Go to UA02 and name it MY BREAK. First, the whole loop on the top key, to keep:

  • 1Press the bottom key, D5 (the last white key). SAMPLE, SAMPLEagain, find BREAK and hold 3USE. Play it: one bar of drums, from Strike.
  • 2Make it a loop that plays while you hold it: TRIM›4TRIGGER›GATE and LOOP›1LOOP›ON. Hold D5: round and round.
  • 3Copy it to C3, to chop: CHOP›2MODE›COPY, 1TO›C3, and hold 4COPY. The screen says COPIED TO C3, and C3 is now the key being edited.

MY BREAK, part 2: chopped

  • 1On C3: CHOP›2MODE›EVENLY and 1SLICES›16. The dashed lines show sixteen cuts.
  • 2Hold 4CHOP. 16 SLICES: the bar is now on the sixteen keys from C3 up, one sixteenth each, every key a 1-SHOT.
  • 3Play the keys from C3 up, one by one, in time: the break, as it was. Now play them in another order. Kick, kick, snare. Hats on their own. A snare twice. That's a new drum part, played by the same drummer.
  • 4Make one slice different: play the slice with the loudest snare, then TRIM›3REVERSE›ON; or TUNE›1COARSE›-5 on a kick slice for a deeper one.

MODE AT HITS works the same way, but cuts wherever the sound jumps up instead of evenly, with 3SENS deciding how small a jump counts. It suits a loose loop, or a spoken line: the factory's WORDS CHOP is made that way, and section 8.11 uses it on your own voice. (A chop puts its pieces on the key being edited and the keys above it, so start low on the keyboard: on D5, the last key, there'd be room for only one.)

8.7 In time with the music

A loop was recorded at one tempo, and your song is probably at another. Taste has two ways to fit it, and they sound completely different.

  • BEATS TUNE, encoder 3, OFF or 1-64 how many beats this key's sample should last. Taste plays it faster or slower so that it does, at the tempo: Step's, when Step is on the chain, otherwise 120 BPM (the screen says which).

TUNETIME (TUNE pressed again) TIME, SPEED and GRAIN

  • TIME encoder 1, CLASSIC or STRETCH CLASSIC: speed and pitch go together, as on the old machines: faster is higher. STRETCH: pitch and speed come apart, so a note keeps its length whatever its pitch, and a loop keeps its pitch whatever its speed.
  • SPEED encoder 2, STRETCH only, 25% to 400% how fast it moves through the sample, without changing the pitch.
  • GRAIN encoder 3, STRETCH only, 10-100 MS how STRETCH does it: it plays the sample as many short overlapping pieces, grains, and this is their length. Longer suits smooth sounds, shorter suits drums.

MY BREAK, part 3: to the tempo

  • 1Play D5, the whole loop. TUNE›3BEATS›4: one bar of four beats. Hold D5. It's faster now, a bar at 120 BPM, and higher, like a record played too fast: the classic sampler sound, and in jungle it's the whole point.
  • 2Now TUNEagain for TIME, and 1TIME›STRETCH. Hold D5: the same tempo, but back at its own pitch. 3GRAIN›30 MS, short, suits drums.

MY BREAK

An empty kit, with:

D5BREAKTRIGGER GATELOOP ONBEATS 4TIME STRETCHGRAIN 30 MS
C3 upBREAK, CHOP EVENLY 16

Play the factory's TWO SPEEDS now: the same loop at four speeds CLASSIC on the first four white keys, and at the same four speeds STRETCH on the next four. Slower CLASSIC is lower and darker; slower STRETCH keeps its pitch and gets a little grainy. Neither is better. They're two different instruments.

8.8 Instruments

Now the other half: one sample, played across all the keys. Press KIT/INSTR on one of your own sounds and it switches to its instrument (the light goes out, and the screen says INSTRUMENT); press it again for the kit. The two are kept separately, so switching never loses either.

  • ROOT TUNE, encoder 4 the note at which the sample plays as it was recorded. If you sampled a C4, ROOT is C4, and every other key plays it that far higher or lower, in tune. The starter set's notes say theirs in their names: KEYS C4, BASS C3.

FILTER CUTOFF, RES and ENV    ENV ATTACK, DECAY, SUSTAIN and RELEASE    LFO RATE, PITCH and FILTER

  • CUTOFF, RES FILTER, 0-10 a low-pass filter on the sample, as chapter 2 described; 10 is wide open. ENV -50 to +50 how far the envelope moves it on each note.
  • ATTACK, DECAY, SUSTAIN, RELEASE ENV, 0-10 the shape of each note, on top of the sample's own shape.
  • RATE, PITCH, FILTER LFO, 0-10 one LFO for the whole sound: how fast, and how much it moves the pitch (vibrato) and the filter.

Build MY KEYS

Go to UA03, name it MY KEYS, and press KIT/INSTR: INSTRUMENT. Then SAMPLE, SAMPLEagain, find KEYS C4, and hold 3USE. ROOT is already C4.

Play a tune and a chord: one recorded note from Glass, playing all 27 keys. Listen to the very high and very low keys: the higher you go, the shorter and brighter (and more chipmunk-like) it gets; the lower, the longer and duller. That's how a sampler plays one note across a keyboard.

  • 1It stops dead when you let go, because an instrument starts on GATE: ENV›4RELEASE›3.5, and it fades instead.
  • 2Softer and warmer: FILTER›1CUTOFF›7.0, and 3ENV›+20 so each note starts a little brighter.
  • 3Three notes at once are loud: MIX›1LEVEL›8.0.

MY KEYS

An empty instrument, with:

SAMPLEKEYS C4ROOT C4
FILTERCUTOFF 7.0ENV +20
ENVRELEASE 3.5
MIXLEVEL 8.0

Loops: a note that lasts for ever

A sample is only as long as it is. KEYS C4 dies away in under two seconds, however long you hold the key. To hold a note for ever, a sampler loops part of it: it plays to the end, jumps back, and plays that part again, over and over, for as long as the key is down.

LOOP LOOP, LOOP AT and XFADE

  • LOOP encoder 1, ON or OFF whether it loops.
  • LOOP AT encoder 2, in seconds where it jumps back to, drawn as a dashed line on the waveform; it loops from there to END. Push to zoom in on it.
  • XFADE encoder 3, 0-1000 MS a crossfade: over its last stretch, the loop fades into the sound just before LOOP AT, so the jump back doesn't click. Most loops need some.

Build VOX PAD

Go to UA04, name it VOX PAD, press KIT/INSTR for the instrument, and USE VOX C4 (Glass's voice-like sound). ROOT stays C4.

  • 1Hold a chord: it fades out after three and a half seconds, as the sample does.
  • 2LOOP›1LOOP›ON and 2LOOP AT to about 1.200 S: the steady middle of the sample. Hold a chord: it goes on for ever. Listen for a tiny bump each time round, at the join.
  • 33XFADE›160 MS. The bump smooths away.
  • 4Make it a pad: ENV›1ATTACK›5.0 and 4RELEASE›6.0; a slow, gentle vibrato with LFO›1RATE›5.2 and 2PITCH›1.2; and MIX›1LEVEL›8.0.

VOX PAD

An empty instrument, with:

SAMPLEVOX C4ROOT C4
LOOPLOOP ONLOOP AT ABOUT 1.200 SXFADE 160 MS
ENVATTACK 5.0RELEASE 6.0
LFORATE 5.2PITCH 1.2
MIXLEVEL 8.0

LOOP AT moves a thousandth of the sample a click, so 1.200 S may show as 1.197 or 1.204: near enough. Try moving it while you hold a chord: some places loop smoothly, some wobble. Finding a good loop point was a craft on the old samplers, and still is.

8.9 STRETCH on an instrument

MY KEYS showed the sampler's oldest habit: notes up high come out short and squeaky, notes down low long and groaning, because the sample plays faster or slower. For drums and keys that's often lovely. For a voice it's a problem: a choir singing a low note shouldn't sound like a recording played too slowly. STRETCH fixes it: every note plays at its own pitch, at the sample's own speed.

Build SLOW CHOIR

Go to UA05, name it SLOW CHOIR, press KIT/INSTR, and USE CHOIR: a real choir singing "aah".

  • 1The choir sings a B4, slightly sharp. Tell Taste: TUNE›4ROOT›B4 and 2FINE›-21. Now B4 on the keys plays it as recorded, and every other key is in tune with Taste's other sounds.
  • 2Play a low chord, around G3. Deep and slow, a choir of giants. Now TUNEagain for TIME, 1TIME›STRETCH, and play the same chord: a real choir's voices again, singing lower.
  • 3Slower than they sang it: 2SPEED›50%. The "aah" now lasts twice as long, at the same pitch. 3GRAIN›60 MS, long, suits voices.
  • 4ENV›4RELEASE›6.5 and MIX›1LEVEL›8.0.

SLOW CHOIR

An empty instrument, with:

SAMPLECHOIR
TUNEFINE -21ROOT B4
TIMETIME STRETCHSPEED 50%GRAIN 60 MS
ENVRELEASE 6.5
MIXLEVEL 8.0

Switch TIME back to CLASSIC for a moment and play the same chord: you'll hear exactly what STRETCH is doing. Then try SPEED at 25%, as slow as it goes: a held chord that takes ten seconds to sing its "aah".

Grains

STRETCH works by playing the sample as a stream of short overlapping pieces, grains, each one read at the note's pitch, while the place they're read from moves at SPEED. Done carefully, as Taste does, you hear the sound, not the grains. Make the grains the point instead, scatter them, freeze them, pile hundreds up at once, and you've got a different instrument altogether: that's Grit, chapter 9.

8.10 CHARACTER

The samplers of the late 1980s had a sound of their own. They stored their samples with less detail than a CD (12 bits instead of 16) and played them back at a lower rate, without smoothing between one sample and the next. That made drums crunchy and gritty, and bass heavier, and producers loved it: it's a big part of the sound of late-1980s and 1990s hip hop. CHARACTER is that, for the whole sound.

  • CLEAN as recorded, read smoothly: the sample as it is.
  • 12-BIT 12 bits at 40 kHz: gritty, a little bite.
  • 12-BIT 26K 12 bits at 26 kHz: grittier and darker, the crunchiest.

Build DUSTY BREAK

Copy MY BREAK into UA06: SOUNDS›2SOUND›UA02›3COPY TO›UA06›hold3, and name it DUSTY BREAK. Then press CHARACTER and turn encoder 1 to 12-BIT 26K. Play the slices: the same drummer, on an old record.

Give the whole loop on D5 a darker filter, as a worn record would: play D5, then FILTER›1CUTOFF›6.0. Now play MY BREAK and DUSTY BREAK one after the other. Two different decades from one sample.

8.11 Recording your own

The starter set is a start. The real fun of a sampler is your own sounds: your voice, a guitar, a chord from another unit, the kitchen. Taste records from the Root's inputs (its built-in microphone, or a microphone or line-level sound plugged in), or from any unit on the chain.

SAMPLE SOURCE, THRESH, LENGTH and REC

  • SOURCE encoder 1 what to record: the Root's LINE IN, MIC IN or BUILT-IN MIC (its own microphone); ALL, everything on the chain mixed together; any other unit by name (GLASS 2...) to sample just that one; or CARD, a WAV file from the Root's card (section 8.12). A meter under the waveform shows how loud the source is.
  • THRESH encoder 2, OFF or -60 to -6 DB OFF: recording starts the moment you push REC. Otherwise it waits (WAITING) until the sound gets louder than this, so nothing's wasted on silence before you start; a marker on the meter shows where.
  • LENGTH encoder 3, 1-60 S the longest it will record. Push the encoder on a Root input to see GAIN instead, how loud the input comes in (the same as SETUP's ROOT GAIN).
  • REC push encoder 4 start (or wait, with THRESH); push again to stop early.

A recording goes on the key being edited (or becomes the instrument), and replaces what was there. Your recordings are kept in Taste's own memory, about 83 seconds of them, and the SAMPLE page shows how much is FREE.

Build HELLO

Your own voice, on every key. Go to UA07, name it HELLO, and press KIT/INSTR for the instrument.

  • 1SAMPLE›1SOURCE›BUILT-IN MIC: the Root's own microphone, the little hole in its top. Talk, and watch the meter move.
  • 22THRESH›-30 DB, so it waits for you, and 3LENGTH›3 S.
  • 3Push 4REC. It says WAITING. Lean towards the Root and say "hello" clearly. It starts as you speak, and stops after three seconds.
  • 4Trim off the silence after it: TRIM›2END back until the dark part ends just after your word. Then make it as loud as it can be: MIX›hold4 NORMAL.
  • 5Your voice plays at its own pitch on C4 (ROOT). Play it up and down the keys: from a giant to a mouse.

Then try it with TUNEagain and TIME STRETCH: "hello" at every pitch, always the same length, a choir of you. Or press KIT/INSTR, record a few words onto keys of the kit, and CHOP AT HITS one of them into syllables.

Sampling another unit

With another unit on the chain, SOURCE can be that unit by name: play Glass or Volt and Taste records exactly what it plays, nothing else. This is how most of the starter set was made. Sample a chord from Ember and play it as an instrument, and every key plays the whole chord, the trick behind house music's chord stabs.

8.12 The card

The Root's memory card is where samples come in from a computer and go out to one. Taste uses a folder on it called TASTE.

  • Loading SAMPLE›1SOURCE›CARD: 2FILE chooses a WAV file from the folder, and pushing 4LOAD puts it on the key being edited. Any WAV will do: mono or stereo, any rate; Taste turns it into its own kind.
  • Saving On the SAMPLES page, hold 4SAVE: the sample shown is written to the folder as a WAV, named after it, to keep or to use on a computer.

8.13 Effects

Taste has no effects of its own, beyond its filter and CHARACTER. With Haze joined on, Taste's sounds get echo and reverb like any synth's, and Haze's DRIVE and DJ FILTER work beautifully on chopped loops.

8.14 Taste's SETUP

  • BEND THIS UNIT, encoder 2, 0-12 how far a MIDI keyboard's pitch bend wheel bends an instrument's notes.
  • WHEEL encoder 3, 0-10 how much vibrato the mod wheel adds.
  • VELO encoder 4, OFF or ON ON: harder is louder, from a MIDI keyboard or Step.

From MIDI, a kit plays from C2 (note 36) upwards: C2 plays the top key, C#2 the next, and so on. An instrument plays the notes as they come.

What you have at the end of this chapter

Seven sounds of your own: MY KIT, MY BREAK, MY KEYS, VOX PAD, SLOW CHOIR, DUSTY BREAK and HELLO. And the sampler's whole bag of tricks: a sound on a key, chopped, reversed, tuned, looped, stretched and roughed up. Now go and record something nobody else has.

Chapter 9 - Grit

A sound broken into thousands of tiny pieces, and played back as a cloud.

Take a sound, any sound, and cut out a tiny piece of it: a twentieth of a second, say, faded in and out so it doesn't click. That's a grain. On its own it's a little blip. Now play another grain, from a slightly different place, and another, and another, dozens a second, overlapping, some higher, some lower, some backwards, scattered left and right. You hear a cloud: the colour of the sound you started with, but frozen, smeared, shimmering or broken into glitter. That's granular synthesis, and Grit is built for it.

Grit's grains come from one of two places:

  • ·A SAMPLE: one of the samples built in (the same starter set as Taste's), one you've captured, or one from the card. Every factory sound from FA01 to FA27 is one of these, so they all play on Grit on its own.
  • ·LIVE: whatever is happening right now, from another unit on the chain, or from the Root's microphone, kept in a rolling recording a few seconds long. Grit plays grains from the last moments, and FREEZE stops time.

Granular synthesis: where it came from, and who uses it

The idea came from physics. In 1946 the physicist Dennis Gabor suggested that any sound could be thought of as a stream of tiny "acoustic quanta", grains, each too short to hear as a note on its own. In 1958 the composer Iannis Xenakis made music from it the hard way, cutting magnetic tape into tiny pieces and splicing them back together by hand. Computers made it practical: Curtis Roads wrote granular programs in the 1970s, and in 1986 Barry Truax ran the first granular synthesis in real time, so it could be played rather than calculated overnight.

For a long time it lived in universities and electronic music studios. Then computers got fast enough to do it on a laptop, and now it's in music software and synthesisers of every size: the frozen pads under film scores, the shimmering textures of ambient music, vocal smears and glitches in electronic music and pop, and stretched-out sounds that last far longer than the recording they came from. Granular synthesis is a method rather than a machine, so there's no one famous instrument to compare Grit with. Learn it here and you'll recognise it everywhere.

9.1 Find a sound you like

Grit has one factory bank, FAC A, with 32 sounds. The first 27 play from samples, so you can hear them all now. The last five, whose names start LIVE, work on whatever's playing: another unit on the chain, or the Root's microphone (section 9.8).

Try this

SOUNDS›2SOUND and go through FA01 to FA27. Hold notes and chords for a while: a lot of them change as they go. Some play on their own as soon as you reach them, without a key (SLOW TIME, RAIN CLOUD, DEEP DRONE, TOM DRONE, CLOCKWORK...): section 9.6 says why. On STUTTER, SCATTER and BROKEN KIT, play the white keys and then the black ones.

9.2 How Grit is laid out

  • 1The left column is where the grains come from and what they are: SOURCE, GRAIN, PLACE and PITCH.
  • 2The middle column is how they play: PLAY, ENV, FILTER, LFO and MIX, then SOUNDS.
  • 3The right column is FREEZE at the top (lit while frozen) and SETUP at the bottom.

The pages in the left column draw the sound the grains come from across the middle of the screen, and every grain on it as a little fade shape, where it's reading and how loud: the cloud you're hearing, as a picture. Turn SIZE or SPRAY and you'll see the shapes change as you hear it.

9.3 The sounds you'll build

Your own slots start as INIT SOUND: Taste's PAD sample, played from the keys, every setting plain, so it makes a sound as soon as you play. This chapter builds seven:

SlotSoundSectionWhat it shows
UA01MIST9.4the grain itself: size, how many, their shape
UA02SLOW BREAK9.5moving through a sound slowly, and lining the grains up
UA03SHIMMER BELLS9.5 and 9.6scattering grains, and pitching them up
UA04BREAK PLACES9.7places on the white keys, stutters on the black
UA05HOVER9.7a sound that plays itself
UA06MIST MOVING9.8the filter and LFO on MIST
UA07MY FREEZE9.9LIVE, FREEZE and CAPTURE, from the Root's microphone

Each one starts from an empty slot of USER A, so just go to the slot. To choose a sample for it, SOURCE: with FROM on SAMPLE, 2SAMPLE turns through every sample Grit has.

9.4 The grain

GRAIN SIZE, DENSITY, SHAPE and ALIGN

  • SIZE encoder 1, 5-500 MS how long each grain is. Short grains, under about 20 MS, are too short to hear the sound's pitch in them: buzzy and gritty. Long ones, over about 100 MS, are smooth and you hear the sound itself.
  • DENSITY encoder 2, 1-200 a second how many grains start each second. Few, and you hear them as separate blips; many, and they melt into a cloud.
  • SHAPE encoder 3, 0-10 how each grain fades in and out: 0 a smooth hump, all fade; 10 sharp, nearly square, so every grain clicks in. The screen draws it.
  • ALIGN encoder 4, ON or OFF ON: each new grain is lined up with the one playing, so their waves join smoothly (the trick Taste's STRETCH uses). OFF: raw, with a little roughness where they overlap.

Try this first

On INIT SOUND, in UA01, hold one note and turn SIZE right down to 5 MS: a buzz, the pad gone. Bring it up slowly and the pad comes back, first gritty, then smooth. Now SIZE at about 50 MS and DENSITY right down to 1/S: one grain a second, a little "blip" of pad each time. Turn DENSITY up and the blips crowd together, then join into a sound. Last, SHAPE at 10.0 with DENSITY around 10/S: every grain starts with a tick.

That's everything granular synthesis is made of: how long, how many, and what shape.

Build MIST

Still in UA01, name it MIST. A soft, wide cloud of the pad:

  • 1Long, smooth grains, plenty of them: GRAIN›1SIZE›315 MS, 2DENSITY›41/S, 3SHAPE›0.0.
  • 2A little scatter, so they don't all read the same place: PLACE›3SPRAY›3.0 (section 9.5).
  • 3Spread wide, left and right: MIX›2SPREAD›10.0, and 1LEVEL›6.0, as a cloud this thick is loud.
  • 4Swelling in and fading out: ENV›1ATTACK›5.0, 4RELEASE›7.0.

MIST

INIT SOUND (the PAD sample), with:

GRAINSIZE 315 MSDENSITY 41/SSHAPE 0.0
PLACESPRAY 3.0
ENVATTACK 5.0RELEASE 7.0
MIXLEVEL 6.0SPREAD 10.0

Hold a chord. The pad you know, but hovering: it doesn't move on through the sample, it stays where it is, breathing. That's section 9.5's subject.

9.5 Where the grains come from

PLACE WHERE, SCAN, SPRAY and REVERSE

  • WHERE encoder 1, 0-100% the place in the sound the grains read from: 0% the start, 100% the end. (LIVE, 100% is now, and lower is further back.) The screen marks it on the waveform.
  • SCAN encoder 2, -200% to +200% how fast WHERE moves on while a note plays. 0% stands still, on one moment for ever; +100% moves at the speed the sound was recorded, so you hear it play through; +10% takes ten times as long; negative goes backwards.
  • SPRAY encoder 3, 0-10 how scattered the grains are around WHERE: 0, every grain from the same place; 10, from all over.
  • REVERSE encoder 4, 0-100% the chance a grain plays backwards: 50%, half of them.

Build SLOW BREAK

A drum loop slowed right down, without slowing its pitch. Go to UA02 and name it SLOW BREAK.

  • 1SOURCE›2SAMPLE›BREAK: Taste's drum loop.
  • 2Start at the beginning and move through it at a tenth of its speed: PLACE›1WHERE›0%, 2SCAN›+10%, 3SPRAY›0.0.
  • 3Grains short enough for drums, lined up so they join cleanly: GRAIN›1SIZE›50 MS, 2DENSITY›41/S, 3SHAPE›2.0, 4ALIGN›ON.

SLOW BREAK

INIT SOUND, with:

SOURCESAMPLE BREAK
PLACEWHERE 0%SCAN +10%SPRAY 0.0
GRAINSIZE 50 MSDENSITY 41/SSHAPE 2.0ALIGN ON

Hold C4. The break plays at a tenth of its speed: each hit of the drums stretched into a long, ringing smear, but at the pitch it was. Hold it and watch WHERE creep along the waveform. Then turn ALIGN OFF and listen to the roughness come in where the grains overlap; and back ON.

Now play with SCAN while you hold the note: +100% and it's the break at its own speed, played by grains; -50% and it goes backwards at half speed; 0% and it hangs on one moment, a drum hit frozen into a tone.

SHIMMER BELLS, part 1: scattered

Go to UA03 and name it SHIMMER BELLS. SOURCE›2SAMPLE›BELLS C4: Glass's bell.

  • 1Read from near the strike, where the bell is loudest, and scatter the grains around it: PLACE›1WHERE›5%, 3SPRAY›4.0.
  • 2Medium grains, plenty of them: GRAIN›1SIZE›199 MS, 2DENSITY›53/S.

Hold a note: not a bell ringing out, but the bell's sound hovering, glittering, as if many bells were being struck very softly. The pitch comes next.

9.6 The pitch of the grains

PITCH PITCH, FINE, RANDOM and JUMPS

  • PITCH encoder 1, -24 to +24 semitones, for every grain. Grit's pitch and speed are apart, as Taste's STRETCH: an octave up doesn't play any faster.
  • FINE encoder 2, -50 to +50 CT fine tuning.
  • RANDOM encoder 3, OFF up to 12 ST each grain detuned at random, up to this much either way: a little, a chorus; a lot, a swarm.
  • JUMPS encoder 4, OFF, OCTAVE or OCT+5TH some of the grains an octave up (or an octave and a fifth): a shimmer above the sound.

SHIMMER BELLS, part 2: the shimmer

On SHIMMER BELLS: PITCH›4JUMPS›OCT+5TH and 3RANDOM›48 CT. Then MIX›2SPREAD›10.0, 1LEVEL›10.0, and ENV›4RELEASE›7.0.

SHIMMER BELLS

INIT SOUND, with:

SOURCESAMPLE BELLS C4
PLACEWHERE 5%SPRAY 4.0
GRAINSIZE 199 MSDENSITY 53/S
PITCHRANDOM 48 CTJUMPS OCT+5TH
ENVRELEASE 7.0
MIXLEVEL 10.0SPREAD 10.0

Play slow chords. The bells now sparkle an octave and a fifth above themselves, each grain a fraction out of tune with the next. Push RANDOM up to 3.0 ST and the shimmer becomes a swarm; take JUMPS off and it settles back down.

9.7 Three ways to play

PLAY PLAY, SYNC, GLIDE and ROOT

  • PLAY encoder 1 NOTES: the keys play the cloud at their pitch, chords and all, as an instrument. PLACES: the 16 white keys are 16 places along the sound, from the start (the top key) to the end, and the black keys stutter: they repeat what was played last, at note lengths in time with the tempo. ALWAYS: the cloud plays all the time, without a key; a key retunes it while you hold it, and lets go back to the sound's own pitch.
  • SYNC encoder 2, OFF, 1/4 ... 1/32 grains on the beat: a new grain every quarter note, eighth, triplet, sixteenth and so on, at Step's tempo (120 without it), instead of DENSITY's steady stream. The stutters always keep time.
  • GLIDE encoder 3, OFF or a time how long the pitch slides from one key to the next.
  • ROOT encoder 4, C2 to C6 the key that plays the sound at its own pitch: C4 to start. The screen says so at the bottom (C4 PLAYS IT AS IT WAS), and while you hold another key, by how much it's moved.

In PLACES, the black keys stutter at these lengths, lowest key first: 1/4, 1/8, 1/8 triplet, 1/16, 1/16 triplet, 1/32; then 1/4, 1/8, 1/16 and 1/32 backwards; and last, 1/64. A stutter repeats whatever was played last, so play a place, then hold a black key to make it stutter, then let go.

Build BREAK PLACES

Go to UA04 and name it BREAK PLACES. SOURCE›2SAMPLE›BREAK.

  • 1PLAY›1PLAY›PLACES. Each place plays on from where it starts, so: PLACE›2SCAN›+100%, at the break's own speed, and 3SPRAY›0.0.
  • 2Short, sharp grains to keep the drum hits crisp: GRAIN›1SIZE›40 MS, 3SHAPE›8.5.
  • 3Each place starts and stops exactly with your finger: ENV›1ATTACK›0.0, 4RELEASE›1.0.

BREAK PLACES

INIT SOUND, with:

SOURCESAMPLE BREAK
PLAYPLAY PLACES
PLACESCAN +100%SPRAY 0.0
GRAINSIZE 40 MSSHAPE 8.5
ENVATTACK 0.0RELEASE 1.0

Play the white keys, top to bottom, one at a time: the break, from sixteen places along it. Tap them in a new order for a new beat, like Taste's chopped break, but with no chopping. Now play a place and hold a black key under it: the hit stutters, a quarter note at a time, then faster and faster as you go down the black keys. A drum roll from one hit.

Build HOVER

A sound that plays itself. Go to UA05 and name it HOVER. SOURCE›2SAMPLE›CHOIR.

  • 1PLAY›1PLAY›ALWAYS. It starts at once, with no key.
  • 2Hold one moment of the choir: PLACE›1WHERE›40%, 2SCAN›0%, 3SPRAY›1.5.
  • 3Long, smooth, lined-up grains, and an octave above: GRAIN›1SIZE›251 MS, 2DENSITY›41/S, 3SHAPE›0.0, 4ALIGN›ON; PITCH›4JUMPS›OCTAVE; MIX›2SPREAD›10.0.
  • 4The choir sings a B4, so tell Grit: PLAY›4ROOT›B4.

HOVER

INIT SOUND, with:

SOURCESAMPLE CHOIR
PLAYPLAY ALWAYSROOT B4
PLACEWHERE 40%SCAN 0%SPRAY 1.5
GRAINSIZE 251 MSDENSITY 41/SSHAPE 0.0ALIGN ON
PITCHJUMPS OCTAVE
MIXSPREAD 10.0

A choir's "aah", held for ever, with an octave floating over it. Now hold a key: the whole cloud moves to that note, and the screen says by how much (G4, say: G4: 3RD DOWN). Let go, and it goes back to B4. Hold a key and turn WHERE: a different moment of the choir, a different vowel.

9.8 Shaping the cloud

ENV ATTACK, DECAY, SUSTAIN and RELEASE    FILTER CUTOFF, RES and TYPE    LFO RATE, WHERE, SIZE and FILTER    MIX LEVEL, SPREAD, DRY and FEEDBK

  • ATTACK, DECAY, SUSTAIN, RELEASE ENV, 0-10 the shape of each note's cloud: how it swells in and fades away.
  • CUTOFF, RES FILTER, 0-10 and TYPE LOW, HIGH or BAND: LOW keeps the bottom, HIGH the top, BAND a slice in the middle.
  • RATE LFO, in Hz one LFO, and how much it moves WHERE (the place, so the cloud wanders through the sound), SIZE (the grains grow and shrink) and FILTER.
  • LEVEL and SPREAD MIX, 0-10 how loud, and how widely the grains are scattered left and right. DRY and FEEDBK are for LIVE: section 9.9.

Build MIST MOVING

Copy MIST into UA06: SOUNDS›2SOUND›UA01›3COPY TO›UA06›hold3. Then make the cloud wander:

  • 1A band of the pad, slightly ringing: FILTER›3TYPE›BAND, 1CUTOFF›6.0, 2RES›4.0.
  • 2The LFO, slowly: LFO›1RATE›0.09 HZ, once every eleven seconds. Then 2WHERE›3.0, so the cloud drifts back and forth through the sample, and 4FILTER›5.0, so the band sweeps up and down.

Name it MIST MOVING, hold a chord and wait. It never sounds the same twice. Watch WHERE's marker drift on the PLACE page while it plays.

9.9 LIVE, FREEZE and CAPTURE

Now the other half of Grit. Set FROM to anything other than SAMPLE, and Grit listens instead: it keeps the last few seconds of what it hears in a rolling recording, the buffer, and plays its grains from that.

SOURCE FROM, BUFFER, GAIN and CAPTURE

  • FROM encoder 1 what to listen to: the Root's LINE IN, MIC IN or BUILT-IN MIC (its own microphone); ALL, every other unit on the chain; one unit by name (GLASS 2...); SAMPLE; or CARD, a WAV file from the Root's card (the GRIT folder).
  • BUFFER encoder 2, 1-20 S how much of the past the grains can reach. With WHERE at 100%, they play what's happening now; at 50%, from halfway back.
  • GAIN encoder 3, the Root's inputs only how loud the input comes in.
  • CAPTURE hold encoder 4 keeps what's in the buffer now as a sample (CAP 1, CAP 2...), to play later as a SAMPLE, here or on Taste via the card.

And then the button: FREEZE, top right. Press it and the buffer stops recording: whatever was just heard is held, and the grains play from it for as long as you like. Press it again and Grit listens once more. When you freeze, the frozen moment's ROOT becomes the lowest key that was held at that instant, on any unit on the chain, so the keys then play the frozen chord in tune.

Build MY FREEZE

This one uses the Root's own microphone, so you need nothing else; wear headphones, or Grit will hear itself through the speaker. Go to UA07 and name it MY FREEZE.

  • 1SOURCE›1FROM›BUILT-IN MIC, and 2BUFFER›4 S. Talk or hum, and watch the level meter and the scrolling waveform.
  • 2Read from just behind now, standing still once frozen: PLACE›1WHERE›95%, 2SCAN›0%, 3SPRAY›1.5.
  • 3Smooth, long grains: GRAIN›1SIZE›158 MS, 2DENSITY›31/S, 3SHAPE›0.0. And a slow swell: ENV›1ATTACK›5.5, 4RELEASE›6.5.
  • 4Now sing one long note, "aaah", and while you're still singing, press FREEZE. Stop singing. Play a key: your voice, frozen, held as long as you like. Play chords: a choir of you.

MY FREEZE

INIT SOUND, with:

SOURCEFROM BUILT-IN MICBUFFER 4 S
PLACEWHERE 95%SCAN 0%SPRAY 1.5
GRAINSIZE 158 MSDENSITY 31/SSHAPE 0.0
ENVATTACK 5.5RELEASE 6.5

Keep it: hold SOURCE›4CAPTURE while it's frozen, and it becomes a sample, CAP 1. Then unfreeze and try again with a different sound: a clap, a whistle, a laugh. A frozen clap is a strange, metallic drone.

The factory's LIVE ICE is a cousin of this one. Try it, and the other LIVE sounds, on the microphone too.

Grit on another unit

With another unit on the chain, FROM can be that unit, and Grit becomes something between an instrument and an effect: it plays clouds of whatever the other unit is playing, as it plays. Two settings on the MIX page are for that:

  • DRY MIX, encoder 3, 0-100% how much of the other unit's own sound the Root still plays. 100%: you hear it and Grit's cloud together. 0%: only the cloud (the factory's LIVE GATE uses that).
  • FEEDBK MIX, encoder 4, 0-10 feedback: some of Grit's own output goes back into its buffer, so grains of grains build up into a shimmering trail. LIVE SHINE uses a little; a lot runs away with itself.

Put Haze on Grit's left to give the cloud echo and reverb as well.

9.10 Samples, the card, and Grit's SETUP

Press SOURCE again for the SAMPLES page, as on Taste: every sample Grit has, your own first (captures, and samples loaded from the card), then the starter set. 1SAMPLE chooses, 2NAME renames your own, hold 3USE to play it, and hold 4SAVE to write it to the card's GRIT folder as a WAV. A sample of yours that no sound uses can be deleted: turn encoder 4 to DELETE and hold it.

  • BEND SETUP, THIS UNIT, 0-12 how far a MIDI keyboard's pitch bend wheel bends the cloud, in semitones.
  • WHEEL WHERE or SPRAY what a MIDI keyboard's mod wheel moves: WHERE, further back through the sound, or SPRAY, more scatter.
  • VELO OFF or ON ON: harder is louder, from a MIDI keyboard or Step.
  • PEDAL SUSTAIN or FREEZE what a sustain pedal does: holds notes, or works the FREEZE button with your foot, so both hands stay on the keys.

What you have at the end of this chapter

Seven sounds of your own: MIST, SLOW BREAK, SHIMMER BELLS, BREAK PLACES, HOVER, MIST MOVING and MY FREEZE. And the whole of granular synthesis: how long, how many, what shape, where from, what pitch, and how to play it. Any sound you can record, Grit can turn into a cloud.

Chapter 10 - Haze

Echo, reverb, chorus and drive: the room, the pedals and the tape, for every synth on the chain.

Every other unit in this book makes sounds. Haze doesn't make any: it takes the sounds the others make and does something to them. It's an effects unit: the echo off a canyon wall, the reverb of a concert hall, the shimmer of a chorus, the growl of a guitar pedal, all in one box, shared by every synth on the chain.

Chapter 2, section 2.5, said what the four main effects are. This chapter is about using them: setting them up, shaping them, and building effects of your own that make a plain sound come alive.

You need two units for this chapter

Haze makes no sound of its own: it needs another unit to work on. So this chapter needs two units joined to the Root, Haze and one other, of any kind (section 10.1 says what to do with it).

If you've only got one unit, you can't use Haze yet, but that's no reason to stop: you can design really good sounds with the one you have, and the chapter on it is where to do it. Skip on to chapter 11.

Effects: where they came from, and who uses them

The first effect was a room. Recordings in the 1930s and 40s got their reverb from where they were made, or from a special "echo chamber": a bare concrete room with a loudspeaker at one end and a microphone at the other. Studios that couldn't build one used a plate, a big sheet of steel hung in a box, shaken by the sound, from the late 1950s. Organ and guitar amplifiers used a spring, which is why surf guitar sounds the way it does.

Echo came from tape. A loop of tape running past a record head and then a playback head plays the sound back a moment later; feed it back round and it repeats, a little darker and more worn each time. Tape echo machines of the 1960s and 70s became instruments in their own right: in Jamaica, King Tubby and Lee "Scratch" Perry built a whole kind of music, dub, out of echoes and reverb, turning a song into space.

Flanging was discovered by pressing a thumb on the flange of a spinning tape reel, to slow one copy of a recording against another (the Small Faces' "Itchycoo Park", 1967, is the famous one). By the 1970s pedals did it, and phasers and choruses with it. Guitarists stood on them; keyboard players ran synthesisers through them. A plain electric piano through a chorus is the sound of half the ballads of the 1980s.

Distortion was a fault before it was a sound: an overloaded amplifier or a damaged speaker. Then it was a pedal: fuzz made the riff of the Rolling Stones' "(I Can't Get No) Satisfaction" in 1965, and overdrive and distortion pedals have been on every rock record since. Electronic music borrowed it too: an acid bass line run into a distortion pedal is a sound of its own.

Dance music added two of its own. DJ mixers grew a single filter knob, turned to make a record go muffled and then bright again, the build before a drop. And producers found that if the kick drum turned everything else down for a moment each time it hit, the whole track breathed in and out with it: the pump, all over French house records such as Stardust's "Music Sounds Better With You" (1998).

Haze has a version of each, and what you learn here will work on any effects unit, pedal or piece of music software you meet.

10.1 What you need for this chapter

Haze needs something to work on, and this chapter uses Glass's factory sounds for every example, so you can hear exactly what the book describes. If your other unit is already a Glass, you're ready. If it's something else, turn it into one for the length of this chapter. Reflashing keeps every kind's sounds (chapter 1, section 1.9), so when you flash it back, your own sounds are just where you left them.

On the other unit (not Haze), press SETUP until you reach the RESET page, then:

1RESET›REFLASH›3BECOME›GLASS›hold4

It starts again as Glass. Glass's factory sounds are in FAC A, and you'll use five of them, chosen on Glass's own SOUNDS page:

Glass's soundCodeUsed for
E.PIANO 1FA11reverb, chorus and the pump
STRINGS 1FA04a big hall
MARIMBAFA22echo
BASS 1FA15drive
BRASS 1FA01the DJ filter

SOUNDS›1BANK›FAC A›2SOUND›FA11 (on Glass)

Which unit is which

From here on, a route on its own is on Haze. When a step is on Glass, the book says so.

10.2 Find a preset you like

Haze's keys don't play notes. The white keys are sixteen presets, one press each: press one and Haze switches to it and sends every synth on the chain into it, so you hear it straight away on whatever you play. They start as the first sixteen factory presets: PLATE, BIG HALL, CAVE, SPRING, TAPE ECHO, DUB ECHO, SLAPBACK, ECHO HALL, CHORUS, FLANGER, PHASER, PUMP, ACID DRIVE, FUZZ BASS, WARM DRIVE and DJ SWEEP, lowest key first.

Try this

On Glass, choose E.PIANO 1 (FA11). Play a few notes and short chords on Glass, and with your other hand press Haze's white keys one at a time, from the bottom up. Some are obvious at once (BIG HALL, TAPE ECHO); some need Glass to play a sound they suit (the drives want a bass). Note down the ones you like.

The black keys are tap tempo: tap two or more in time and the echoes that follow the tempo (section 10.8) follow you. The TAP button does the same. Their lights flash the beat.

Haze has 32 factory presets in all, FAC A, on the SOUNDS page: SOUNDS›1BANK›FAC A›2PRESET. The white keys are your own copies of the first sixteen, USER A 01 to 16, so you can change them; the factory ones stay as they are.

10.3 How Haze is laid out

  • 1The left column, COLOUR, works on one synth you choose: SOURCE (which synth), DRIVE (distortion), FILTER (the DJ filter) and PUMP. Under them, BYPASS switches COLOUR off for a moment, to compare.
  • 2The middle column, SPACE, is shared by every synth: SENDS (how much of each goes in), MOD (chorus, flanger, phaser), ECHO and REVERB. Under them, FREEZE, and SOUNDS at the bottom.
  • 3The right column has TAP at the top and SETUP at the bottom.

Every setting reads 0 to 99, or a time, or a name; turn its encoder. Two pages have a second page: press ECHO or REVERB again.

10.4 Two halves: SPACE and COLOUR

First, two words you'll meet all through this chapter, and on any effects unit. A sound with no effect on it, just as the synth makes it, is dry. The effect's part of the sound, the echoes or the reverb's tail or the chorus's moving copy, is wet. Most effects are a mix of the two: the dry sound you play, with some wet around it.

On Haze, WET is also the name of how much of a synth goes into its effects: turn a synth's WET up and more of it goes in, so more echo or reverb comes out around it. Its dry sound doesn't change.

Haze has two halves, and they work in two different ways, the two ways a mixing desk uses effects.

  • ·SPACE is for the effects that add something around a sound: chorus, echo, reverb. Each synth sends Haze a share of itself, its WET, and Haze adds only the effect. The synth's own sound still plays at the Root, as it always does. So turning a synth's WET up adds more echo or reverb without taking anything away, and every synth can share the same room.
  • ·COLOUR is for the effects that change a sound itself: drive, the DJ filter, the pump. They only make sense on one sound at a time, so COLOUR works on one synth you choose, and plays it in place of the synth's own sound. MIX says how much: at 100% you hear only Haze's version.

The two connect: the synth that COLOUR works on can also be sent into SPACE at its WET, after its drive and filter, as a guitar's pedals come before the amplifier's reverb.

10.5 The presets you'll build

This chapter builds eight presets of your own, in USER A 17 to 24. Those slots start as INIT FX: a plate reverb at a moderate level and everything else off, a plain place to start. (USER A 01 to 16 are the white keys; you can copy your favourites there at the end, section 10.14.)

SOUNDS›1BANK›USER A›2PRESET›UA17

Name each one as you build it, on the SOUNDS page with 4NAME (turn for the letter, push for the next one), as on every unit. By the end, USER A will hold:

SlotPresetSectionOn Glass'sWhat it shows
UA17MY PLATE10.7E.PIANO 1a plate reverb, and pre-delay
UA18MY HALL10.7STRINGS 1a big, dark hall
UA19MY ECHO10.8MARIMBAa tape echo in time with the tempo
UA20MY DUB10.8MARIMBArunaway repeats, ping-pong, a spring, and FREEZE
UA21MY CHORUS10.9E.PIANO 1chorus, flanger and phaser
