10.6 Sending a sound into Haze

Choose UA17 on Haze, and on Glass choose E.PIANO 1 (FA11). Play: you hear the electric piano, dry, just as before. Nothing goes into Haze until you send it.

SENDS›1GLASS›30

SENDS has one encoder for every other unit on the chain that makes a sound (Step, which only plays the others, has none), four to a page (press SENDS again for the next four), each named and with its MIDI channel underneath. Turn Glass's to 30 and play again: now there's a room around the piano. That's INIT FX's plate reverb. Turn WET up and down while you play: 0 is none, 99 is drenched. WET belongs to the synth and the chain, not to the preset, so it stays where you put it whichever preset you choose.

WET and LEVEL

Two things set how loud an effect is: how much of each synth goes in (its WET, on SENDS), and how much of the effect comes out (each effect's LEVEL or VOLUME). WET is how a synth sits in the room; LEVEL is the room itself. Set LEVEL for the preset, and WET for each sound.

10.7 Reverb

A reverb is thousands of echoes so close together that they blur into one tail. Haze's REVERB page has four settings:

  • TYPE REVERB, encoder 1 PLATE: bright and dense, the classic studio sound, flattering on almost anything. HALL: bigger and slower, a large room. SPRING: twangy and bouncy, with a chirp on sharp sounds.
  • DECAY REVERB, encoder 2 how long the tail lasts, as a time: 0.3S to 8.0S for a plate or hall, 0.4S to 4.0S for a spring.
  • TONE REVERB, encoder 3, 0-99 how bright the tail stays. Low: a tail that darkens as it fades, like a big soft room. High: bright and splashy.
  • LEVEL REVERB, encoder 4, 0-99 how loud the reverb is.

MY PLATE

On UA17, with Glass's E.PIANO 1 sent at 30, turn REVERB›2DECAY from 1.0S to 1.1S, and 3TONE down from 60 to 55. Play short chords and listen to the tail: the piano now sounds as if it's in a small, bright studio.

Now press REVERB again for its second page:

REVERBREVERB 2›1PRE-DLY›20MS

PRE-DLY is a short wait before the reverb starts, 0 to 198 ms. In a real room the first reflections take a moment to come back from the walls, and a bigger room means a longer wait. It also keeps the start of each note clean: the piano's attack is heard on its own, and the reverb blooms just after. Try 100MS and play short notes: you can hear the gap. Then go back to 20MS, just enough to keep the piano clear. Turn REVERB›4LEVEL down to 50 if it's grown, and name the preset MY PLATE.

MY PLATE (UA17)

A small, bright studio around an electric piano.

REVERBTYPE PLATEDECAY 1.1STONE 55LEVEL 50
REVERB 2PRE-DLY 20MS
SOURCEKEY WET 30
SENDSGLASS 30

MY HALL

Choose UA18 on Haze and STRINGS 1 (FA04) on Glass. A hall wants a long, slow sound to fill it. Set:

REVERB›1TYPE›HALL›2DECAY›4.3S›3TONE›40›4LEVEL›60

Hold a chord, then let go and listen to it hang in the air for seconds. TONE at 40 makes the tail darker than the strings, so it sits behind them rather than on top. On REVERB 2, set PRE-DLY to 60MS: a big room, a long wait. Then on SOURCE›4KEY WET›35 (section 10.14 explains it), and name it MY HALL.

MY HALL (UA18)

A big, dark hall behind slow strings.

REVERBTYPE HALLDECAY 4.3STONE 40LEVEL 60
REVERB 2PRE-DLY 60MS
SOURCEKEY WET 35

Less than you think

Reverb is the easiest effect to overdo. A sound with too much sounds far away and washed out, and on a busy track every part blurs into the next. Turn LEVEL up until you can hear it clearly, then back until you only miss it when it's gone.

10.8 Echo

Haze's echo works the way a tape echo does: the sound is recorded onto a loop and played back a moment later, and each repeat goes round again, a little darker and more worn. Its page:

  • RATE ECHO, encoder 1 how long until each repeat: 1000MS down to 60MS (FREE), or pushed, a note value that follows the tempo (below).
  • REPEATS ECHO, encoder 2, 0-99 how much of each repeat goes round again: low, one or two echoes; high, a long trail; near the top, more than ever went in (below).
  • VOLUME ECHO, encoder 3, 0-99 how loud the echoes are. INIT FX starts at 0: no echo.
  • TONE ECHO, encoder 4, 0-99 how bright the echoes are. Lower is darker and more like old tape.

MY ECHO

Choose UA19 on Haze and MARIMBA (FA22) on Glass, and make sure Glass is still sent (SENDS, 30). Short, sharp notes show off an echo best. Turn ECHO›3VOLUME›60 and play a single note: it comes back every 321 milliseconds, quieter each time.

Echoes sound best in time with the music. Push RATE:

ECHO›push1›1RATE›1/8 D

Now RATE is a note value, 1/32 up to 1/2 (T for triplets, D for dotted), at the tempo shown under it. With Step on the chain it's Step's tempo; without it, tap one in on TAP or the black keys, two taps or more. Play a simple tune at 120 beats a minute (tap it in), and the dotted eighth's echo makes its own rhythm against yours: the trick behind a thousand guitar riffs.

Set 2REPEATS›40 and 4TONE›45, turn the reverb down on REVERB›4LEVEL›15 so the echoes stay clear, and name it MY ECHO.

MY ECHO (UA19)

Echoes in time with the tune, a dotted eighth apart.

ECHORATE 1/8 DREPEATS 40VOLUME 60TONE 45
REVERBLEVEL 15
SOURCEKEY WET 30

MY DUB

Dub engineers played the echo like an instrument. Choose UA20, keep MARIMBA, and set an echo a quarter note apart, dark, with lots of repeats:

ECHO›push1›1RATE›1/4›2REPEATS›75›3VOLUME›65›4TONE›25

Play one note and listen: the repeats go on and on, getting darker. Now turn REPEATS up slowly, past 90. Somewhere near the top more goes round than came in: the echo stops dying away and grows, howling and distorting on its own, the way a tape echo does when it's pushed. Turn it back to 75 before it gets out of hand. That edge, turned up and down by hand, is a dub sound.

Press ECHO again for ECHO 2:

ECHOECHO 2›1PINGPONG›ON

Now the repeats bounce from left to right and back, which is best heard on headphones. (Ping-pong reads the tape twice, so each side's gap can't be longer than half a second: at slow tempos the longest values are shortened.)

Last, the room: REVERB›1TYPE›SPRING›2DECAY›1.6S›3TONE›40›4LEVEL›45. The echoes go into the reverb, so each repeat lands in its own twangy space. Name it MY DUB.

Now play a phrase and press FREEZE, the button under REVERB. Its light comes on, and the echo and reverb stop taking anything new in and hold what they have, round and round, for as long as you like. Play over the top: your new notes are dry against the frozen wash. Press FREEZE again and the wash fades away as normal. It's a performance button: it isn't kept with the preset.

MY DUB (UA20)

Dark echoes bouncing side to side into a spring; ride REPEATS and FREEZE by hand.

ECHORATE 1/4REPEATS 75VOLUME 65TONE 25
ECHO 2PINGPONG ON
REVERBTYPE SPRINGDECAY 1.6STONE 40LEVEL 45
SOURCEKEY WET 30

10.9 Chorus, flanger and phaser

The MOD page holds three close relatives, all made by mixing a sound with a copy of itself that moves:

  • MODE MOD, encoder 1 OFF; CHORUS, two copies swaying slightly in pitch, one left and one right, for width and warmth; FLANGER, a very short echo fed back into itself, the jet-plane whoosh; PHASER, harmonics cancelled out by a sweeping filter, a softer, rounder swirl.
  • RATE MOD, encoder 2 how fast it sways: 0.08HZ to 4.00HZ, or pushed, once per note value, from 1/16 to 16/1 (sixteen whole notes), following the tempo.
  • DEPTH MOD, encoder 3, 0-99 how far.
  • LEVEL MOD, encoder 4, 0-99 how loud the moving copies are against the synth's own sound.

MY CHORUS

Choose UA21 on Haze and E.PIANO 1 on Glass again. Set a slow, gentle chorus:

MOD›1MODE›CHORUS›2RATE›0.21HZ›3DEPTH›55›4LEVEL›60

Play chords and hold them. The piano spreads out across both speakers and gains a slow, liquid wobble. Turn LEVEL down to 0 and back up to hear the difference: dry, it's a plain piano. With chorus it's the sound of a thousand records. Turn the reverb down to REVERB›4LEVEL›20, set SOURCE›4KEY WET›45 (chorus likes more), and name it MY CHORUS.

MY CHORUS (UA21)

A wide, warm, swaying electric piano.

MODMODE CHORUSRATE 0.21HZDEPTH 55LEVEL 60
REVERBLEVEL 20
SOURCEKEY WET 45

Try this

On MY CHORUS, turn MOD›1MODE to FLANGER, then PHASER, holding a chord. Then push 2RATE and turn it to 2/1: the sweep now takes two whole notes, a slow rise and fall that keeps time with the music. Turn MODE back to CHORUS and RATE back (push it again for 0.21HZ) before you move on, or keep the version you like best: it's your preset.

10.10 COLOUR: choosing a synth

The left column works on one synth. First you choose it:

SOURCE›1SYNTH›GLASS

  • SYNTH SOURCE, encoder 1 NONE, or any other unit on the chain.
  • MIX SOURCE, encoder 2, 0-100% how much of Haze's version you hear. The Root plays the rest of the synth's own sound, so at 100% you hear only Haze's, and at 50% half and half, the way a pedal's blend knob works.
  • KEY WET SOURCE, encoder 4, 0-99 the preset's send for its white key (section 10.14).

Like WET, SYNTH and MIX belong to the chain, not the preset: they stay as you set them whichever preset you choose.

BYPASS, under PUMP, switches COLOUR off and on. While it's lit, the chosen synth plays clean, all of it from the Root (and still sent into SPACE at its WET). Use it to compare: does the drive make the sound better, or just louder?

10.11 Drive

Drive is what happens when a sound is pushed harder than it can go: the tops of the wave are squashed flat, and the squashing adds new harmonics. A little sounds warm and thick; a lot sounds hard and aggressive. DRIVE has three kinds, after the three classic kinds of pedal:

  • MODE DRIVE, encoder 1 OFF; OVERDRIVE, the gentlest: mostly the middle of the sound breaks up, the bass stays clean; DISTORTION, harder and buzzier; FUZZ, the most extreme, a thick, square buzz.
  • DRIVE DRIVE, encoder 2, 0-99 how hard it's pushed.
  • TONE DRIVE, encoder 3, 0-99 darker or brighter.
  • LEVEL DRIVE, encoder 4, 0-99 how loud it comes out.

MY DRIVE

Choose UA22 on Haze and BASS 1 (FA15) on Glass, and make sure SOURCE's SYNTH is GLASS and MIX is 100%. Play a few bass notes. Now:

DRIVE›1MODE›DISTORTION›2DRIVE›55

The clean, round FM bass turns gritty and hard. Press BYPASS on and off while you play. The driven version is louder, and louder always sounds better at first (chapter 2, section 2.6), so it isn't a fair test. Turn DRIVE›4LEVEL down until switching BYPASS on and off changes the sound but not how loud it is: about 31. Now you can tell whether you like it. Try OVERDRIVE and FUZZ too, and TONE: each needs LEVEL set again.

Finish with a touch of room, REVERB›4LEVEL›15 and SOURCE›4KEY WET›15, and name it MY DRIVE.

MY DRIVE (UA22)

A gritty, distorted bass, no louder than the clean one.

DRIVEMODE DISTORTIONDRIVE 55TONE 50LEVEL 31
REVERBLEVEL 15
SOURCESYNTH GLASSMIX 100%KEY WET 15

10.12 The DJ filter

The FILTER page is a DJ mixer's filter: one knob that goes both ways.

  • FILTER FILTER, encoder 1 OFF in the middle. Turn it down and a low-pass filter closes, from LP 17.8K down to LP 60, taking the top off until only a muffled thud is left. Turn it up and a high-pass filter opens, from HP 17 up to HP 6.0K, taking the bass away until only a thin fizz is left.
  • RESO FILTER, encoder 2, 0-99 resonance: a peak at the filter's edge, which makes a sweep sing.

MY SWEEP

Choose UA23 on Haze, BRASS 1 (FA01) on Glass, with Glass still chosen on SOURCE. Hold a note, and turn FILTER›1FILTER slowly down from OFF, then all the way back up past OFF and on into the high-pass, and back to OFF. That's the DJ's move: down to build tension, back up to release it, or up through the high-pass to thin a sound out before the drop.

Turn 2RESO up to 20 and sweep again: the edge of the filter whistles as it moves. More RESO whistles more, but it also makes the sound louder at the edge: a big, loud chord through a lot of RESO can go over the top, and Haze rounds it off rather than letting it crack. If it starts to sound harsh, turn RESO down.

Leave FILTER at LP 2.0K, a warm, muffled brass to sweep up from; add REVERB›4LEVEL›20 and SOURCE›4KEY WET›20, and name it MY SWEEP. When you call it up, sweep the filter to taste: it's meant to be moved.

MY SWEEP (UA23)

A muffled brass, ready to be swept open by hand.

FILTERFILTER LP 2.0KRESO 20
REVERBLEVEL 20
SOURCESYNTH GLASSKEY WET 20

10.13 The pump

The pump turns something down each time another sound plays, and lets it back up after. Its page:

  • KEY PUMP, encoder 1 the synth whose sound does the ducking, NONE or any unit on the chain. Like SYNTH, it belongs to the chain, not the preset.
  • DEPTH PUMP, encoder 2, 0-99 how far it ducks.
  • RELEASE PUMP, encoder 3 how long it takes to come back up, 40MS to 800MS.
  • TARGET PUMP, encoder 4 what gets ducked: COLOUR (the chosen synth), SPACE (the echo and reverb), or BOTH.

In a dance track the KEY is the kick drum, and everything else pumps in time with it. That needs a drum unit as well as a synth, three units in all, and the Music Production manual does it. With one synth, the pump has a cleverer use: the synth can duck its own echoes.

MY DUCK

Choose UA24 on Haze and E.PIANO 1 on Glass, sent on SENDS at about 35. First an echo and a hall:

ECHO›push1›1RATE›1/4›2REPEATS›55›3VOLUME›70

REVERB›1TYPE›HALL›2DECAY›2.2S›4LEVEL›40

Play a busy phrase: it's a mess, echoes piling on top of the notes. Now the pump:

PUMP›1KEY›GLASS›2DEPTH›80›3RELEASE›182MS›4TARGET›SPACE

Play the same phrase. While you play, the echoes and reverb duck out of the way; the moment you stop, they bloom up into the gap. Your notes stay clear, and the space fills in around them. Engineers do this to vocals all the time. RELEASE sets how quickly the space comes back: shorter for fast playing, longer for slow. Name it MY DUCK.

MY DUCK (UA24)

Echoes and a hall that get out of the way while you play.

PUMPKEY GLASSDEPTH 80RELEASE 182MSTARGET SPACE
ECHORATE 1/4REPEATS 55VOLUME 70TONE 50
REVERBTYPE HALLDECAY 2.2SLEVEL 40
SOURCEKEY WET 35

10.14 The white keys, KEY WET and Haze's SETUP

A white key does two things: it calls up its preset, USER A 01 to 16, and it sets every synth's send to that preset's KEY WET (SOURCE, encoder 4). That's why each recipe in this chapter has a KEY WET: it's how much of everything goes in when you call the preset up with a key, so a reverb comes in gently and a chorus strongly. Choosing a preset on the SOUNDS page doesn't touch the sends.

To put one of your presets on a white key, copy it over one of the sixteen: on the SOUNDS page, choose it, then 3COPY TO the slot of the key you want (UA01 is the lowest white key, UA16 the highest) and hold3. The preset that was there is replaced; the factory ones are always on FAC A to copy back.

Haze's SETUP has one setting of its own, on THIS UNIT beside the MIDI channel:

  • KEYS encoder 2 + SENDS: a white key calls up its preset and sets every synth's send to its KEY WET, as above. PRESET: a white key only calls up the preset, and every synth's send stays where you set it.

What you have at the end of this chapter

Eight presets of your own: MY PLATE, MY HALL, MY ECHO, MY DUB, MY CHORUS, MY DRIVE, MY SWEEP and MY DUCK. Between them they use every page on Haze. They work on any synth, not only on Glass: flash your other unit back to what it was (its own sounds are all still there), send it into Haze, and try each one on its sounds. A good effect changes how you play, so play.

Chapter 11 - Where next

You know how sound is made now. The rest is up to you.

11.1 What you've learned

Think back to chapter 2. Pitch, tone, shape, movement, effects, loudness: six things that every sound is made of. Since then you've built sounds out of each of them, from scratch, by hand.

You've built tones from sine waves, one operator modulating another, the way the bell-like sounds of the 1980s were made. You've started from bright, buzzy waves and carved them with a filter, the way the classic analogue synthesisers did, for basses, leads, pads and brass. You've made drums from nothing but oscillators and noise. You've moved a sound between four waves at once, played back recordings across the keyboard, and broken sounds into thousands of grains and scattered them. And you've put all of it into a room, an echo, a chorus and a distortion pedal.

If you've worked through every chapter, you now know more about how sound is made than most musicians ever learn. Plenty of people play synthesisers for years without knowing why a filter whistles, what an operator does or where a reverb's tail comes from. You do. And you know it the best way there is: not from reading about it, but from turning the encoders and listening to what happened.

Two things to take away from all of it, the same two the book started with.

The first: a good sound is one you like. Not the one that's most like a famous record, not the one with the most going on, not the one somebody else told you was right. Every recipe in this book is a starting point. If you turned something further than the recipe said and liked it better, you were right and the recipe was wrong.

The second: the best sounds are found, not planned. Remember the beginning of the book: some of the most famous sounds in music were accidents, a machine used the wrong way, a setting turned too far, a mistake somebody liked. Every time you turned something past where it was meant to go, just to hear what happened, you were doing what those people did. Keep doing it. Turn things too far. Send a sound somewhere it was never meant to go. Try the setting that can't possibly work. Most of the time it won't. The times it does are the sounds that will be yours.

11.2 Your unit, from now on

Start with the biggest thing you've got out of this book, which isn't in the box at all. What you've learned works on every synthesiser there is. Operators, filters, envelopes, LFOs, wavetables, samples, grains, sends and inserts: these are the same ideas, with the same names, on every synthesiser, every effects unit and every piece of music software you'll ever sit down at. The knobs will be in different places and the screens will look different, but you'll know what they do, and you'll know where to start. Most people faced with a new synthesiser scroll through its presets. You can make your own.

And the unit in front of you isn't finished with you just because the book is. It was never only a way to learn: it's an instrument, and it's yours.

  • ·Play it. A unit and a Root are a complete synthesiser: headphones or speakers on the Root, a power bank or a phone charger for power, and you can play anywhere, on its own keys or from a MIDI keyboard. Turned sideways (chapter 1), it's a little keyboard instrument for a desk, a sofa or a train.
  • ·Play it from a computer. Plug the Root's USB-C into a computer and the computer sees it as a MIDI device: music software can play your unit, from a recorded part or from the keyboard plugged into the computer, and an editor or librarian can send it sounds (Glass's, chapter 3). The sound itself doesn't travel over USB: take it from the Root's LINE OUT into the computer's audio interface, or into a mixer, and record it like any other instrument.
  • ·Play it with other instruments. The Root's MIDI IN takes notes from any keyboard, sequencer or drum machine with a MIDI OUT, each unit on its own channel (chapter 1, section 1.10), so your unit can be one voice in a bigger setup. MIDI OUT passes a copy of what comes in on to the next instrument (THRU), and once you have Step it sends Step's notes and its clock out too, so your other instruments can play along and keep time with it.
  • ·Keep building. Every one of your banks has room for sounds you haven't made yet. Back them up to a card (chapter 1, section 1.9), swap them with friends, and when you're ready, flash the unit as something else and start on its sounds too. Your sounds are never lost: every kind keeps its own.

11.3 The whole Tessel

This book has been about making sounds, one unit at a time. But a Tessel was never meant to be limited to just one unit. Units snap together side by side, as many as eight on a Root, and the moment you join a second one, everything changes.

Join a Volt and a Strike and you have a bass line and a beat. Add Ember or Glass for chords, Haze for the room, Taste for a vocal chop, Grit for a texture drifting underneath. Each unit is a complete instrument with its own screen and its own keys, so there are no menus to dig through: everything you've learned in this book, on every unit, at your fingertips at once. And because every unit can be flashed as any other, the set you own can change shape with the music you're making: today a techno rig, tomorrow an ambient one.

There are two modules this book hasn't covered. The first is the one that turns a row of synths into music: Step, the sequencer. Step plays every unit on the chain at once, sixteen tracks of notes on a timeline of bars and beats, with accents, slides, chords, an arpeggiator, swing and a mixer, and it remembers which sound every unit was on, so a whole song comes back at the press of a button.

The second is Pilot, the controller. It makes no sound of its own: it gathers the knobs you reach for most, from any units on the chain, onto pages of four, so a filter on one unit, an echo on another and the tempo can all sit under your fingers together. Its keys call up scenes, every unit switching sound at once. Pilot's changes are always temporary, so you can twist a sound as far as you like in the middle of a set and it's still waiting, untouched, for next time.

Step has a book of its own: Making Music, the companion to this one. Where this book taught you how sounds are made, that one teaches you what to do with them: how Step works, and then how real tracks are built, one style of electronic music at a time, from techno and acid to house and beyond, starting with just three units and growing as your setup grows. Each chapter says which modules it needs, so you can always start with what you've got.

Put it together and a Tessel is whatever you need it to be:

  • ·A synthesiser, on its own, in your bag, ready wherever you are.
  • ·A groovebox: Step, a drum unit and a bass, everything in one row, no computer anywhere.
  • ·A live instrument: songs that come back at a press, sounds you can grab and twist with your hands, Haze's FREEZE and DJ filter, Pilot's pages and scenes, every part of the music in reach on stage.
  • ·A whole studio: write, arrange, mix and play out a finished track from first idea to last note, without ever opening a computer. Sample your own voice through the Root's microphone, record a friend's guitar into Taste, and it's all in the same row.
  • ·A part of a bigger setup: MIDI in, MIDI out, a computer over USB, a mixer on the LINE OUT. A Tessel plays well with others.

Start where you are, with what you've got, and add a module when the music asks for one. Every one you add makes every other one do more.

Now go and make something

That's the end of the book, and the start of the good bit. Make sounds nobody's heard before. Make music with them. Get things wrong on purpose and keep the mistakes you like.

And when you've made something, we'd love to hear it. Tell us what you've done with your Tessel: the sounds, the tracks, the strange setups and the happy accidents. Write to us at Utopian Instruments, [address to come].

Enjoy what you make.

Every button, every page, every encoder, on one page per unit.

For when you know what you want and just need to find it. Each unit's map shows its buttons as they sit on the panel, with the four boxes of each page in the corners where they'll appear on the screen: encoder 1 top left, 2 top right, 3 bottom left, 4 bottom right. A button with a second page shows it underneath (press the button again to get there). Under each map, a line on every control.

WHEELwhat moves the WHEEL encoder: MOD WHEEL, BREATH, EXPRESSION, AFTERTOUCH or OFF
VELOOFF: every CLASSIC note equally loud; ON: harder is louder

Strike

The white keys are the drums, the same on every kit: 1 KICK, 2 PERC, 3 SNARE, 4 TAMB, 5 RIM, 6 CLAP, 7 CL HAT, 8 OP HAT, 9 LO TOM, 10 MID TOM, 11 HI TOM, 12 CRASH, 13 RIDE, 14 COWBELL, 15 CLAVES, 16 MARACAS. In one of your own kits, hold a key: turn any encoder for that key's drum from another kit, or NONE.

EDIT the drum last played; encoder 1 is always LEVEL. Push: the factory's value
BOOMkick: TUNE, DECAY, TONE. snare: TUNE, TONE, SNAPPY. toms: TUNE, TYPE (TOM or CONGA). open hat: DECAY. cymbal: DECAY, TONE. cowbell: TUNE. the rest: LEVEL only
PUNCHkick: TUNE, DECAY, ATTACK. snare: TUNE, TONE, SNAPPY. toms: TUNE, DECAY. hats: DECAY. crash and ride: TUNE. the rest: LEVEL only
SPARK, VELVETLEVEL only, on every drum
NEONevery drum: TUNE, BEND (how fast the pitch falls), DECAY
TIMBERkick: TUNE, DECAY, BEATER. snare: TUNE, DECAY, SNARES (0: off). hats, toms, crash, ride: TUNE, DECAY. rim, cowbell, claves: TUNE. clap, maracas, tambourine: DECAY
THIS UNIT Strike's own setting (SETUP)
ACCENThow much louder an accented step from Step is: OFF or +1 to +10 dB

Ember

Every setting is for all six voices at once. Sliders read 0-10.

LFO the slow wobble, shared by every voice
RATEhow fast, 0-10
DELAYhow long it waits before fading in, from the first key of each phrase, 0-10
DCO the oscillator
RANGEthe octave: 16', 8', 4'
LFOvibrato: how far the LFO moves the pitch, 0-10
PWMthe pulse's width (MANUAL), or how far the LFO moves it (LFO), 0-10
PWM MODELFO or MANUAL
WAVES what the oscillator makes
PULSE, SAWeach on or off
SUBa square an octave below, 0-10
NOISEhiss, 0-10
VCF the low-pass filter, and the high-pass after all six voices
FREQwhere it starts to cut, 0-10
RESresonance, 0-10: near the top it whistles
KYBDhow much it follows the keys, 0-10
HPF0 a little bass boost, 1 flat, 2 and 3 cut the bass
VCF MOD what moves the filter
ENVhow far the envelope opens it, 0-10
POLARITYNORMAL opens it; INVERT closes it
LFOhow far the LFO moves it, 0-10
ENV the one envelope: the filter (by VCF MOD's ENV) and the loudness (unless VCA is GATE)
A, D, S, Rattack, decay, sustain level, release, 0-10
VCA the loudness
VCAENV: shaped by the envelope; GATE: on while the key is down
LEVELthe sound's volume, 0-10
CHORUS the two buttons
Ia slow, gentle sway
IIfaster
I+IIboth on: a fast, shallow shimmer
THIS UNIT Ember's own settings (SETUP)
BENDhow far pitch bend goes, 0-12 semitones
VCF BENDhow far the same wheel moves the filter, 0-10
WHEELhow much vibrato the mod wheel adds, 0-10
VELOOFF: every note equally loud; ON: harder is louder

Axis

On every envelope page, push encoder 1 for its loop: SUSTAIN, LOOP AT, REPEATS, BOUNCE (push again for the points). The VECTOR page's top boxes are empty: the diamond is drawn there.

OSC A-D each corner's oscillator
WAVEwhich of the 128 waves, 0-127 (eight families of 16)
COARSEpitch, -24 to +24 semitones
FINE-100 to +100 cents
LEVELhow loud this corner is, 0-10
VECTOR the diamond (press again for its envelope)
Xtowards A (-100) or C (+100)
Ytowards B (-100) or D (+100)
VECTOR ENV moves the point while the note plays
POINTwhich of the five points, 0-4
TIMEhow long to get to it, 4 ms to 41 s
X, Ywhere it is on the diamond
FILTER the resonant low-pass filter
CUTOFFwhere it cuts, in Hz
RESresonance, 0-10
ENVhow far FILTER ENV moves it, -100 to +100
KEYBOARDhow much it follows the keys, 0-10
FILTER ENV, AMP ENV five-point envelopes
POINTwhich point, 0-4
TIMEhow long to get to it, 4 ms to 41 s
LEVELits level, 0-10
SUSTAINthe point it holds at while the key is down
LOOP ATloop view: where a loop goes back to
REPEATSloop view: OFF, 1-7 or FOR EVER
BOUNCEloop view: ON, back and forth
LFO 1, LFO 2 two slow wobbles (what they move is set on MOD)
RATEhow fast, in Hz
SHAPETRIANGLE, SAW UP, SAW DOWN, SQUARE or RANDOM
DELAYhow long before it fades in
MOD six connections: a source moving a destination
SLOTwhich connection, 1-6
SOURCELFO 1, LFO 2, FILT ENV, AMP ENV, VELOCITY, WHEEL, KEY, PRESSURE or NONE
DESTPITCH, CUTOFF, RES, LEVEL, X, Y, PAN, WAVE A-D or WAVES (WAVE SCAN)
AMOUNThow much, -100 to +100
CHORUS the stereo chorus (press CHORUS again: on or off)
CHORUSON or OFF
RATEhow fast, in Hz
DEPTHhow deep, 0-10
SPREADhow wide the voices sit, 0-10
KEYS how it plays
MODEPOLY (8 notes), UNISON (all eight on one) or MONO
DETUNEUNISON: how far apart, 0-10
GLIDEOFF or a time
LEVELthe sound's volume, 0-10
THIS UNIT Axis's own settings (SETUP)
BENDhow far pitch bend goes, 0-12 semitones
VELOON: harder is louder; OFF: every note the same

Taste

In a kit the pages work on the key last played (its name is in the top bar). On TRIM and LOOP, push a marker's encoder to zoom in on it. SAMPLE from CARD: encoder 2 is FILE and encoder 4 LOAD; from a Root input, push encoder 3 for GAIN.

SAMPLE recording onto the key being edited (or the instrument)
SOURCELINE IN, MIC IN, BUILT-IN MIC, ALL, a unit by name, or CARD
THRESHOFF (start at once) or -60 to -6 dB: wait until the sound is this loud
LENGTHthe longest take, 1-60 s (push on a Root input: GAIN)
RECpush to record, push again to stop
SAMPLES every sample (SAMPLE pressed again)
SAMPLEwhich one; your own first, then the starter set (*)
NAMEyour own: turn for the letter, push for the next
USEhold: on the key being edited (or the instrument)
SAVEhold: onto the card's TASTE folder as a WAV
TRIM which part plays
START, ENDwhere it starts and stops, in seconds (push: zoom)
REVERSEON: backwards
TRIGGER1-SHOT (plays to the end) or GATE (while held)
LOOP holding a note for ever
LOOPON or OFF
LOOP ATwhere it jumps back to (push: zoom)
XFADEthe crossfade over the join, 0-1000 ms
CHOP slices onto the keys from this one up
SLICEShow many, 2-27 (COPY: TO, the key to copy onto)
MODEEVENLY, AT HITS, or COPY
SENSAT HITS: how small a jump counts, 0-10
CHOPhold: do it (COPY: copy it)
TUNE pitch
COARSE-24 to +24 semitones
FINE-50 to +50 cents
BEATSOFF or 1-64: last this many beats at the tempo
ROOTan instrument's own note
TIME TUNE pressed again
TIMECLASSIC (speed is pitch) or STRETCH (apart)
SPEEDSTRETCH: 25% to 400%
GRAINSTRETCH: the grains' length, 10-100 ms
FILTER the low-pass filter
CUTOFFwhere it cuts, 0-10
RESresonance, 0-10
ENVhow far the envelope moves it, -50 to +50
ENV each note's shape
ATTACK, DECAY, SUSTAIN, RELEASE0-10 each
LFO one for the whole sound
RATEhow fast, 0-10
PITCHvibrato, 0-10
FILTERhow much it moves the filter, 0-10
MIX the key's level and place
LEVEL0-10
PANL50 to R50
CHOKEkits: OFF or GROUP 1-4 (cut each other off)
NORMALhold: your own sample as loud as it goes
CHARACTER the whole sound
CHARACTERCLEAN, 12-BIT (40 kHz) or 12-BIT 26K
THIS UNIT Taste's own settings (SETUP)
BENDhow far pitch bend goes, 0-12 semitones
WHEELhow much vibrato the mod wheel adds, 0-10
VELOON: harder is louder

Grit

On a SAMPLE sound, SOURCE's second box is SAMPLE (turn to choose) and CAPTURE is empty. In PLACES, the white keys are 16 places and the black keys stutter (1/4 to 1/32, backwards, 1/64). SETUP's second page: PEDAL.

SOURCE where the grains come from (SOURCE again: SAMPLES)
FROMLINE IN, MIC IN, BUILT-IN MIC, ALL, a unit by name, SAMPLE or CARD
BUFFERLIVE: how much of the past, 1-20 s (SAMPLE: which sample)
GAINa Root input: how loud it comes in
CAPTURELIVE: hold to keep the buffer as a sample
SAMPLES every sample
SAMPLEwhich one
NAMEyour own: turn for the letter, push for the next
USEhold: the sound plays it
SAVEhold: onto the card's GRIT folder (turn clockwise for DELETE, an unused sample of yours)
GRAIN the grain
SIZEhow long, 5-500 ms
DENSITYhow many a second, 1-200
SHAPEthe fade: 0 smooth to 10 sharp
ALIGNON: each grain lined up with the last
PLACE where in the sound
WHERE0-100% (LIVE: 100% is now)
SCANhow fast WHERE moves, -200% to +200% (0 stands still)
SPRAYhow scattered, 0-10
REVERSEthe chance a grain plays backwards, 0-100%
PITCH the grains' pitch
PITCH-24 to +24 semitones
FINE-50 to +50 cents
RANDOMeach grain detuned at random, OFF to 12 semitones
JUMPSOFF, OCTAVE or OCT+5TH: some grains above
PLAY how the keys play it
PLAYNOTES, PLACES or ALWAYS
SYNCOFF, or grains on the beat: 1/4 ... 1/32
GLIDEOFF or a time
ROOTthe key that plays it as it was, C2-C6
ENV each note's cloud
ATTACK, DECAY, SUSTAIN, RELEASE0-10 each
FILTER after the grains
CUTOFF0-10
RESresonance, 0-10
TYPELOW, HIGH or BAND
LFO one slow wobble
RATEhow fast, in Hz
WHERE, SIZE, FILTERhow much it moves each, 0-10
MIX
LEVEL0-10
SPREADgrains scattered left and right, 0-10
DRYLIVE from a unit: how much of its own sound still plays, 0-100%
FEEDBKLIVE: Grit's output back into its buffer, 0-10
THIS UNIT Grit's own settings (SETUP)
BENDhow far pitch bend goes, 0-12 semitones
WHEELwhat the mod wheel moves: WHERE or SPRAY
VELOON: harder is louder
PEDALsecond page: SUSTAIN (holds notes) or FREEZE

Haze

White keys: USER A 01-16, one press each, every synth sent at the preset's KEY WET (unless SETUP's KEYS is PRESET). Black keys: tap tempo, as TAP. SYNTH, MIX, KEY and the sends belong to the chain, not the preset.

SOURCE COLOUR's synth
SYNTHNONE, or the unit COLOUR works on
MIXhow much of Haze's version you hear, 0-100%; the Root plays the rest dry
KEY WETthe send every synth gets when the preset's white key is pressed, 0-99
SENDS SPACE's input
each unitits WET: how much of it goes into MOD, ECHO and REVERB, 0-99
DRIVE distortion on COLOUR's synth
MODEOFF, OVERDRIVE, DISTORTION or FUZZ
DRIVE, TONE, LEVELhow hard, how bright, how loud, 0-99
FILTER the DJ filter on COLOUR's synth
FILTEROFF in the middle; down, a low-pass (LP 17.8K to LP 60); up, a high-pass (HP 17 to HP 6.0K)
RESOa peak at the filter's edge, 0-99
PUMP ducking, in time with another sound
KEYNONE, or the unit whose sound does the ducking
DEPTHhow far, 0-99
RELEASEhow long it takes to come back, 40MS-800MS
TARGETCOLOUR, SPACE or BOTH
MOD chorus, flanger, phaser
MODEOFF, CHORUS, FLANGER or PHASER
RATE0.08HZ-4.00HZ; push: a note value, 1/16 to 16/1, following the tempo
DEPTH, LEVELhow far, how loud, 0-99
ECHO the tape echo
RATE1000MS-60MS; push: a note value, 1/32 to 1/2, following the tempo
REPEATShow much goes round again, 0-99: near the top it runs away
VOLUME, TONEhow loud, how bright, 0-99
PINGPONGECHO 2: the repeats alternate left and right
REVERB the room
TYPEPLATE, HALL or SPRING
DECAYhow long: 0.3S-8.0S (a spring: 0.4S-4.0S)
TONE, LEVELhow bright the tail, how loud, 0-99
PRE-DLYREVERB 2: the wait before it starts, 0-198MS
THIS UNIT Haze's own setting (SETUP)
KEYS+ SENDS: a white key sets every synth's send to its KEY WET; PRESET: it only calls up the preset
